1.	Why has J. A. Michaud, engineer employed on the Intercolonial railway at Rivifere du Loup, been suspended seven months after having been suspended once and put hack to work, for the same offence, in connection with an accident at Carrier ?
2.	Was he proved guilty? If so, who by?

4.	Has a regular train with a schedule time got to make tha,t time, and is the line supposed to he clear for him ? If so, how long before?
5.	Why was that man, as alleged, blamed for going too fast when he was not going fast enough to make that time?
6.	On whose recommendation was he punished the first and second time?
7.	When the main line is obstructed is the superior train or any other train leaving a terminal or any other station, supposed to be advised of it? If so, why was not this man advised of it?
8.	Is the minister prepared to go through the records of the accident at Carrier the 8th January, 1913, so that he may see for himself that the investigation was conducted according to the usual rule, and the punishment given such as conclusions would guarantee, in order that the poor employee with a family shall not stay seven months without employment?

1.	The first suspension was until his case had been decided; the suspension of seven
months is the punishment adjudged in his case. The whole time of his suspension including the first is counted in, as part of the seven months.
He was punished for approaching a semaphore at a rate of speed, so fast, that he could not stop within his vision, and for passing a semaphore standing at danger,, and for accepting a clearance order at Chaudiere Junction, not properly made out.
2.	Yes, by the investigation held by Superintendent McDonald and confirmed by the General Superintendent.
3.	Three swore it was down and eight, swore it was up.
4.	A regular train is expected to make its schedule time having due regard to weather and other conditions, and the engineer and others in charge of the train are expected to observe all the rules of the railway, made to insure the safe operation of trains. The line cannot always be kept clear and the rules of the railway provide that the engineer and others in charge of trains have to observe care and look out for signals, for obstructions which may be in the track. There is usuallv an interval of from ten to twenty minutes maintained between trains iollowing one another excepting when thev are closing up at stations. Rule 17 of the time table says ' Special ana working trains must be kept, at least, ten minutes clear of the time of all regular trains.'
5.	The engineer is ordered and expected to regulate the speed of his train according to the place and circumstances, and J. A. Michaud was shown to be going at too great a rate of speed, approaching Carrier Junction, so that he could not stop train but ran .past the semaphore which was standing at danger.
6.	J. A. Michaud was only punished once, his first suspension being pending decision [DOT] in his case, and the time being counted as part of the seven months' suspension. The punishment being decided by the General Superintendent, upon the evidence.
7.	Whenever it is possible trains are notified of an obstruction on the track, but the want of notice does not relieve the official of the train from keeping the proper lookout and running trains in accordance with the rules. J. A. Michaud ran past the semaphore, which was standing at danger, in violation of the rules. The clearance order, which he received at Chaudiere Junction, told him that the train he ran into had not reached Carrier Junction, and he should have ueen keeping a very careful lookout for it.
8.	The investigation was conducted according to the usual rules and the punishment given was such as the evidence and the circumstances and conditions required in 'the opinion of the officers of the railway, who are responsible for the train service.

On motion of Hon. W. T. White (Minister of Finance) House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide for an increase, from a sum not exceeding $75,000 to a sum not exceeding $110,000, of the annual amount payable out of tbe Consolidated Revenue Fund for the maintenance of the Ottawa branch of the Royal^ Mint and the refinery forming part thereof.'
(Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The abject of this resolution and of the Bill founded upon it which I shall ask leave to introduce is to increase the amount of the annuity payable out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund to the [DOT]Ottawa branch of the Royal Mint in connection with its operations. When the establishment of a branch at Ottawa was under consideration in 1901, it was arranged with the Imperial authorities that statutory provision should be made for its upkeep, nnd in consequence of that understanding the Ottawa Mint Act of 1901 was passed. By section 2 of that Act it was provided that:
A sum or sums not exceeding in the whole in any year seventy-five thousand dollars, for defraying the salaries, contingencies, retiring and other allowances and expenses connected with the maintenance of the Ottawa branch of the Royal Mint

Should be payable out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. In course of time that sum was found to be inadequate, and since the year 1910 a,n additional amount of $25,000 has been provided in the estimates, making a total appropriation of $100,000 to defray the expense of the maintenance of the Mint. Of that sum, there was expended last year about $95,000.

How many employees
are there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think I have that information at the present time, but I can get it later.. The work of the Royal Mint has been increasing steadily during the past, few years, and no doubt it will increase in the same or a greater ratio in the future. Of course the refinery has been added since the mint was originally established, and its expenses have been considerably increased. At the present time there is no place in Canada, except Vancouver, where manufacturers and others can have an authoritative assay of precious metals, and it is the intention now that the refinery here shall do that work, of course charging fees therefor. At the present time, if any manufacturer desires to have an assay of precious metals, he is obliged to send them to New York. I may say that the fees charged for that and other services of the mint are very small. It is also necessary to increase to some extent the staff of the mint proper, and the *deputy minister has asked us to introduce legislation which will give assurance, as was done in the year 1901, that statutory provision will be made for the increased expenditure. It is estimated that the sum will not exceed $110,000. They may not use that amount entirely; in fact I do not anticipate that they will for some time, ' otherwise the amount to be inserted in the
Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
statutes should be larger. The sum of $110,000 is intended to be provision which will satisfy the requirements of the mint for some time to come. I have not full particulars as to the number of the staff at the present time, but I have some figures here which I thought might be of some interest to the House, as showing the increase in the work which has been done by the mint. In the year 1908 5,000,000 pieces were struck. In 1909 that had grown to 9,000,000 pieces, in 1910 to 19,000,000 pieces, in 1911 to 13,000,000 pieces, and in 1912 to 17,000,000 pieces; so that during a period of five years the number of pieces struck by the mint has been doubled. For the year 1912 they handled worn silver coin to the amount of $88,000, of a coinage value of $83,000. The total Canadian coinage struck for 1912 was about $3,000,000, or, to be accurate, $2,910,000. The revenue derived from fees and charges is of course very small, but there is a very substantial profit upon the operations of the mint in the sense that the Dominion obtains the seigniorage upon the silver. Last year that amounted to a profit of about $800,000. That is to say, out of a coinage of silver of $1,383,000 there was a profit of $801,000. or between 50 and 60 per cent. Possibly that may be all the information that is required by the committee, but on the second reading I shall be glad to give anv further information that may be desired.
What_is the regulation or the practice of the mint affecting the handling of old coins? Are they purchased from the holder at face value, or at silver value5

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are purchased at face value, that is to say they are redeemed. Silver that is worn is redeemed at par value, hut of course it must be worn. Then it is recoined, and there is a loss on that operation, as I think the figures I have given will indicate. For example, the worn coin handled in 1912, was $88,000 at par value, while the coinage value was $83,000.

There is some information which my hon. friend might give, if not now, later on. I would like to know how many of the 19,000,000 pieces coined were of gold, silver and copper, respectively. I would like also to know where the metal is procured, the sources from which we get our raw material, gold, silver and copper, and what price is paid to the miners. Where, for instance, is the principal source of supply of our gold? Does any of it come from the Yukon?
Mr. W7HITE: Most of it.

And does the silver come from Cobalt? The public would be interested to know the sources of sup-

ply, and what is the price paid by the Government for the raw material which comes annually to the mint. I suppose that at the present time the output of gold from the Yukon goes principally to the United States, and only a small portion comes to the mint in Ottawa. One would also like to know what was the total production of gold in the Yukon last year, how much came to the mint, and how much went outside of Canada. The same information respecting silver would be interesting. I do not remember having seen anywhere the total output of silver last year from the Cobalt district, and it would be interesting to know how much came to the mint and how much went to the United States. If this information could be given in concrete form, it would he interesting to the general public.

As to the source of our gold supply in the mint, I think I can say accurately that the greater part is obtained from the Yukon, but we have received some gold from Nova Scotia and Ontario. I shall endeavour to get the information as accurately as possible before the second reading of the Bill, so that my hon. friend will be in possession of all the facts. My hon. friend also spoke of the gold of the Yukon going to American cities for the purpose of assay and naturally also to be coined. I think 1 am correct in stating-the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Thompson) will be able to put me right if I am not- that the great bulk of the gold of the Yukon has gone to the United States to be assayed. During the past year, on representations made to me by the hon. member for the Yukon, we changed the
regulation by which fees were payable for assaying in the assaying plant or refinery at Vancouver, the expectation being that that would cause the gold of the Yukon to be detained there for that purpose and that there would be a corresponding increase in trade by reason of that between Vancouver and the Yukon. I have not had an opportunity yet of studying what the effect of that 'change in the regulation has been.

What was
the change?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was arranged that gold should be assayed without payment of a fee. In the United States, where the gold of the Yukon is coined, there is no fee charged for assaying and in consequence the city of Vancouver was at a disadvantage as compared with the American cities by reason of the charges which were made. They were comparatively small charges, but they were still of some consequence in connection with the assaying of gold. That has been changed and we hope in consequence that the gold of the Yukon may go to Vancouver instead of Seattle and San Francisco. As far as the other information required by my hon. friend is concerned, I will undertake to obtain it before the second reading of the Bill.

I would
like to point out that we have in Canada two metals which are characteristic of this country, namely, cobalt and nickel, both of -which are splendidly adapted to subsidiary coinage. Two years ago I brought this matter up in the House. I pointed out that, inasmuch as we had a national mint in this country, we ought to give preference to the metals that were characteristic of the country and that were adapted to coinage purposes. Canada has the leadership of the world in the_ matter of the production of nickel and nickel is the best metal, outside of cobalt, for a 'subsidiary coinage. Why not, if we are to have a national policy in this country, and if we are to have a national mint, make our subsidiary coinage out of either nickel or cobalt, perhaps out of cobalt, and in that way advertise the fact to the world that Canada can supply enough cobalt and nickel for subsidiary coinage? May I ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance wliat is the capital investment up to date on account of the branch of the national mint in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
I would observe to my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) that if we were to have the additional coinage of nickel, for instance, in this country, it would not dispose of

one-tenth, or one-hundredth part of the nickel which we produce. We would have a better way -still of disposing of our nickel if we built our own ships in this country.

Yes, if we were to do
that; but we .have to take control of the production of nickel in this country and see that it is refined in Canada under our national policy and not sent out of the country.	[DOT]

Do you mean the
Nationalist policy?

No, I mean the national policy. Perhaps my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) does not see the significance of that term. But it is high time that we let the world know how much nickel we have, and, by the national policy, compelled its refinement- in this country. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition says that we would not use it all in coinage. Perhaps we could use some of it in coinage and we could induce other countries to buy nickel from us in the market, but certainly we ought to set the example ourselves by using it at home.
Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax!: I would like to ask -my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to explain the method by which a profit is made to the country in the operation of minting.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend, no doubt refers to how the profit accrues from the seigniorage on the silver. The mint- coins from silver five, ten, twenty-five and fifty-cent pieces. A twenty-five cent piece is only worth intrinsically, say, ten, or twelve cents, and if the mint buys 'silver at current prices, mints it into coinage and it is worth twice the cost of the metal intrinsically in the coin, of course, it is a fairly profitable business for the mint -and for the country. The silver coinage, when it leaves the -mint, goes to the several offices of the Receiver General and is there paid out to the banks as they require it for Dominion notes. These notes are only issued as against gold. The result is that we get in Dominion notes which are secured against gold in exchange for this silver at its par value and the profit to the Dominion by way of seigniorage comes from that operation.
A kind of gold brick.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is better than a gold
brick. The profit to the Dominion by way of seigniorage on the issue of this silver really comes to it from the amount of gold that is in the vaults of the Receiver General throughout the country over and above Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
the .amount of the Dominion notes outstanding. I am not quite sure that I make that clear. There are Dominion notes outstanding against gold. We issue silver and get in Dominion notes. These notes, when they come in. may be cancelled and the Dominion will own the resultant amount of gold that it holds in the vaults over and above the amount of the Dominion note circulation that is outstanding. In that- way it is an automatic process. That is the way the Government obtains the reserve which it holds against its government savings banks and post office savings banks deposits. We are obliged to carry a ten per cent reserve.

The coin has a value fixed by law; it is not the actual value of the metal in it. I asked the minister if he could tell me what is the actual price paid to the Mint for gold, for silver and for other metals. The minister told me that the business of the mint had increased and would continue to increase. On what basis does he assume that the business of the Mint will increase? Is it because of an extra demand for bullion or for coin? The bank note is the chief medium of circulation in Canada, whereas in Europe the circulating medium is gold. Does the minister expect we shall export our bars of silver to Europe? I do not know that we can export gold, but surely we ought to be able to export silver.

It may be turned into coin, and it may be sold as bullion. The value of gold bars prepared for and sold to various manufacturing companies and banking institutions, has increased from $9,410 in 1910 to $296,592 in 1912. Hitherto the whole of such gold bullion has been obtained from

I took up the question with the master of [DOT] the Mint a short time ago and he quite acquiesced in the view that it is very desirable that Canadian manufacturers instead of sending the gold to New York to be assayed, with all the attendant troubles of customs and transportation, should have the work done here. What is the seigniorage; is it the royalty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the royalty the Government takes by reason of the value of the coin as a coin being greater than the intrinsic value of the metal. It does not apply in the case of gold because the intrinsic value of gold is supposed to be equal to the coin value.

It may be remarked that the profit coming to us is not because we have established a mint but because we have established the seigniorage which is independent of the Mint. If we had no Mint at all we would have the seigniorage or profit but the fact that the mint is gradually extending its usefulness is probably justification for its maintenance.

The circulation of large
quantities of American silver in Canada must be a loss to the country. Has the Government taken any steps to stop the circulation of American silver?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My predecessor, Mr. Fielding, made an arrangement, which continues, by which the banks are given a small percentage-I think three-eights of one per cent commission-together with the cost of expressage, in order to encourage the return of American silver to the United States and obtain there its equivalent in gold.

effective?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think so.

precious metal and the sale of the coin done at the mint or through the Finance Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is done at the mint. I am informed that tenders are called for the supply of the precious metals and they aTe
purchased at their market values. On account of the situation of the Mint at Ottawa I am not sure whether we shall be able to overcome the advantage the American refiners, have for the reason of being closer to the Yukon.
Are the new coins supplied directly through the mint?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Mint supplies the new coins to the Department of Finance.

If a defence were ever required for the establishment of a mint in this country, it has been given this afternoon by the Minister of Finance when he informed us that the capital invested in the mint is $700,000 and the profit for one year is $800,000. That strikes me as a very direct result and as a rather profitable investment for the country.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition asked how much gold the Yukon has produced and what percentage of that gold came to the mint. The output of gold in the Yukon is increasing. Last year we produced a little over $5,000,000. Some three or four years ago the production was between two and three million dollars. Of that $5,000,000 about a million and a quarter came to the Mint at Ottawa. The Minister of Finance informed the House that $1,470,000 was minted here in 1911, of which amount about one and a quarter millions was composed of Yukon gold. I am sorry to say that gold from the Yukon has not come to Canada to a very large extent.
Why is that?

Because the United
States Government realized before our Government did the value of getting Yukon gold. Although the state of Washington and the Pacific coast states north of California were not gold-producing states, the United States Government established in the city of Beattie a purchasing assay office, while we had no purchasing assay office, nor in fact any assay office at all, in our Pacific cities. As a result, gold from the Yukon was shipped to the Seattle assay office and no charge was made for assaying it. As we had no assay office on the Pacific coast, Yukon gold to a large extent went to United States cities on the Pacific coast and passed our own. The Dominion Government placed an assay office in Vancouver where any man might bring his gold and have it assayed, and the assay office would give him a certificate which he would take to the bank and receive legal tender. When the Government established that office, they permitted a discriminatory charge over the assay office which was

established at the mint here; that is to say, until last fall any man who took his gold to the assay office in Vancouver had to pay one-eighth of one per cent more than was charged in Seattle, San Francisco, Philadelphia, or in Ottawa. The result was that, while we had in Vancouver a magnificent assay office, properly equipped and well manned, we did not get the gold. I brought that fact to the attention of the Minister of Finance, as did some of the other members for British Columbia, and he removed that discriminatory tax so that at the present time the assay office in Vancouver is on the same basis as the assay office in the mint at Ottawa. Therefore, gold coming from the Yukon can be sent to the assay office in Vancouver and it will bring the same price as at any other place. We want all that Yukon gold to come here. We do not want even five or ten per cent of that gold to go to the United States.
A very interesting phase of this question developed recently in the Banking Committee. I asked some of the witnesses who testified there why our banks should not use our own gold. Opinions differed. One gentleman testified that it could not be used in our banks because the gold reserves were sometimes sent to New York on call loans. Gold seems to be in a state of flux. He said that our coin would not circulate in the United State because it was not considered as legal tender there; that the British gold coins and the American gold coins were the only ones that circulated there. Another gentleman, high up in banking circles, testified to the opposite effect. He said that there was no reason why the gold reserves of our banks should not be in our own coin. That seems to me to be a reasonable proposition. As to the amount of gold which we have in our reserves, I am informed by gentlemen of the banking profession who testified before the Banking Committee that we have about $37,000,000 in gold coins in our banks. Seven millions of that is composed of British sovereigns and therefore $30,000,000 of the gold which rests to-day in the vaults of our banks is American gold. That state of affairs should not exist when we are producing from the Yukon, from Porcupine, from British Columbia and from Nova Scotia gold in very large quantities?

How would you remedy it?
Mr. THOMPSON': By doing the same thing with American gold coins as has been done with their silver coins, namely: ship them out of the country and replace them with our own coins. We have a Mint here to manufacture the gold. There is no reason why in the interests of our country as a whole we should not do this. When the Bank Bill is up for consideration, I am going to submit to the Minister of Finance a proposition to that end. Take the Government reserves. The argument which was advanced by one gentleman that Canadian gold could not be used by our banks certainly does not apply to our Government reserves, because they are kept here and do not go to New York. I fail to see why those reserves should not be altogether composed of Canadian gold.

I wish to congratulate the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Thompson), on the increasing production of gold in his district. I should like, however, to tell the House that in one little camp in the province of Ontario, in Porcupine, the production of gold next year will be at least $8,000,000, probably $12,000,000, and the production is steadily increasing. For the first time the province of Ontario has proved to be gold producing so that the output of Porcupine is almost phenomenal. As long as the world is engaged in the pursuit of gold, there is no more promising field than in the new country of Ontario now known as Cobalt. It ought to he a matter of satisfaction to the people of this country to know that Canada, so rich in other natural products, is now proved to be rich in precious imetals.

In answer to my hon. friend from the Yukon (Mr. Thompson), I may say that at his request I gave very careful consideration to the question as to whether the Dominion could put itself in a position to hold Canadian gold as reserves against the deposits in the post office savings banks and the Government savings banks. I am afraid there are considerable difficulties in the way. My hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin) touched upon one which had occurred to me and which I investigated rather fully. At the present time, tire gold reserve in the offices of the Assistant Receiver General represents the amount of gold deposited by the chartered banks of Canada in exchange for Dominion notes, either the 9mall notes or those of large denomiations -' legals ' as they are called. In other words, these reserves of the banks are practically carried in the offices of the Receiver General. The total gold so held is in excess of $100,000,000, and of this $90,000,000, I am informed by the controller of the treasury, is in American gold. The reason for thi3 is obvious. It is only within
recent years that we have minted Canadian gold. New York, being like London an international money market, a centre of exchange for America, it is very natural that the gold held by the banks should be principally American gold rather than British sovereigns. American gold is legal tender in Canada, though Canadian gold is not legal tender in the United States. So, 'the advantage tq tha bank in holding American gold is that it is legal tender here and can be exchanged for Dominion notes, and it is legal tender a'so in New York and can be used to meet their obligation® there. That gold is of the same fineness as British sovereigns. To meet the point raised by my hon. friend from Yukon, we should have to melt that gold down and recoin it into Canadian coin. For, if you send it to the United States to exchange, what do you get back? You cannot go any further; gold is the ultimate. You could only get back exchange or else get other American gold coin-you could not get Canadian coin. The cost of recoining this gold would run into large sums of money. I had the controller of the currency go into that and give me the figures. Those figures I have not here, but I wilt ask the House to accept what I say, that a very heavy .sum would be expended in recoining these American coins into Canadian coins. So, even if the banks could make as good use of the gold in this other form, there would be difficulties in the way. And they could not in every case make as good use as they can of the American gold, for the reason I have given, that our coinage is not legal tender in the United States while American co,inage is legal tender here as well as in New York.

This matter has been under the consideration of the House and of the Senate during the last ten years. The object of the legislation is to protect the public from fraud and misrepresentation and also to protect honest manufacturers. The first Bill introduced in the Senate some years ago was suggested by the manufacturers and passed the Senate but representations were made by wholesale and retail dealers that there" were objectionable clauses in that Bill and it was withdrawn. Afterwards it was brought up again by the late Government; in both the Senate and the House of Commons the public were given an opportunity of being heard and eventually an Act was passed in 1908 which is now on the statute-book. In order that provisions of this Act might be carried out an inspector was appointed, a practical man, familiar with the technical details involved in this question. In a prosecution in Toronto not long ago, the judges of the Court of Appeal pointed out that some of the wording in the Act was defective, and that the meaning was not plain. The Bill now before the House does not differ substantially from the present Act. I think I am safe in saying that the principles of this Bill are exactly the same as those of the Act at present in force, but in certain cases the wording has been changed, and the Bill has been redrafted in order to place things in clearer

My idea was that this provision was a condition of the establishment of such elevators.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. A statute speaks all the time and when those interior terminal elevators have been established then this statute, speaking as of that time, would by its very terms exclude such terminal elevators from its operation.

In addition to what the Premier has now mentioned, the resolution applies, as I understand, only to a place which is not a terminal point. If the hon. member from Edmonton would refer to section (y) of the interpretation clause he would see what a terminal is:
A terminal elevator includes every elevator or warehouse which receives or ships grain and is located at any point declared by the Governor in Council to be a terminal point.
Then section 13:
The Governor in Council may authorize the minister to construct, acquire, lease or expropriate for His Majesty any terminal elevator if Parliament has granted money for that purpose.
So that if at any time a point is declared to be a terminal point, then the provisions in this resolution will not apply.

Certain penalties are
prescribed in section 245 of the Act and these penalties apply to farmers who sell their right to get cars or who take possession of cars wrongfully. I have some correspondence from tile Grain Growers' Association of Aberdeen, in my riding, in which it is alleged that the railway employees have been placing cars at the disposal of farmers at another station near there or at a siding on payment of a sum of money by a farmer to the railroad men. My correspondents seem to be satisfied that that is the case. They say on the other hand, that it is difficult to get evidence which they can present to the railway company, which has asked for the evidence, because the farmer himself, under the law as it stands at present, would likely be liable to the penalty of the section and they have asked that some legislation be passed amending this penalty clause so that it would punish any employee of a railway company who committed an offence of that kind but that the punishment should not be imposed. on the informer. They make the following suggestions:
That the following be added to the Canada Grain Act of 1912, section 245:
(e)	An employee of any railroad who either directly or indirectly sells the right of loading a car, whether in or out of turn, shall upon summary conviction, be liable to a fine of from $50 to $1,000 or to imprisonment not exceeding six months, or both.
(f)	The purchaser or informant in such cases to be judged not guilty of a misdemeanor.

Is the suggestion that the farmer who buys the right from the railway employee should not he punished for it?
Mr. MeCRANEY:	For the purpose
of getting evidence against these railway Mi-. BORDEN.
men they say it will be necessary to exempt the farmer who gives the money, otherwise you will never get the evidence.

If my hon. friend will
write a letter to the department on the subject we will see that it is taken up with the Grain Commission.
Mr. MeCRANEY:	Has the Government
under contemplation the establishment of a terminal elevator system under Government control? We have had this matter before the House on previous occasions and we in the West have had reason to believe that when the present Government came into power they would take immediate steps to operate elevators at Port Arthur, Fort William and the transfer points between those ports and the Atlantic seaboard. I would like to know from the hon. minister whether that policy is the policy of the Government, and whether they purpose carrying it out.

We are building a large
elevator at Port Aithur at the present time for the purpose of controlling the rates, to a certain extent at all events, and so on. The further construction of elevators at Fort William has not been considered up to the present time.
I would like to know the reason for the increase in the fees mentioned in this resolution. Naturally, as the fees are a burden on the trade, it is our business to know why they are being increased.

The increased fees suggested for the elevators and for the track buyers are for the purpose of paying the cost of printing the licenses, keeping up the office, distributiug the licenses, and so on. Under the present Act the fee is $2, but that has not yielded enough to pay for the cost of printing the licenses, and rules and regulations, and for the keeping of a proper record of them in the office. Hitherto the revenues have been administered through the Warehouse Commissioner's office, and the license fees were the only source of revenue. The result has been a large deficit every year, and it was thought that if the grain department is to pay its way, the license fees must be increased, or else the fees for the inspection and weighing of grain must be increased, and the Government do not think it would lie wise to increase the fees for weighing and inspection. It was thought that the elevators and the dealers in grain could pay this small increase without feeling it.

Is it the policy of the
Government, or of the department, to fix the fees at such a figure as shall carry the whole cost of the administration of the

Grain Act, or are the fees merely an incident in the provision for the cost?

So far as the Government are concerned, we do not propose to fix the fees with the intention of entirely meeting the expenses of the Grain Commission. But the Grain Commissioners would like, as far as possible, to have their board placed on a self-sustaining basis, and as the $2 fee for licenses for country elevators and terminal elevators, and so on, seemed to be very small considering the large amount of business done, the board recommended that this -small increase be made.
Is it considered that these fees will be a substantial contribution towards the cost of administration?
Yes.

What is the capacity of
the elevator that, is under construction at Fort William, and how soon will it be completed?

I think the capacity is
three and a quarter million or three and a half million bushels, and under the contract-it is to be completed by the 15th or the 30th of September next. Speaking from memory, I think these aTe the terms of the contract.

I understood the minister to say that there was a provision in this Bill that if the fees did not amount to a sum sufficient to pay for the upkeep of the office, the person who owned the grain would pay the difference. Am I correct?

Not exactly. If the
owners of a mill wish to get an inspector for themselves, the new provision is that the applicants shall make up the difference between the ordinary fees and the salary of that inspector whose services are required entirely for the use -of that mill.
Who has the authority to fit that difference?

Application would be
made to the Board of Grain Commissioners, and if they thought the application was a reasonable one, they would allot a certain inspector to the mill on condition that the applicants would pay his ordinary salary.
Resolution reported, read the first and the second time, and concurred in.
I beg to move that this resolution be referred to the committee appointed to consider Bill No. 163, to amend the Canada Grain Act.

Does my hon. friend think that he can proceed in this way with a resolution containing a money
275J
clause? It seems to me to be contrary to all the rules.

That Bill came from the Senate, and I referred to the law offices of this House the question whether it was necessary to move by way of resolution in this House. They gave the opinion that it should be done in this way, and I moved, the resolution in accordance with that advice.

The point I
raise for your consideration is this:	No
doubt this money clause has to be moved by resolution, but to refer it to a committee dealing with a Bill which has already passed the Senate seems to me to be rather against the rules.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
My attention not having. been drawn to the matter, I would not be prepared to say offhand that this procedure is quite regular. If I had further time to look into the matter I would reach a conclusion.

House in Committee on Bill No. 26, respecting Radiotelegraphy.-Mr. Hazen.
On section 4-certain passenger steamers to be equipped with apparatus; exceptions:
I was not in the House when my hon. friend brought up this Bill. I understand it is simply to control of this radiotelegraphy.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

What is the
meaning of this exception?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I intend to propose an
amendment to the first line of this section, which reads ' from and after the first day of July, 1913.' I am going to ask that it be amended so as to read, ' from and after the first day of January, 1914.' It will be impossible for these vessels to get equipped with wireless before the first day of July next and it is proposed to extend the time until the first of January, 1914. When this Bill was introduced in November last we supposed that there would be very little delay in getting it through the House and under those circumstances we thought that the 1st of January, 1913, would be sufficient.

There was considerable discussion on two occasions on this Bill, it was referred to the Select Standing Committee on Marine and Fisheries and after a good deal of consideration they agreed to recommend the Bill in its present form.
What is the principal object of the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Bill is made necessary in consequence of the increasing part that wireless telegraphy is playing everywhere. We have an Act now regarding radiotelegraphy, under which licenses are granted by the Minister of the Naval Service, and the provisions of which still remain in this Bill. The principal provision of the Bill is the compulsory equipment with wireless apparatus of three different classes of passsenger steamers. That is what the section now under consideration refers to. It provides that three classes of steamers shall be equipped with wireless: First, passenger steamers licensed to carry fifty or more persons that ply between ports more than two hundred miles apart; second, passenger steamers licensed to carry 250 or more persons plying betweeen ports more than ninety miles apart; and, third, passenger steamers that are licensed to carry 500 or more persons and plying between ports more than twenty miles apart. Another provision has reference to the forwarding and delivery of radio-telegrams by Canadian land lines and the employment of British subjects as operators at land stations. There is a penalty for the trans-misssion of a false distress call or for wilful interference. The Governor in Council is given power to fix the fee to be paid for licenses, to accede to any international convention with respect to wireless telegraphy and to make regulations to carry out the same. He is also empowered to make regulations for the censorship of radio-telegraph signals and messages. Power is given to the minister to classify stations and to specify what equipment the stations in each classification must have; to issue licenses for stations and to fix the period for which they shall be valid; to prescribe the form of the licenses and the conditions and restrictions they shall contain; to examine persons for operators' certificates, to prescribe the form of the examinations for these certificates and to prescribe what class of operator will be required to work at the different classes of stations; to specify the -watches to be kept at the different stations and the number of operators which shall comprise their staff; to make regulations for the inspection of all stations; to make regulations to govern the working of installations on ships within the territorial waters and to make regulations to govern the working of all stations in the Dominion with reference to Mr. HAZEN.
intercommunications. Power is given to His Majesty to assume possession of a station at any time and to work the same in the public service. Adequate penalties are prescribed for any violation of the different provisions of the new Act. With regard to the question of my right hon. friend as to the exceptions, I may say that that was fully considered by the committee. The exceptions aTe as to steamers calling at Canadian ports for bunker coal, provisions, or repairs, or from stress of weather. The reason for that exemption is obvious. Steamers plying on the rivers or inland waters other than the great lakes are also exempt. It is felt that steamers plying on rivers and being at all times practically within sight of land, could if an accident should occur, run ashore and provide for the safety of passengers. There is not the same necessity for these steamers being equipped with radio-telegraphy as oceangoing ships. Then steamers plying on Northumberland straits are exempt. They hardly ever lose sight of land; the land on each side is inhabited, there is not much fog as a rule, and the committee thought they should be exempted. Then steamers plying on the Georgian bay are exempt.

For what
reason?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It was represented to the committee that boats plying on these waters are not financially able to bear the expense of this equipment. Most of them do not carry any passengers, and the boats, which do never go any great distance from land. Vessels plying on the lakes of Canada other than the great lakes are excepted. The steamers running along the shore from Toronto to Hamilton would be exempt, also the steamers from Toronto to Niagara which practically go round the shore and are never more than seven miles out. The shore i3 inhabited, and the committee felt there was little danger in allowing these boats to operate without having wireless telegraphy.
On section 7-penalty for sending false messages:
The penalty provided is not exceeding $500 in costs and six months' imprisonment. Is not that drastic?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is very mild compared with the penalty in the United States, which is not exceeding $2,000 or five years' in-prisonment.
Yes, but the word is ' and ' in this case, and there is no alternative but fine and imprisonment.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That word should be ' or.' My hon. friend is quite right; we will amend it "by substituting the -word 'or' for 'and.'
Amendment agreed to.

I would like to call
the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to section 4 read in connection with section 9. The precaution is taken in section 9 that no proceedings can be taken under that section except by order of the minister. The criminal proceedings under section 4 are even more serious than those covered by section 9. I would suggest that the same_ provision be made with regard to this section as in section 9,-no proceedings to be taken except by order of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think it would be almost better to strike it out of section 9. For, after all, if these proceedings are only to _ be taken under the approval of the minister, the person who violates one of these provisions will resort to all sorts of expedients to have political pressure brought to bear upon the minister to prevent the order being given for the taking of proceedings. It would be better to let each case stand on its merits.

I would like to see
some discretion left with the minister, because circumstances might arise where this discretion might be very important. When the Quebec Centenary came off, a regular fleet of steamers came in from the United States with passengers desiring to see the sights. Steamers making such a trip might often have apparatus not in accordance with our law, and so they could not leave port until they paid a fine. I am only pointing out that there may be cases in which it would be well that the minister should have discretion in these matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This Bill was before a
committee of which both my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) and my hon. friend from Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie) were members, and was fully discussed by that committee, lit may be that the suggestion of the last speaker was made there. For my own part, I should be opposed to that suggestion. I do not think the proceedings should be taken without good reason, and I do not think discretionary power should be left with the minister. The question whether a man should be subject to a penalty under this law should be decided by a magistrate. I would far sooner see the Bill left in its present state. If, after we get working under the Bill we find reason for varying this provision, I would not hesitate to come back to Parliament and ask that the change be made. I would leave it as it is, especially as it has been gone into by a special committee.
Bill, as amended, reported.

House in Committee of Supply. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
Customs-salaries and contingent expenses of the several ports of the Dominion, including pay for overtime of officers, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $3,125,000.
['I handed in the departmental answer. I will make inquiries as to how the mistake was made.']

There is an
increase of $600,000 in this item.

Owing to the unprecedented increase in the revenue last year, it was found necessary to employ very many new officers at the different ports throughout the Dominion. The total number of new officers thus employed was 477, at salaries aggregating $405,985. The increases of salary to deserving officers amounted to $152,110; the number of officials receiving these increases being 1,355. The increase in payments for overtime amounted to $12,340, and the increase in contingencies, cartage, &o., $49,085. This makes a total increase of $619,520.
These additional officers, I imagine, were chiefly in the larger ports ?
Yes.
How many in Montreal ?

There were forty-eight in
Montreal. Though the greater number of the increases were in the large ports, the smaller ports had to have additional officers in many cases.

What class of small
ports ?

For instance, there was one at Berlin, one at Bowmanville, six at Brantford, one at Brockville, one at Fort William, seven at Hamilton, three at Kingston, five at London, one at Midland, thirteen at Niagara Falls, one .at Sudbury, sub-port to North Bay, one at Huntsville, sub-port to Orillia, twelve at Ottawa.
The hon. member appointed seven new men at Hamilton, six at Brantford and thirteen at Niagara Falls. What is the increase in revenue at these points which necessitated that increase in stall?

At Brantford in the fiscal
year 1911-12 the revenue was $529,787. In the last fiscal year it was $604,618, an increase of $74,829. In Hamilton there was an increase of $628,204 in the last fiscal year, and at Niagara Falls an increase of $146,848, that is, from $318,505 in 1911-12 to $465,353 in the last fiscal year.
Would the men at Niagara Palls have the same duties to perform in the last year as they had in the year when they collected $318,000?

That is a manifesting port
and owing to the general increase in business throughout the country there would be much more work to be done in the manifesting branch and of course there was a great increase in the revenue throughout the Dominion.
How many men had you there in 1911-12?

We had thirty-three in the
previous year anu now we have forty-six.
What was the increase in the amount of manifesting?
I could not say that unless I had the books of the port before me.

I think the fact is that
some few holes have been filled up with people who wanted positions at Niagara 'Falls. It is extraordinary that thirty-three men could collect $318,000 in 1911-12 and that forty-six men were required in 1913-14 when there was only $120,000 additional revenue. It looks as if the minister was taking more care to make new appointments than to look after the collection of the revenue.
I did not appoint a man at any port without a recommendation from the inspector or from the collector in case the inspector had not visited the port.
What were the names and salaries of the thirteen men appointed at Niagara Falls?

The names of the officers
are:	Burton, $800; Byers, $1,200; Chamberlain, $800; Day, $80u; Emery, $800; Fisher, $800; Gardiner, $750; Hanna, $800; Hern, $700; Pattison, $800; Prest, $800; Shriner, $800; Thompson, $800.
How many officers were appointed to replace that old Grit at Marie-ville, whom my hon. friend dismissed?
Just one man.
Have customs ports been established at Athabaska Landing and at Eason?

At Athabaska Landing, not
at Edson.

When was it established
at Athabaska Landing?

An Order in Council was
passed some time ago to take effect on the 1st of May. No one has yet been appointed to the position but an officer of the department is there now prepared to open the [DOT]office.
Mr. REID (Grenville)
What will the salary be?

The relieving officer who is
going there gets $1,200 per annum, I think.

What will be the salary
of the officer to be appointed?
That has not been determined yet. We are simply sending a relieving officer to open the port.
Will buildings be erected?
We are sending an inspector there to rent a building that will be suitable.

I am very glad that a
port is being opened there, as it is a very important shipping point. It is the point to which practically all the traffic to Peace river, Athabaska, and Mackenzie river now goes. It goes to Athabaska Landing by rail, and is there transferred to steamers, and since the railroad has been completed to that point customs accommodation has become very desirable. There should be facilities in the way of buildings, for the officer who may be appointed will certainly have a considerable amount of work, and he should receive reasonable remuneration. I want to impress upon the minister the fact that it is not by any means an ordinary outport, but an extraordinary one, and one which will call for a good deal of service. It is very desirable that there should be no delay in passing goods through the customs there. Part of the freight which leaves Athabaska Landing goes nearly to the Arctic ocean. Only one trip is made in the year, and it is in every way desirable that the freight reaching the landing should leave on its long journey with the least possible delay. The same remark applies to Peace river, where the freight is taken up stream by steamers and over portages, and some times a little delay, in the fall particularly, means a very great handicap to the people.	_	.
I wish to draw the ministers attention to the desirability of establishing a customs outport at Edson, which is on the Grand Trunk Pacific and is a divisional point west of Edmonton. The particular need for accommodation at Edson is that at that point there is a direct waggon and sleigh road to Peace river, and while the freight generally goes by way of Athabaska Landing, there is a great deal of settlers' traffic which leaves the road at Edson, particularly in the winter time. Edson is practically the railway point for the Grand Prairie settlement, distant about 200 miles, and as people from the States shipping right through would ship by rail to Edson, and take their goods off there, it would be very desirable if they could get customs accommodation. In addition there are tributary to Edson a nnm-

ber of coal mines. There is a branch railroad fifty miles in length [DOT]which leaves the Grand Trunk railway at Biekerdike, a few stations west of Edson. There are three or four mines in operation on that branch now, and another mine is in full operation about fifty miles further west, on the main line. Edson is the nearest business point to these coal mines. In view of these facts, that Edson is the starting point for the Grand Prairie settlement, both in summer and winteT, but particularly in winter, that it is the business point nearest the coal mines, that it is a divisional point on the Grand Trunk Pacific and very close to that will be a divisional point on the Canadian Northern railway as well, I would urge very strongly that the facilities of a customs outport be given to Edson. I do not say it is less important than Athabaska Landing, possibly it is less important, but it is much more important than many other points, which have been given facilities for a customs service.

I realize that Athabaska
Landing is likely to be a very important port, and for that reason, we sent an officer who had had considerable experience to open it up in order that every facility would be given to the importers. I am under the impression that before very long we will need another officer there. With reference to Edson, I shall make a note of what the non. member said and look into it. My hon. friend will remember that we have opened several offices in that district during the last year. We are trying to open as many as we can with the amount voted. We have opened several around Edmonton, and I feel that if another office were to be opened, it would probably be further west of Edmonton, on the Grand Trunk Pacific.

I am sure that if the hon. minister chooses to make inquiry he will find that what I have said in regard to Edson is absolutely correct. It is a stategic point which renders customs facilities more desirable in the public interest than at many of the other points I have mentioned, although the facilities granted at these points are very acceptable. In regard to the Athabaska Landing. I am glad to know that the minister is posted as to the necessities there, and I would simply urge upon him that it is not in the same class as the ordinary country customs outport.
I realize that.
It is a place at which he might very well give ample accommodation because the necessity for it is there.

Yes.

revenue at Montague?

$385.94 for the fiscal year

The number of vessels

Inwards 130; outwards 3;

there at that port?

Has there been any

No, I do not know of any change unless it has taken place lately.
Mr. HUGHES. There has been a change made.

just now indicating a change but if my hon. friend has any information he might tell me if there has been one.
Mr. Thomas W. Morrissey has been appointed collector of customs.

Yes.

since I have had this memorandum prepared.

Mr. HUGHES (Kings. P.E.I.).
I wanted to know really what it was costing you to collect the revenue there. I think there must be some mistake in the number of vessel given. They must be fishing boats.

This is the official report
that I have here.

Can I get that information?
Mr. EElt): I will get whatever information the hon. gentleman wants to-morrow.

What salaries are paid
the customs officers at Georgetown; what is Mr. Owen's superannuation allowance, and what is Mr. Morrissey's salary?
What salary is paid the officer appointed about fifteen months ago at Spry Bay, Halifax county?
$900 a year.

Along the coast for quite a distance.

To whom does he
report what work he does?

Do you say a seizure
was made by this officer?

With all due deference
to the minister, 1 do not see on what ground he can justify the appointment of this official. A new office was created for him. He lives in a place where it would be impossible almost for him to perform any service

in the way of prevention which could possibly he a return for his salary. The minister will find that if he made any seizure he was associated with some superior officer. Mr. Bowen was receiving
$1,150 and the officer appointed in his place only gets $1,000; Mr. McGill was receiving $1,200 and the officer appointed in his place only gets $1,000.

Yes, hut Mr. Bowen was in the department for thirty years and Mr. McGill for thirty-four years. I am not finding fault with the salaries paid the new officials for I think $1,000 a year is little
enough, but I leave it to the fair play of the Minister of Customs to say whether these three gentlemen who nave had long service should not be placed at least on the same footing as the new officials. I hope the minister is not making that difference because the new men are political friends of his and the others have been Liberals in the past.

I think the Liberal
officials in the Customs Department all over Canada will agree that I have treated them fairly in the matter of increases last year. There is supposed to be a uniform salary for landing waiter's work and the clerks in the office get slightly higher salaries, but they do not get overtime. For that reason it is very difficult to increase the salaries of the landing waiters, say at Yarmouth, and not do it throughout the Dominion. I have been trying to increase the salaries wherever I can, but the hon. gentleman knows that it takes a lot of money to increase them throughout the Dominion. I personally have _ always taken the ground that the salaries everywhere are very small. Last year we gave increases to the extent of $152,000. So far as we can, we want to give some more increases this year. I shall be very glad to give increases where they are deserved, and where we have the money to do so.

I have' been trying to get
into the minister's head that Mr. Boyd is a preventive officer who attends on the boats as they come in from Boston twice a week, or every day in the summer time. He receives extra pay the same as Mr. Kirk and Mr. Pothier. I maintain that the Minister of Customs should put these three gentlemen on the same footing as the others. He will not be overpaying these two new officials and will only be doing justice to the old and efficient servants.

Mr. Bowen, the officer who
died, was receiving pay for over-time too, so that Mr. Rogers who was appointed in his place was appointed at $50 a year less than Mr. Bowen was getting, and he is doing the same work. I do not see that it is unfair to appoint him at a salary of$l,000.

I am not complaining that
it is unfair. I maintain that the salaries that the Minister of Customs is paying Mr. Boyd and Mr. Rogers are not too high but, when Mr. Boyd is getting $1,000 and other preventive officers who have held their positions for some years are only getting $800 or $850,1 think that the minister should put them all on the same basis.
Their salaries will be considered with the other increases which we are giving.
Will the minister give me the total customs receipts for the last fiscal year?

I have only the unofficial statement here. The commissioner tells me that the official figures will be a little larger. The total revenue up to March 31, 1913 was $113,817,578.29; for the previous year it was $86,397,943.70; showing an increase of $27,419,634.59.
The additional officers in the inside service are twelve.
Is Mr. Breadner one of these?
No, Mr. Breadner is in the outside service.
Are these twelve for the inside service appointed by Civil Service examination?
They are appointed through the Civil Service Commission. The Commissioner of Customs goes to the Civil Service Commission and gets those to be appointed to the inside service.
Then, their salaries are not part of this increase of $600,000?
No.
That makes this increase all the more glaring.

I do not know whether the hon. gentleman was present when I explained that this was for officers appointed throughout the whole Dominion.

Mr.'GUTHRIE: I was here. But I cannot see why it should take 477 new officers to collect $27,000,000 of additional revenue. I can understand that by following the plan he seems to have adopted in Welland and Niagara Falls the minister could spend a good deal more than $600,000 throughout the Dominion. But the minister's experience in this House, for he has had a long career as a member of Parliament, and also as a professional man and businessman,, for I believe he has been actively engaged in business, must have shown him that there is no justification for any increased expenditure as he now proposes. As I have stated, the percentage of cost ought to go down, and as a matter of fact it is going up. That shows there is something radically wrong about the system. I submit that the difficulty is that the minister has over-manned his department very largely with what I think we may call political heelers. I have no doubt he has been hard pressed to find places for the many applicants who have thronged about him. He has given way, and so has increased the cost of collecting the customs revenue. Unless he can give some assurance that in the future he is going to restore the old proportion and revive the old descending scale as between revenue and cost of collection, I do not think this House should agree to such an increase unless more justification is forthcoming. This increase, I contend, is largely due to the making of political appointments and providing jobs for political heelers at the expense of the Government.

I have a case in a small way in my own constituency that may explain the system the minister has adopted. In the little town of Mulgrave there was a preventive officer by the name of Hattie, who was receiving $75 a year for duties that were practically nominal. The minister dismissed Mr. Hattie and appointed in his place a very worthy old gentleman who has been a faithful friend of his party for many years Mr. David Murray, at a salary of $400, to do, I presume, the same work that Mr. Hattie was doing, and was glad to do, for $75. I have no doubt that appointment is political-it cannot be anything else. I have no complaint to make about Mr. Murray getting the appointment. He is a fine old gentleman, and a friend of my own. But there can be no reason that I can see for the increase from $75 to $400 for almost nominal duties. I would like to know from the minister if other small preventive officers in little harbours along the coast who are now being paid from $75 to $150 a year are to be increased to $400, as in the case of Mr. Murray. If my hon. friend intended to give a general increase, I could understand why he should give $400 to Mr. Murray; but, if
the others are to be kept at the same salary, the only explanation that can be given of such a case is that it is political.

Mr. Murray was dismissed
some years ago when the Liberals came into power, and, as far as I can understand, without cause, and we simply appointed him on the same salary as he was receiving when he was dismissed.

That is not the case.
Mr. Keating is the customs officer at Mulgrave who was appointed to Mr. Murray's place and he is still in the same position. Mr. Hattie, preventive officer at Mulgrave, was getting $75 and he was dismissed and Mr. Murray put in his place at a salary of $400.

The case of Mr. Hattie was
investigated by Mr. Duchemin, who found him guilty of political partisanship. I suppose they should have dismissed Mr. Keating also and put Mr. Murray back in his old position.

No, I do not think so, because you could not get any evidence of political partisanship against Mr. Keating. Mr. Keating is a good officer who has filled his position very well and cannot be accused of political partisanship. If you could have found any case against Mr. Keating probably this would not have happened. I mention this as a sample of the way the minister is conducting the business on the coast and the only explanation I can find of his action in asking such a large increase in the amount for salaries is that he desires to reward his political friends.

As I understand, Mr. Murray fifteen or sixteen years ago occupied the position of collector of customs. He was dismissed by the Liberal Government after investigation. He was in receipt of $400. Since this Government came into power, they investigated the case of a minor official, Mr. Hattie, who was receiving $75. I suppose that salary was quite sufficient for the work he was performing. He was dismissed and Mr. Murray was put in his place to do his work, but instead of getting the same salary as Mr. Hattie was getting Mr. Murray was given the salary which attached to the position of collector of customs which he held fifteen years ago. Is that what the minister said?

I said Mr. Murray was
forced to resign, and he could not get his superannuation.

I did not think that
Mr. Murray was very fairly treated at the time. I tried to get his superannuation allowances arranged for.

He was on the superannua-
. tion list and I think the people in the vicinity felt that he was hardly fairly treated and the salary of $75 for an official there is really

That is all Mr. Hattie
got.

But it was too small for an existence and Mr. Murray was re-appointed at probably a little higher salary than Mr. Hattie had but he had been unfairly treated, he had lost his superannuation for fifteen or sixteen years and he is getting up in years.

He got a salary five
times what Mr. Hattie had been getting.

The hon. member would feel that $75 is not a fair salary to any man doing preventive service. At all events, Mr. Murray really had a fair claim against the Government for having lost his superannuation and we felt that we should give him probably a little more salary than we could have got another officer for in order to try to do justice to him for losing his superannuation.
Mr. SINCLA-lR:	It would have been
better to give him his superannuation than to take the course that has been taken. If there was any injustice done in the old case and he was entitled to superannuation, he should have got his superannuation.

It was impossible to grant
the super annua uon when his resignation was in.
With reference to the situation at Niagara Falls, I may say to my hon. friend that we had no person in the county of Welland asking that officials in Welland county or at Niagara Falls should be dismissed. No investigations were held there.
Were there no dismissals there?
Is there anything new in this.
With new country being opened up we require more officers.
The hon. minister makes up this item on a basis of $494,000 for contingencies.

Last year we employed 477 new officers at an aggregate salary of $205,985. Then, the increase of salaries to deserving officers amounted to $152,110. That was distributed among 1,355 officers. The increase in payments for overtime service to additional officers was $12,340. The increase in contingencies rent, &c., at various ports amounted to $49,085, making a total of $619,520.
That is all for last year?
For the fiscal year ending Alarch last.
Then is the $600,000 to be voted for next year additional?
The hon. member is aware that we had a vote last year, and the supplementaries for this year amount to $600,000, so that the $600,000 we ask for is what the salaries were last year up to March 31.

The item $2,525,000
covers supplementaries as well does it not? If you are right, there is an increase of $1,200,000.
There is a great deal more than $600,000.

That item should certainly embrace the supplementaries as

well as the main estimates for last year. You are adding $600,000 this year in addition to what you had last year.
The officers that we have added account for $619,000, and the increase last year amounted to $600,000.

The total last year, as appears in the first column, which includes supplementaries, was $2,525,000. This year what is asked for is $3,125,000, which is an increase of $600,000. Does it mean that since this Government has come into office there has been an increase of 50 per cent in the cost of collecting customs?
We had $200,000 in the supplementaries that we passed a few days ago.
That is all in the first column.
No, the supplementaries were passed only a short time ago.

It should be in that column.
. Mr. REID: These estimates were prepared last November, and the supplementary estimates for 1913 were passed only a short time ago.

Then this item leaves an entirely erroneous impression. The first column is intended to show to the committee the total expenditure under this item last year in the main estimates, the supplementaries and the extra supplementaries, so that the committee can make a comparison between the cost of running that particular branch of that department last year and the estimated cost for the current year. If the first column does not show the total expenditure for last year we ought to have some explanation.

These estimates were prepared last October. They were estimates of the expenditure expected up to March 31, 1913. Then we brought down the supplementary estimates for 1912-13, which included the item of $200,000.	.

We ought to have an
explanation in respect to each item. Unless we have a memorandum in each case, we can form no accurate judgment as to the increased cost.

I think that has always
been the case when estimates have been brought down early in the session and supplementary estimates for the previous year have been subsequently brought down.
