The difficulty would be obviated if the minister would give us accurately the amount of each item.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think he can do that.

On page 92 of last year's estimates, in the column headed 1912-13, it is stated that the main estimates were $2,425,000. Then in the supplementary estimates, which were recently passed, the Customs item for salaries, contingencies &c., was $285,000.
The $100,000 in the supplementaries of last year makes up the $2,525,000.

The	item $2,525,000
does not include everything for last year.
It includes the supplementary estimates that were voted a month ago.
Where does the minister get the $100,000?
In the main estimates there was $2,425,000 and in the supplementaries $100,000, making $2,525,000. Then, this year we have $200,000 for salaries, contingencies and so on, which makes $2,725,000.

What was the amount
in 1910-11?

You are asking for
nearly $900,000 more than was asked in the estimates for 1911-12.
If the hon. gentleman looks at the revenue for the year 1911-12 he will find that it amounted to $73,000,000.
I am not talking about the revenue; let us get the facts with regard to the expense first.
Take each year; in the first year $73,000,000 was the revenue.

Am I right in the
figures that the cost during the current year is nearly $900,000 greater than it was in 1911-12 ?
I do not know; I have not the figures before me.
If that is not the case the minister should be able to tell us.

I can get the information
for the hon. gentleman. I have only the information here for the	two
years 1912-13 and 1913-14. The hon. member asked me for the figures for the year previous and I will be glad to get the information. In the year about which the hon. gentleman was speaking the revenue was $73,000,000, and in the year following it was $86,000,000. There waS an increase

of $27,000,000 last year. If the revenue is going to increase we must have a larger staff and the cost of collection will be greater.
Not in the same proportion.

The officers are all asking
for increases, and the increases granted each year are added to the cost of collection.

That is a small item,
only about $150,000.

There has been increases
during two or three years, and the hon. gentleman will have to add these increases when comparing the cost of collecting the revenue of to-day with what it was three years ago. We must give larger salaries to customs officers and to officers on the staff if we are going to keep them. Some of our best officers have left the service during the past year on account of the salaries that we were paying. I think that the cost of collection is being kept as low as it possibly can be, taking into consideration the increased revenue that is coming in.
Does the hon. gentleman admit that there is an increase of $900,000?
No, I will not admit it unless I have the figures.
Will the minister undertake to look up the figures and let us have them ?
Yes.

I think we can take
the report of the Department of Customs for some of the figures, anyway. I find on page 12 of the Report of the Department of Customs that the total amount of the revenue for the year ended March 31, 1911, was $73,312,367.59. For the same year, in the estimates which I have in my hand, page 88, the expenditure was $1,950,000, or the percentage of expense of collection of the customs revenue was 2-98 per cent. Take the next year from the same authority. For the year ended March 31, 1912, the total revenue from customs was $87,576,036.52. The appropriation for the year was $2,225,000, and the percentage of cost of collection was 2 -78 per cent. Then, for last year the appropriation was $2,425,000, with a supplementary estimate of $100,000, which I do not happen to have, and a further supplementary estimate, which is shown on page 9 of last year's supplementaries, of $285,000. The point I made at the outset was that in the present year the total customs revenue is about $113,000,000, and the percentage of cost of collection is about 31 or 3i per cent.

The revenue was $115,039,602.
Mr. REID (Grenville)

I took it down as

Mr. REID I said that was not quite official but I nave had the figure handed to rae since.

Well, the percentage of cost will be about three and one-quarter per cent. The increase is very marked when you look at the amount and, if these figures show anything, they show that m the last few years the cost of collection, salaries, contingencies and expenses, has gone up over $900,000, or $1,200,000. I cannot quite figure out in my own mind how these supplementaries are worked in. I thought they all showed in these estimates before me now. If they do not I do not know why they do not. This statement before us only shows that in 1912-1913 there was an appropriation of $2,525,000, but as the minister says, there was a supplementary of $285,000. Then he proposes for this year an appropriation of $3,125,000 for the same item or an increase of $600,000. Are we to have more supplementaries in addition to the vote proposed for this year and if so that would make the increase still greater. Would the minister say whether this would be final or whether there would be supplementaries?
If we have to give any more increases there will have to be supplementaries.
Or appoint more officials.

Or appoint more officials.
We are opening more ports, the revenue has increased from the time of hon. gentlemen opposite by sixty per cent.
And the pressure to appoint becomes greater.

No, we are not appointing
officials unless the inspectors report that we must have more officials to collect the revenue and do the necessary work at the different ports.
I understood the minister to say that he had 477 additional officers last year. Were they not paid out of the appropriation of $2,525,000 and the supplementary vote of $285,000?

Yes, they were paid out of
those votes.

What are you going to
do with this $600,000 additional that you are asking for now?

More ports, more salaries,
more officers.
We have no particulars of that so far.

There have been very much larger increase than we expected, and this year, if these increases go on, we will certainly require even more than we have now. If the revenue continues to increase and if we .grant increases to deserving officers, we must have a larger vote in order to pay the staff necessary to perform the duty.

I do not object to the moderate increases made last year by the minister in the salaries of officials, I think they were very proper and they would be proper again this year, but it only took about $150,000 to do that. Another increase of salaries may take $175,000, but how he makes up a total of $600,000 on that single item I cannot see. He may guess at it, but surely he must have some data.
We had 470 new officials last year.
Their pay was included in the $2,525,000 and the $285,000 supple-entaries voted last year.

Some of these officers have
only been on for a month or two months or three months and so on.
It still is a fact that in two years you have increased the cost of collecting the customs revenue about $900,000. It looks like an extraordinary increase when it should be a decrease.
According to the figures given by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Guthrie) himself, there was $40,000,000 more collected for an increased expenditure of $900,000.

The hon. gentleman
(Mr. Guthrie) is mixed in his figures. He says that in 1910 the total revenue collected was $87,776,000 and the customs staff cost that year $2,225,000 or 2.7 per cent of the collection. Now, last year the customs revenue collected amounted to $115,000,000 and it cost $2,800,000 to collect. If the hon. member figures on that he will find that there is a decrease in the percentage of cost of collection rather than an increase.
Who is the present preventive officer at Red Island, Richmond county, N.S.?
There is no officer there.

Last year the total on which the percentage is figured (estimates, page 95) was $3,070,000, in addition to which there was $285,000 in the supplementary estimates. This year the total is $3,830,000, or an increase of $760,000. Last year the percentage was 2.78 and this year it is 3.24 if computed upon receipts of $115,000,000.
The hon. gentleman is mistaken; he is taking the figures for this year at $115,000,000, and he should charge against that sum the estimates of last year, $2,070,000.

I have been figuring on the $115,000,000, which was collected up to the 31st of March last; I can only take the figures before me. The greater the revenue the more cheaply it should be collected proportionately. That has been the rule since Confederation with the exception of two or three years. It decreased from six per cent to 2.78, and now it is going up again under this new Conservative Administration. If the minister would assure the Houise that there will be no supplementaries this year, his statement may be correct, but will he give such an assurance as that?
I hardly think he will.
What change has been made at New Glasgow, N.S.?
We have appointed J. M. Bailey, salary $1,200 and C. A. Cameron, salary $900.
You dismissed an officer named Kavanagh.

He was appointed after
September 21, 1911.

The reason given for
the dismissal of Kavanagh was that there was not sufficient employment for him. But after dismissing Kavanagh who was getting much smaller salary than either of the new appointees, the minister appointed Cameron at $900 a year and Bailey at $1,200 a year, although there was not enough work for Kavanagh to do. That is another explanation why we are asked for such a large amount of expenditure in the Customs Department.
Kavanagh was dismissed because he was appointed some time after the Government was defeated on September 21.

I think the minister is not correct in that. Mr. Kavanagh was in the office months prior to that date. I do not know whether or not his appointment was by Order in Council. If the minister will look over the documents relating to Kavanagh, I am sure he will find the statement that Kavanagh was relieved from duty because there was not sufficient employment for him in the office. Why it takes two men to do the work that was not sufficient for one, puzzles me,

Does the minister consider it a sufficient ground for dismissal
8711 .

that a man was appointed after the elections of 1911 and before the present Government came into power?
That was what was done by my predecessor in 1896.

Is that the policy of
the present Government?

When I do not consider a
man's services satisfactory, I let him go.
I would like to ask the minister why he dismissed Mr. Joseph Macdonald, customs officer at Sydney?

He was appointed the day
before the former Government went out of office. That is the reason why he was dismissed.
Had the minister anything against the services of Mr. Macdonald?
He was not in the department long enough for me to know much about him.
This man could not be accused of offensive partisanship, because he was appointed subsequent to the 21st-of September, 1911, and before the present Government came into power.

He was appointed acting
officer during the pleasure of the minister.

It must be the policy
of the (Government to dismiss persons who were appointed subsequent to the 21st of September, 1911, and before the present Government came into power. Is that correct in Mr. Macdonald's case?
Mr.' REID:	He was an acting officer
appointed during the pleasure of the minister.

No, he was not.

The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) dwelt for a considerable time on a statement which he made that the percentage of cost for collection of revenue in 1912 was 2.78, and he asserted that the percentage had increased in the next year to about 3.25 per cent. I am not able to discuss that because I have not the official reports on which we can rely and without which we are almost always apt to get into trouble. I do not know how the hon. member made up his figures, and I do not dispute his calculations. I have the official returns for 1909,1910,1911 and 1912. In 1908, the percentage of cost for collection of revenue was 3.30; in 1909, under the Mr. CARROLL.
same Government, the percentage had increased to 4.15, a very material difference. How does the hon. gentleman explain that? The hon. member will see that there was an increase of .85 per cent m one year, whereas the contention is that the increase from 1912 to 1913 is only .47, or the difference between 2.78 and his figure of 3.25.
My official tells me that the percentage last year was 2.92 and the previous year 2.78.

That is not a very large difference. The hon. minister has opened a great many ports. These ports have been necessary. There is room for difference of opinion on that _ point. The Hon. Mr. Paterson, when Minister of Customs, stated plainly that customs houses were not opened for the public convenience; that they were opened for the purpose of collecting revenue. I do not think he was always right in his policy.
I think he should have taken into consideration the public convenience as well as the collection of revenue. There has been a demand during the last two years for opening more customs houses for public convenience. I am one of the guilty parties in that regard. A customs house was opened in my own county. I have not the figures before me; but the last time that I was in conversation with the collector after the expiration of nine months from the opening of the office, the imports amounted to a figure which would indicate for twelve months about a million and a quarter dollars, whereas in the previous year there were no imports at all. I admit that a great many of the imports were free goods; but the opening of the port was of immense advantage to the people doing business there, and saved them the necessity of entering their goods through Guelph, Georgetown or Toronto. The minister is perfectly right in taking into consideration the public convenience as well as the collection of revenue in opening these additional ports. I do not see any reason for complaint as the difference is so slight, in comparison with the great convenience to the public. The minister has given us a very fair statement and there i3 nothing in the contention of the hon. member for South Wellington. I think he must have got astray in his figures. I would suggest that he revise them because I have no doubt that the commissioner of customs, a very careful man, who had charge of such matters for a great many years, is absolutely correct in the statement that he has given us.

I submit that there is not a particle of evidence in the report which I have read which would justify the Minister of Customs in dismissing Captain Paschal Poirier on the ground of offensive partisanship. I call your attention to the nature of the charge made by Mr. Gillies, the Conservative candidate, in which he extravagantly asserted that Poirier was guilty of very offensive political partisanship, not only in discussing politics but in driving voters to the poll. There is no evidence of that and the only evidence against him is that he took passage on a steamer to the nominating convention. But there^ is the further inconsistent act of the Minister of Customs in dismissing Captain Poirier for political partisanship and appointing a more offensive partisan in his place, a man who since his appointment has been selected to fill the position of vice-president of the Conservative Association of Richmond county. He is still there, and, in addition to being collector of Customs, he was appointed postmaster at the port of Descouse. I also find he was appointed inspector of the breakwater that is being constructed by the Department. of Public Works a few miles from Descouse. I submit that that man should he dismissed from office for offensive partisanship. It ought not to make any difference in the estimation of the Minister of Customs, whether he is an offensive Liberal partisan or an offensive Conservative partisan. I submit that the present holder of the position of Customs 'collector at Descouse ought to be dismissed because he is actually an offensive partisan and not a partisan in the sense that Mr. Poirier was proved to be in the investigation held by Mr. KYTE.
Mr. Duchemin. In regard to what rights public officials have with respect to the discussion of public questions, I beg to refer to the statement made by the right hon. the Prime Minister in the House of Commons in the session of 1896. It will be found on page 338 of ' Hansard ' of that year, and is ae follows:
The fact that these officials work for either party; so long as they work openly, honourably, and fairly, ought not to weigh against them, if at the same time they do not neglect their duty as public officers. It seems to me that those gentlemen who are in the civil service of this country ought to have the same rights as other electors, not only to vote, but to work during elections, subject to certain limitations which I shall endeavour to submit to the House.
Again he said:
It does not seem to me that a public officer discussing in an honourable and straightforward manner a public question of absorbing interest with a gentleman who afterwards succeeds to office as a minister hf the Crown, ought necessarily on that account to lose his office.
I have no doubt in my mind that the right hon. the Prime Minister was absolutely sincere when he subscribed to that doctrine in the House of Commons in 1896. He stated that a public officer had the right not only to attend public meetings, but to discuss political matters, provided he did so honourably and without giving offence to any person. In the case of Captain Paschal Poirier the late collector of Customs at Descouse, there is no evidence whatever that he ever was a partisan. There is his own statement that in twenty-seven years he polled only two votes, one vote for a Conservative candidate, and the ether for a Liberal candidate, that he did not canvass in public, that he did not drive anybody to the polls, that he did not attend any public meeting for the purpose of taking part in public discussion. He took passage on a steamer from Descouse to St. Peters and went to the meeting where there was a strange speaker, and the moment that the strange speaker concluded his remarks, he left the meeting. If, in the judgment of the right hon. the Prime Minister a public official has the right not only to attend public meetings, but to discuss public questions with the electors, without forfeiting his office, surely there is no justification in the world for the dismissal of Captain Paschal Poirier, on the ground of political partisanship.
My hon. friend referred to this being half of Mr. Poirier's living. What is his other occupation?
He has a little bit of a farm that he works on, and at one time he was a sea captain.

I would like to understand exactly what the standards are which govern in the neighbourhood referred to by my hon. friend. In the province of Ontario, the standards are somewhat different, if those described by my hon. friend are to be taken as the standards which exist throughout his province. In the province of Ontario poll clerks are usually appointed because of their well known political proclivities.
Are they sworn to discharge their duties faithfully?

I presume they are, but that is not the point. As a rule they are not appointed from the official class. I think it inconceivable that such appointments should be made. I have never heard of such a case in the province of Ontario, and I can speak for that province so far as my knowledge goes. To see a member of the Customs staff in the province of Ontario going to a political convention would be shocking to the people of that province, but it seems to be quite common glace and regular from the point of view of the member for Richmond. .
What does the hon. member say about the present collector of Customs at Descouse, who is vice-president of the Conservative association.

It is probably a sign
that he is a very capable man. My hon. friend has referred to Mr. Poirier giving some evidence of his going from home on a vessel, and he has stated that he did not pay his own fare. It would be interesting to know who did pay it. I did not hear my hon. friend say whether it was in his interest that Mr. Poirier went, but there is a very strong suspicion that he went to see that the hon. member for Richmond had fair play at that convention.

That is no justification for
dismissal, according to the Prime Minister.
Not being a delegate why did he go?
To listen to the speaker.

Some strange speaker
without a name. Had he ever heard of the hon. gentleman before? He was not a delegate, and he went to the convention without any reason, and in going in office hours, I fancy he would come under the definition of the right hon. the leader of this House, and that if could be said that he was neglecting his duties in attending that convention. The coolness with which the hon. member for Richmond has attempted to justify such flagrant conduct as this man has been guilty of, is quite shocking to me, coming as I do from Ontario where such things would not be permitted for a moment.

I do not know how it
is in the experience of my hon. friend, but in a good many cases in Ontario men under age are appointed poll clerks if they are bright young fellows.
Customs officers?

No, hut their appointment would not be a sign of political partisanship because a good many are not of age. The hon. minister has laid down a very strong rule that if a customs officer goes to a convention and takes no part in the discussion, but listens to a speech, he is guilty of offensive partisanship and of neglect of duty. If it be true that this officer at Descouse has been appointed an officer of the Conservative Association, and that he is an active officer of that association, does the minister propose to permit him to hold office in his department? If he does, this talk of political partisanship is all rubbish.
Is there any evidence that he has been appointed an officer of the Conservative Association?

I say if it be true that he is now an active officer of the Conservative Association, does the minister propose to allow 'him to hold a position in the department and still hold office in the Conservative Association?
I have no evidence that he has 'been appointed an officer of the Conservative Association.
But if he has been?
He may have been vice-president and may have resigned. If he has not resigned-

The hon. member for
Richmond says he has been appointed since he got the position of collector.
I have no doubt that he has resigned since he got the appointment of collector.

The hon. member for
Richmond says he has been appointed an officer of the Conservative Association since he was appointed customs collector.
The hon. member would not likely know the members of the Conservative Association there.
If it is shown that he is now an offcer of thq Conservative Association, will the minister see that he is retired from that position or retired from his department.
He will have to retire from the position of officer in the Conservative Association or else retire from the office of collector.
Hear, hear.

I was out of the House for a few moments during- which I understand the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) made some remarks. He seems to have said that my calculation as to the percentage of the cost of collection was wrong and he has pointed out, as I understand, that in the year 1909, according to the returns of the Customs Department, the percentage of the cost of collection was 4-15 while in 1912 it was 2-78. It is true that in 1909 the proportion was high but there was a reason for it; 1909 was the year of the financial panic.

I do not think the hon. gentleman put that quite fairly. In the year 1911-12 the cost of collection was 2.78 per cent. For the year 1912-13 the appropriation was $3,070,000 in the main estimates and $285,000 in the supplementaries, or a total appropriation of $3,355,000 on a collection of $115,000,000 or 2.92 as against 2.78 per cent for the previous fiscal year. For the present fiscal year we have $3,830,000 in the estimates and, of course, we cannot foretell what the revenue for the fiscal year ending on the 31st March next will be.
Does the minister anticipate that the supplementaries will be any less this year than last?
Yes, the supplementaries will be very much smaller.

What is it estimated they will be?
Mr. RE>ID: I have not that with me. There will be some supplementary estimates but they will not be as large as they were last year.
The assistant commissioner could no doubt tell the hon. gentlemen.
They will probably be $200,000 as against $285,000 last year.

The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) made the statement that during the past two years the increase in the estimates had amounted to $900,000. During the same period the receipts of the Department of Customs increased by $42,000,000 or, in other words, this $42,000,000 has been collected ati an average cost of 2.13 per cent. He also contrasted the estimates for the years 1913-14 with the cost of collection for the previous year. Since then I find that the hon. member was absolutely incorrect and that the returns made by the Customs Department are for the actual expenditure for the current year, thus corroborating the statement made by the minister. I have in my riding a couple of officers who were appointed since the change of Government and who do not collect a cent of revenue, but who are yet absolutely necessary.

That has been so at
other points even since Confederation.

One of the officers is
at a point whence the ore from the Canadian Northern mines is exported and he has to be there as a preventive officer, and to make the returns; the other has charge of bonded baggage for American tourists, and neither collects any revenue, although they cost the department $600 a year. Many such cases must occur throughout the Dominion in this growing time.
My contention was that the percentage of cost of collection should decrease rather than increase.
It has not increased.

The minister admits it
has increased from 2-78 last year to 2-92, and the supplementaries will certainly increase it further. Estimating it on the returns to the 31st of March, the cost of collecting is 3-33 without taking into consideration what may be asked in the supplementaries. If the minister is going to increase his staff by 470 a year and have thirteen officials tumbling over themselves at Niagara Falls, the revenue is bound to increase.
Does the hon. gentleman say the salaries of the customs officers should not have been increased ?
I have commended the minister for increasing the salaries, and I think another increase should be granted this year, but before we vote these lump sums we should have some explanation.

I am sure the hon.
member (Mr. Guthrie) wants to be fair and I cannot see how he says the cost of collection is 3-33 when the minister tells us it is only 2-92. The minister is not going to run away with the $400,000 increase and hide it; if it fs not spent it will not be taken out of the treasury.

Oh, he will spend it,
do not have any doubt of that; he will appoint a lot of fellows in your county.

There is a collector of customs in Picton who is the son of an ex-Lib-eral member of this House, and he work, ed for twenty-one years- m the summer months, from five o'clock in the morning until midnight, for a salary of $1,400 a year. I asked the present Minister of -Customs to give him an assistant and he did so. The customs officer had to apply for sick-leave because -of over-work. I can tell my hon. 'friend (Mr. Guthrie) that we do not propose 'to work our men like that. If we are to judge other counties in the past by what has taken place in my county, then I say that it is a crying shame the way customs officers have been treated.

Can the Minister of
Customs give me a definition of ' offensive partisanship '? Edouard Chiasson, a collector in my county, was dismissed last year on the ground of offensive partisanship. The minister first held an investigation at which no evidence was given against Mr. Chiasson, and he was not dismissed. Not long after my generous friend the Minister of Marine wrote to the Minister of Customs asking him to hold another investigation, as he thought some evidence might be brought up which would prove active partisanship. The second investigation was held. One of the witnesses deposed:
I reside at L'Amecque; I am a voter; Mr: Edouard Chiasson resides at L'Amecque; T remember the federal election in 1908 and I do not Temem-ber that Mr. Chiasson took part; do not remember his taking part in the' election of 1911. I was at the Turgeon meeting at the Catholic Mutual Benefit Associa-' tion hall at L'Amecque. Mr. Chiasson was on the platform; I do not remember that he spoke; he applauded Mr. Turgeon's speech; I was at the polls on election day; did not notice Mr. Chiasson; did not notice his canvassing during the campaign; know nothing further; I am a Conservative; hard to say what side Chiasson was on.

-Five or six witnesses gave' similar evidence. Mr. Chiasson was appointed collector of customs in 1903 on the ground of his ability. He was one of the best educated men in the locality; he had been a school teacher and had given satisfaction; he belonged to one of the most respectable families. I did not know with what political party he was affiliated; he was recommended by me on account of his qualifications for the position and his high standing in the community, and witnesses have deposed that they never heard of him taking part in politics when he held office. In the elections of 1911, they did not know whether he was a Conservative or a Liberal. There was a meeting in that .municipal district held by myself, only a few hundred yards from his own residence. He came to my meeting. I have been addressing meetings throughout the county of Gloucester for the last forty years. He ap-lauded some of my remarks. Even if he ad applauded something that I might have said on a Canadian navy, I do not think that constitutes offensive partisanship. His dismissal would signify that a man appointed by a Liberal Government must be dismissed. The Prime Minister stated here a few years ago that a man who did not take an active part but who merely expressed his opinion should not be dismissed. The hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) will remember that, when he was on this side of the House, he said that no official Should be dismissed except for neglect of duty. I made no complaint when the Minister of Customs dismissed the official at Bathurst, because I knew that he had been taking part in an election. In this case, however, the evidence shows that the only possible fault of the man was that he had attended a public meeting in his own district without saying a word. Nobody saw him at the poll on polling day. He canvassed no one; he expressed his opinion on political piat-ters to no one. Yet, because he was appointed by the Liberal Government, he was dismissed. I would ask the Minister of Customs if he places that in the category of active or offensive partisanship.
Mr. E. D. C. Knowles, the commissipner appointed to hold these investigations, found against Mr. Girroir. He reported that he had been guilty of political partisanship.

I would ask the Minister of Customs to look over the evidence. It amounts to what I have stated, and was given by men who belong to the Conservative party. The gentleman who has been appointed in his place was at the time one of the most active men on Conservative committees, still belongs to those commit-Mir. TURGEON.
tees, and has been active in making recommendations since his appointment.
If he has done anything of the kind, I will certainly see that he discontinues it.

I would like to ask
the minister whether any change has been made in the position of sub-collector at the sub-port of Raie-Verte, and incidentally whether representations have 'been made to him as to the necessity of establishing a port of entry or the placing of an official at Cape Tormentine. For a number of years there has been an agitation to change tire office from Baie-Verte, which was one of the first settlements in that section of the 'country, but which has now gone down materially, the business having been transferred to the town of Port Elgin, which is a very active and thriving community. The distance between those two places is about two and a half miles. At that time there was a very strong movement on the part of the people of Cape Tormentine which is a port for the shipment of deals, to have an officer at that point. In fact, they wanted to have a sub-office established there. There is a larger export business done at Cape Tormentine than perhaps at any other port along that north shore, with the exception of Shediao, and I believe that more lumber i.s shipped from Cape Tormentine than from Shediac. Have any applications been made with respect to closing the Baie Verte office and opening one at Port Elgin, and also with respect to establishing an additional office at Cape Tormentine? It would be a great convenience to the shipping interests at Cape Tormentine, as many large steamers come there to load. It is the nearest point to Prince Edward Island along that strait. Steamers ply between Cape Tormentine and Prince" Edward Island. The tea captains and shippers find it very inconvenient to travel twenty odd miles from Cape Tormentine to Baie Verte in order to attend to their customs business. This agitation has been going on for a number of years. 1 have received during the past five or six years a number of petitions, end I have brought them to the notice of my hon. friend's predecessor, but no change has so far been made.

If I remember rightly, there have been , some communications with respect to changing the office from Baie Verte to Port Elgin and superannuating the old gentleman who is now at Baie Verte. Nothing has been done so far, as the matter is only under consideration. With reference to Cape Tormentine, nothing has been done. The difficulty is that many hon. members are asking for new offices, which would be a great convenience to the public. If I were to carry out their wishes and those of

other gentlemen who have been applying for offices, I would have to ask for much more than I am asking in the estimates. The hon. member for South Wellington is grumbling because I am increasing the cost of collecting the revenue on account of opening new offices. I would like to open very many more than I am able to do with the estimates that I have here to-night. I think there are a great many ports That should have officers, and yet I have not felt quite justified in coming to the House and asking for a large enough estimate to provide for these places. Take Tormentine, for instance, there is no doubt that it would be a great convenience to the vessels going there and to the public also but I have not made an appointment there. In all places where officers have been appointed on account of increase of revenue, it is on the report of inspectors and collectors that appointments have been made. The main part of the increase in cost of collection is in the large offices.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me how many new officers have been appointed in Montreal, and how many in Three Rivers?

While the minister is looking up the figures, I desire to occupy a few minutes. I think the minister has misunderstood the hon. member for South Wellington. I understood that hon. gentleman to advocate the principle of increasing the number of outports. He complained that in his own county there were two important places which had not either port or outport. I think the hon. gentleman is quite right; I often wondered how it was that- during the fifteen years of Libera] rule the hon. gentleman did not do more for his county in the way of securing accommodation for the people. The Minister of Customs of the late Administration held to the principle that customs ports were opened for the collection of revenue and not for the convenience of the public. He told me that time and again when I made appeal to him for a customs house in my own town, and I assume that that is the reason the hon. gentleman from South Wellington did not get the increased accommodation for his people of the lack of which he now complains. But the peculiar part of the hon. gentleman's remarks is that he complained of the increased cost of collecting the revenue, yet urged on the minister to open more ports or outports, and so, of necessity, increase the cost of collection.
Not necessarily.

That is a new theory to me. If it would not, then I say the minister is justified in every way in doing what he has done, increasing the number of officers for the collection of revenue. Nor
do I say he has overdone it, for I fancy in no place has he opened a port or outport where it was not required for the public convenience. I repeat that the Minister of Customs in the late Administration made a mistake in insisting that the ports should only be open for the collection of revenue and not for the convenience of the public. I hope the hon. member for South Wellington will get the new offices. Both Elora and Fergus are important towns and would justify an extension of customs accommodation, and possibly Erin Village also. In the county of Wellington are also the towns of Palmerston and Harriston that need increased accommodation. In my own county after a new outport was opened the people were delighted, and none more so than some	of the friends of the
hon. gentleman who has been decrying the increased cost of collecting the revenue. In my town amongst the chief importers were Liberals who voted against me. But notwithstanding that fact, it was a matter of public convenience. I thought the Minister of Customs did right in acceding to the request which, I confess, I made to him regardless of how it could affect the cost of the collecting of revenue. I had appealed to the minister's predecessor, but was turned down. I said then that the Liberals were not going to be in power for ever, and the time would come when my grievance would be redressed. I did not know I was so good a prophet, for in six or eight months my grievance was redressed, a Government having come into power which believes in dealing with the public on the lines of public convenience and not merely on the lines of what money they can get out of them. I heartily justify the action of the minister in opening these ports for the public convenience, even though it may have the effect of increasing the 'cost of collection.
I do not object to the opening of these ports, and I think my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) ought to know that. He says I advocated it.
The hon. gentleman advocated both ways-a decrease in the revenue and an increase in the ports.

The villages that I
mentioned-and I hope now that I have the support of the hon. gentleman I may have the arrangement completed-both have substantial Government buildings. So, there will be no cost for accommodation, nor need a new civil servant be appointed, but a man can be sent from Guelph when goods are to be passed. It is a short railway trip with a fare of about 75 cents.

A man could not do that
and attend to his duties in Guelph.

I think he could. I
have watched the government officials. It would take perhaps an hour and a half and the trip would only have to be taken perhaps once a week. So, the expense would be small.

But it is not a question of
expenses only. I understand that the officers now are so busy that I have been requested to send them another officer.

No doubt about that.
That is what I object to. We have 477 additional men put on the pay roll at the instance of the present minister. That is where the money has gone. I have not objected and do not object to new offices, nor do I object to the increase of the staff necessary to carry on the work. But I think such cases as I have mentioned before account for this great increase. ^ I think there is no justification for the increase at Niagara Falls. I do not think there is any justification for the increase at Hamilton or at Brantford. I do not know about Ottawa. The customs returns have increased largely in my own city and there has been no increase in the staffs. Berlin and Waterloo have also shown large increases, with the appointment of only one man. But at Niagara Falls they have simply tumbled the men in to satisfy their political friends. That is what has increased the cost of collection.

The
minister is evidently disposed to deal generously with the public and provide foi their convenience according to the assurances of himself and the member for Hal-ton.	He	has	started a	new	policy,	that	of	consulting	the	convenience of the public in deciding these offices, and not merely the collection of revenue. That is what governments are for. That being the case-and he has carried out that policy to a considerable extent, judging from the number of people he has appointed in the last year or two and from the fact that he wants this large amount of money now to establish new offices-I would remind him of a petition which has been sent to this office from the district of Tracadie asking for a sub-collector there. This would cost a trifle and would afford a great convenience to a large section of the people of the county of Antigonish as well as of a considerable portion of the county of Guysborough.	The fact3 setforth'in that petition and the correspondence I have had with the minister myself must strike the minister as indicating	a condition	wnich would
justify a sub-collector of customs at that port. There would be no difficulty in get-Mr. GUTHRIE
ting an officer with * the proper qualifications and the man recommended for the position is a good 'loyal Conservative. That I suppose, is in his favour and he is a good man in other respects. I am sure that such an appointment would be viewed with favour by both Liberals and Conservatives in that community. Such an office^ is really a necessity and I hope the minister will find it in his power to establish it.

I
was pleased to hear the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) speak as. he has in regard to the advantages of subofficers in Fergus and Elora. He also m-terjected a remark that there had been established an office in Harriston. That is not the case. I would say for the information of the minister, if for nothing else, that to my knowledge there is not a customs office in Wellington apart from the one in the city in which the hon. member for South Wellington resides; and, as the hon fnember for Halton (Mr. Henderson) has stated, I am surprised that he did not take this matter into consideration when he was in a better position to have offices established in the riding which he represents. We have at least three better towns in the north riding than either of the villages to which he referred:	The Minister of
Customs has seen fit to establish offices in those towns which are much more deserving than these villages. I am quite agreeable to assist him in establishing customs offices in the south riding of the county which the hon. member has the privilege of representing.

About the time of appointment, if the minister will look into it I think he will find that in a good many cases appointments which were made after September 21 were simply confirmations of the appointments of officials who had been temporarily appointed but whose appointments had not been made by Order in Council. Some of these officials had been there for years.
No, not at all. All the officers who had been there for years in that way are still there.

I hope that is the case. I have a complaint to make with regard to the dismissal of a man in Colborne. My information from two sources is that he was dismissed without any notification except what was handed to him on the day of his dismissal. There was no investigation and he denied the charge or political partisanship. If that is the case it can hardly be justified on any grounds. He denies that he took any part in politics, he was not given any investigation; _ nothing was proven against him. That is treat-

ment such as the minister would not offer to the most menial servant in his own employment. He would hardly dismiss any man or woman without giving at least a few days' notice or some reason that was a real reason.

The officer at Colborne was dismissed for political partisanship on the evidence of the member sitting for that riding. The hon. member knows that the rule has been followed by the House that if the member representing a riding assures the minister that an officer is an active partisan, that officer is to be dismissed; after that evidence has been submitted to the Governor in Council an Order in Council is passed and the officer notified. The officer at Colborne was not treated any differently from all other officers who were dismissed in that way.
I pity the others.

The member for the
county to that extent becomes minister.
The hon. member knows that has been the rule for years. That was the rule carried out by the Liberal Government since 1896.

Against which the
House unanimously passed a rule.
What is the rule followed in case a defeated candidate having the patronage of a county recommends a dismissal?

If there is a vacancy in the
county I follow my own judgment.

Shortly after the minister took office he was asked by the junior member for Halifax what rule he would adopt in case of a recommendation by a defeated candidate. At page 1076 Mr. Maclean said:
Mr. Maclean (Halifax): If a customs officer is charged with .partisanship is he given an opportunity to defend himself?
Mr. Reid (Grenville): I am following the policy laid down by the House. When a member charges that an official has been an active partisan in his constituency I ask for ffiis dismissal. But in the case of another constituency where there is not a member to represent the constituency, if a charge is *made, I have an investigation, and if it is proven that the official has been an active partisan, of course he is dismissed.
That was the rule laid down by the minister very shortly after he assumed office. I find that in my own constituency the minister has not been carrying out that rule.
To what case do you refer?

To the dismissal of W. A. Girrior, on a complaint made against
him by G. A. Rowlings, the defeated candidate in that constituency. The letter is dated Sydney, N. S'., November 6, 1911:
Hon. J. D. Reid,
Minister of Customs,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Sir,-I beg to request the dismissal of W. A. Girrior, preventive officer, of customs at Larry's river, county of Guys-borough. I regret to say that' this official' displayed offensive partisanship towards myself by interrupting me .in my address at' Larry's river, during the recent compaign. I would recommend the immediate appointment of William J. Murphy of Larry's river in his place.	<
Yours very truly,
(Sgil.) G. A. Rowlings, Liberal-Conservative candidate, Guysborough County, September Election.'
Then the minister's commissioner addressed a letter to Mr. Girrior, dated Ottawa, November 10, 1911:
Mr. A. Girrior,
Customs Officer,
Larry's River, N.S.
Sir,

Representations have been made to" this department to the effect that you have displayed offensive partisanship towards Mr.-Rowlings, a candidate during the recentj campaign, interrupting him at Larry's river, -your action being thus in contravention of the regulations respecting the interference of customs officers in political questions. I am therefore directed to ask for your statement as to whether these representations are correct or not. An early reply is requested.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) John McDougald, [DOT] Commissioner of Customs.
Mr. Girrior replied to that letter under date November 15, 1911:
John McDougald, Esq.,
Commissioner of Customs,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-You favour of the 10th to hand, to the effect that I had displayed offensive artisanship towards Mr. Rowlings, a can-idate during the recent campaign. He, Mr. Rowlings, said in his speech that if reciprocity would take place that our fishing bounties would be excluded and cut off. I was at his meeting when he said so, and I only said that I would bet $20 it would not interfere with the fishing bounties, and I can bring proof that was the only word I said. I then left the meeting and got home without saying one word more, so I fail to see* how Mr. Rowlings can claim that I interrupted him. As I have been to all meetings of Conservatives and never did interrupt any, I think Mr. Rowlings should pardon such a small offence, which in the future might do him no hurt. Still, I am at their disposal. Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) William A. Girrior, Preventive Officer.
The next document is one from the minister to His Royal Highness the Governor General in Council:

The undersigned, Minister Customs, has the
honour to recommend that Mr. William A. Girrior, preventive officer of customs at Larry's river, N.S., be dismissed from the customs service for active political partisanship during the late Dominion election. The evidence as to such partisanship appears on customs file No. 77333 herewith.
Respectfully submitted,
(Sgd.) J. D. Reid, Minister of Customs.
Then we have on record a letter from the commissioner of customs addressed to Mr. Girrior notifying him of his dismissal. You will note Mr. Chairman that the only partisanship charged against this man was the remark which he made in the meeting in the sehoolhouse of his native village, when Mr. Rowlings had made a statement which everybody of any intelligence knew was not correct. He said that if reciprocity was passed, there would be no further fishing bounty. That was not true. Anyone -who has read the correspondence that led up to the reciprocity agreement knows that there is no foundation whatever for that statement. This man Girrior made the innocent remark that he would bet $20 that the fishing bounty would continue. I would not call that a very serious matter especially when the statement made by the candidate was without the slightest foundation in fact. I think it was the duty of this man to make some protest. At all events it was a case in which the minister ought to have had an investigation. If he had had all the facts investigated, he would not have dismissed that officer, but he has not carried oiit the principle which he laid down in this House. Even at this late date, he ought to give Mr, Girrior a chance to establish his innocence for I have no doubt he could do so. I would like to know if the minister intends in the future to adhere to the principle which he laid down during last session in this House that in a case where complaint was made by the defeated candidate, he will order an investigation.

I think in almost every case where a complaint has been made by a defeated candidate we have had an investigation. There have been a few exceptions, but very few. In cases such as that mentioned by the hon. member where an official admits that he took part in politics one way^ or another, we have not held an investigation, but I do not suppose that these oases amount to more than four or five. In this case where an officer admits that he attended a meeting, interrupted the speaker and found fault with what he was saying, we considered that the evidence was sufficient to justify dismissal without holding an investigation. The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) asked me a question about the number of extra officers at Quebec and Montreal. The number is Mr. SINCLAIR.
twenty at Quebec and forty-eight at Montreal.

How many at Three

I submit to
my right hon. friend that this motion is altogether premature. It seems to me that the House has not reached that period of the session when morning sittings would Mr. CHISHOLM (Inverness!.
be justifiable. First of all, as I am informed, the committees have not yet completed their labours. Meetings of four of the committees are called for to-day [DOT] Banking and Commerce, Public Accounts, Old Age Pensions and Railways, Canals, and Telegraph Lines. Then, to-morrow the Banking and Commerce Committee and the Special Committee on Old Age Pensions are to meet. As I understand, the Committee on Banking and Commerce will not have completed its labours by to-morrow and may require some more sittings. If this motion as moved is agreed to, the Committee on Banking and Commerce would have to sit during the sittings of the House in order to complete its labours.
I do not know when the Committee on Railways, Canals, and Telegraph Lines and the Special Committee on Old Age Pensions are likely to complete their labours. It is important to know whether or not all the committees will have finished their labours before we commence morning sittings. The Government has not yet informed us whether or not it has any new legislation to bring down. It is usual, when we commence morning sittings, that all the legislation of the Government has been introduced, with the possible exception of railway subsidies, which are generally brought down at a late period. When my right hon. friend was in opposition, he found fault with us in that respect, but I do not know that he has improved on the former order of things. If we were not to commence morning sittings until the railway resolutions were ready, we would have to sit very late in the summer and perhaps in the fall. Before we adopt this motion, we should have this information from the Government. The business of the House, as shown by the Order Paper, is not sufficiently advanced to justify this premature motion. The most important measures of the session have not been disposed of. We have not yet had the budget speech. We should have the budget speech during the ordinary sittings and not after we are compelled to sit in the mornings. The fact that we are sitting in the mornings is an admission on all sides that the House is approaching prorogation, and I am sorry to say that I do not see that we have yet reached that desirable period.

Hon. G. H. PERLEY moved the third reading of Bill No. 28, respecting an agreement between Canada and certain of the West Indian colonies. He said: We have had word from all the West Indian colonies, except one, that this Act has

been confirmed and would be brought into operation on proclamation, as provided in their several ordinances and Acts. The only colony from which we have had no definite assurance yet is British Guiana. However, I have no doubt that they have considered the matter, and a cable was sent yesterday making inquiries. We had a cable from the Island of Grenada on April 20, which says:
At a meeting of Grenada Legislative Council to-day resolution passed to join Canadian reciprocity agreement.
This is one of the islands which was not represented last year at the conference held in Ottawa, and which was given the option under our statute of taking advantage of this agreement.

Before this Bill passes I desire to call the attention of the House to one phase of the matter which in my judgment requires further consideration, and in respect of which I hope the Government will see their way clear to accept an amendment which I intend to propose. I refer particularly to those clauses of the Bill which have reference to transportation. I think hon. gentlemen on both sides of this House are agreed as to the advisability of passing this legislation; it will be an advantage to Canada and, I think, to the British West Indies. Any steps taken to increase the trade of this country cannot but be a benefit to the country as a whole. If I were to blame the Government at all in regard to this matter, I would charge them with being niggardly in their treatment of these colonies. I think that instead of making a reduction of twenty per cent in the duty upon certain imports, many of these things might have been admitted free, thus increasing largely the trade between Canada and the West Indian colonies and, to some extent, reducing the cost of living to the Canadian consumer. I think that practically everything coming from the West Indian colonies to Canada should be admitted free, because, viewing the matter from the standpoint of the protectionist, the articles which we would import from the West Indies are not produced in Canada, and die re would be no competition in that respect; and, viewing it from the standpoint of the consumer, we would be getting a cheaper living. I believe that the only way we can make this proposal a success and justify the course being taken is to work up a direct line of business between Canada and the West Indies; in other words, the benefits which we hope to obtain by this agreement would be better secured by establishing a means of direct communication. We have not done much business with the West Indian islands during the last ten or fifteen years; the figures are so small that I think the Minister of Finance must be surprised when he realizes how infinitesimal has been the Mr. PERLEY.
business between Canada and the West Indies as compared with that between Canada and other countries of the world. I think, therefore, that whatever we do should be done along the line of stimulating the trade between Canada and the West Indian colonies. In the Maritime provinces we have had, along certain lines-particularly in fish-a large business with the West Indies for a great many years. I might mention that the Maritime provinces have tried to carry on a business, not so much with the British West Indian islands as with Cuba, in respect of potatoes, and I think ihat in this regard a special subsidy was given-and I believe it is still in force-to a steamship line running direct between the port of St. John and the Island of Cuba. The result has been that a market has been found for a very large quantity of potatoes which under other conditions would not have been marketed. I notice in the press that only within the last week a ten-thousand barrel shipment of .potatoes was sent from St. John to Cuba; this was no doubt due to the subsidy to which I have referred. If you want to stimulate trade between Canada and the West Indian Islands, you must have direct steamship communication between Canada and those colonies, otherwise, if the steamships call at United States ports, you will establish a trade between the United States and the West Indies rather than between Canada and the West Indies. The articles exported from Canada -hay, oats, flour, and general farm produce-almost invariably go to the West Indies through United States ports. In some cases these might be Canadian goods trans-shipped through United States ports, but it will be found that three-fourths, and probably nine tenths, of all such goods as are produced by Canada and shipped to the West Indian markets go through United States ports, simply because in the United States they have splendid transportation facilities It is true that they have the transportation facilities because they have the business; they carry on not only an export but an import trade in the way of fruit, sugar, and the other tropical products of the West Indies. We can work up a large business between Canada and the West Indian Islands, just as they are doing in the United States, but we can do it only by means of a direct steamship service. A statement was made by one of the delegates of the Ottawa conference-I speak now from memory-that the rates were about four cents a hundred pounds less via New York to Montreal or Toronto than via the direct route. If that be the case, this business, unless something is done, will find its outlet through United States ports, and not through Canadian maritime ports. If the Canadian Government is going to subsidize

these steamship lines-and I think they are -I contend that these steamships should be compelled to ply direct between Canadian and West Indian ports. The Government will be able to control the rates by means of a subsidy contract; they can make the rates as cheap as they are via United States ports; they can drive the business through our Canadian ports, and will not only work up,a trade betweerathe producers of the respective countries, but will encourage the development of ,all the activities incidental to navigation and railway transportation. This is a very important matter indeed as affecting all of Canada, and, if we are desirous of obtaining the full benefit of this treaty, I think this business should be done through our own and not through United States ports. I believe also that the subsidies must be sufficiently large to make the work attractive to a big steamship company, and one that will give us an up-to-date service. If I have any objection to offer to the subsidies we have been granting in the past to Cuba and -the West Indies, it is that they have been too small; certainly tbev have not produced the results that should have been obtained, and we have had a very inefficient service. When I say that, I think I am using as mild language as a man could use who knows anything about it. I know something about the service between St. John and Halifax and the West Indies in the past, and I have no hesitation in saying that it has been entirely unworthy of Canada, one which has been almost a disgrace to Canada, and certainly of no benefit to the Dominion from the point of view of transportation, or from any other standpoint. The service was so bad that no person has been known to take advantage of it a second time. It might be said that this is pretty strong language, and I admit it is, but I think I have reasons for making the statement. Possibly the subsidy was not large enough to justify any better service. If that was the case, then give a bigger subsidy, but if the subsidy was large ' enough to justify a better service, then I think the department has been remiss in its duty. I am not applying my remarks to the present minister so much as to previous ministers. Whatever may have been the cause, the result has been a very inferior service, which has been of no benefit to Canada from any standpoint whatever. If I am right in my statement, I think the service requires a much larger subsidy. I do not believe that we shall ever get satisfactory results from a service of steamships starting at Halifax, calling at St. John, and thence proceeding to the West Indies, or calling at St. John on the way back and then proceeding to Halifax. Such a service is too slow. We are living in an age of progress, and there is no use of talk-277
ing about a steamship service which takes about a week to get started. The vessel is partly loaded at Halifax, and then it goes 1 to St. John to finish the loading, which usually takes about a week. That is too slow for this progressive age. In my judgment, the service should either he from St. John alone or from Halifax alone; or, if there is jealousy between the two ports- and I am afraid my hon. friend from St. John would not agree to the service being from Halifax alone-and if we cannot have a single service, let there be two services. The service should be of some benefit to the people of Canada, and should stimulate trade between Canada and the West Indies, and I am afraid that the present service has done neither the one thing nor the other. We have simply been paying out large sums of money to transportation companies and getting no benefit. I do not say that the transportation companies have not given as good a service as they could afford in the circumstances, hut there should be a service that would be of benefit to exporters and to Canadian commerce in general.
I believe that the contract should be made with a real transportation company and not with some local company which might organize itself into a transportation company, hire steamers, and do what I might almost call a tramp business. I do not wish to pass any reflections on the service we have had in the past, but I know there has been at least one service between the Maritime provinces and a portion of the West Indies that has not been the success it might have been simply because the company who were carrying it on did not own vessels. They were not a real transportation company, and consequently were not in a position to give the people the benefit they were entitled to receive. I am satisfied that those gentlemen gave all the service they could afford to give; the difficulty was that they were not a transportation company. They hired a vessel here and a vessel there, paid big prices for rentals and had little or nothing left for themselves, with the result that the *exporters had to pay bigger freight rates than the business justified. I do not know what ideas the minister may have. We have heard reports about the Government entering into a contract with the Elder-Dempster Line and also with the Canadian Pacific railway. I believe there is no company in Canada in such a good position to undertake this service as the Canadian Pacific railway. I hold no brief for the Canadian Pacific railway. When the elections come round they are about the hardest competitors I have, but they are a good transportation company, and whatever they do they do well. If the Canadian Pacific railway entered into a contract with the Government to give a fortnightly service.



or a three weeks' service, or a monthly service, they would carry it out loyally and from a business standpoint. They would be able to give a through bill of lading from any point in Canada to any point in the British West Indies because they would have a continuous service both by rail and water. For these reasons, I think they are in a better position to carry on this service than any other company. I repeat ithart I am casting no reflections upon any company which has been carrying on business between Canada and the West Indies, or which may intend to do so in the future. I merely mention this to support my original proposition that if this service is to be a success we must (tarry it on through Canadian ports, and we must be able to give a service as cheap as or cheaper than the service through American ports. If there is a difference of four cents in one hundred pounds in favour of the New York route, that is almost prohibitive against Canadian traffic, but if we gave a sufficiently large subsidy, and the business was carried on by a Canadian company which had a through service, from a point we will say in the Rocky mountains to Trinidad, we would have a service which would be a real competitor with that from New York and Boston. We all know that if we have the transportation facilities we will get the business. I do not have to argue to this House that good transportation facilities always produce a paying business, and the better and cheaper the transportation facilities are, the more business we will secure. Therefore, I submit it is important in the interests of the trade of the West Indies and of Canada that we should have a service between either St. John and the West Indies, or between Halifax and the West Indies, or from both St. John and Halifax, and that it should be carried on by a company who would own and operate their own boats and be able to give a service up-to-date, so that the shipper would know exactly what to figure on. That service should be from Canadian ports and Canadian ports alone. Therefore, I move,
That the said Bill No. 28 he not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House, with instructions to amend the same, by adding to section 5 thereof the following sub-section, namely:
(3) All steamships so subsidized shall be required to ply direct between Canadian port or ports and the said British West Indian colonies.

Before the Minister of Trade and Commerce left for Australia, he made the statement that when this Bill came up for third reading, he would inform the House as to the conditions of the West Indian service and also would give informa-Mr. CARVELL.
tion as to the tenders and contract which would be made, if such contract should be made. We have had a good many rumours in the newspapers and we would like the acting minister to give us full information upon the subject.

I have listened with
a great deal of interest to the observations of my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Car-veil), with regard to the steamship service between Canada and the West Indies. We are all anxious to carry out our understanding with our West Indian friends in good faith and in a way that will accomplish the best results from this trade agreement. There is, and has been, a great deal of difficulty about arranging a proper fast service with the West Indian islands. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) gave much time to the matter before he went away and I havd given considerable tinie to it since then. Before I give to the House the details of this contract that we have entered into_ for this service between the lower province ports and the West Indies, I will say a few words in regard to some of the remarks that have been made by the hon. member for Carleton. He advocates a direct steamship service between our ports and the West Indian islands and moves an amendment to the Bill now under discussion which embodies that idea. The Government never seriously considered subsidizing any service except a direct one between the West Indian islands and Canada. One of the tenders that was put in provided that the steamers should be allowed to stop at American ports under certain conditions. This matter was discussed 'by the Government and we felt that it would be a mistake to subsidize a steamship service of that kind. As I think I stated in the House before, in answer to a question by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), we have not made a contract which permits stopping at American ports, nor have we any idea of making a contract of that kind. This agreement which we are considering to-day on the third reading is one that was entered into with the West India delegates and it seems to me that it does not permit of amendment in this shape. The policy of the Government is that the steamers shall run direct from the British ports in the West Indies and in Bermuda to Canadian ports and I think we will all agree in this House that it is a wise thing to do in -the national and imperial interests.
My hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) says that our trade largely comes through United States ports. As a matter of fact, I do not agree with that statement made by my hon. friend to the extent to which he makes it, but I do know that we have a good deal of trade from the West Indies coming through

United States ports. The main reason for that is that there are in the United States, and particularly in New York, large business firms which have been carrying on trade with the West Indies for a number of years and who control that trade and it suits them better to ship flour from our Northwest through New York," through the port where their business house is situated, than it does to ship it through Halifax. I know it has been stated that the rate by New York to Montreal is less than by Halifax, but I would like to sue that substantiated more than by mere statement, because I am assured by the contractors for the service from Halifax and St. John to the West Indies that such is not the case. There is in the contract a very carefully drawn clause which distinctly prevents anything of the kind. In the contract which exists to-day, and which is an extension of one made by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in power, and in this new contract which we have made, this provision is there in carefully drawn language. If it can be shown that goods coming from Barbados, for instance, to Montreal are brought more cheaply via New York than via St. John or Halifax, we have the power, and it is in the agreement, to rectify that.

Would the minister
read that clause?

May I be permitted to say that I spoke, of course, without knowing the contents of the agreement. Perhaps the minister would give the House the agreement, and then we would be able to more intelligently understand what we are referring to.

An order of the House
has been passed, on a motion of the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), for certain papers, in connection with this service, and if my hon. friend would put in a supplementary motion, I would be glad to bring down the papers up to date, including the contract and the Order in Council authorizing it. I will try to expedite the return so that the papers will be brought down as soon as possible.
The minister might give all the particulars of the arrangement now.
I would be very glad to do so, but it would hardly be wise to read the whole contract at the present moment.
Is the minister reading from the new agreement now?

Yes, this is the new
agreement. I will just read the portion that has particular reference to the point that we were discussing.
277i
It is agreed and understood that the freight rates on south-bound trips, sailing from Halifax or St. John as hereinbefore provided, on through bills of lading from any places in the provinces of Ontario or Quebec or from any Canadian points farther* west, shall in no case be greater than from the same place via any United States routes or ports; and on north-hound trips the rates from any port in the British West Indies to any place in Ontario or Quebec or other Canadian points farther west, shall be as favourable as via any United States route or port to the same place.

I would like to ask the minister if there is any clause in the agreement which provides that the rates from the West Indies to Halifax and St. John shall be as low as the rates from the West Indies to New York. I am informed that on certain classes of goods the rates to St. John are nearly double what they are to New York and there is no possibility of getting the grievance remedied. The people interested feel that it is a very great hardship.-

If the hon. gentleman
will permit me, I will leave that question for the moment. I may say that there is in all these contracts a general provision that the minister has authority over the freight and passenger rates and if they are found to be unreasonable, he has, nominally and technically, at all events, the right to see that they are reduced. I do not think there is anything that definitely covers the point mentioned toy the hon. member for St. John.
Does the minister think there ought to be?

I believe the rate to St. John ought not to be greater than the rate to New York. I discussed the matter with Mr. Black and I understood from him the rates were the same. No doubt complaints were made in certain cases that the rates now charged are higher than those of last year, but as my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) knows, all the steamship rates have gone up somewhat, and in speaking with Mr. Black he simply -told me they charged to Halifax and St. John the same rate that was charged to New York. If there is any discrimination it should be carefully looked into. After considering carefully this new contract we have entered into for the West Indian service, endeavouring to get a contract for a term of years which would be satisfactory, we decided to make the contract for merely one year. The present contract expires on the last day of June and the new contract made with the present contractors, runs for twelve months, to expire on the 30th of June, 1914. These contractors have undertaken to join with others, and Mr. Black is now in England

with that end in view. Our arrangement with Messrs. Pickford and Black is that this contract shall be transferred to a new company with other people in it and these other people are to be approved by the department. The boats are to run every twelve days and it will take four boats to perform the service. Two of these boats are to be the same as the contractors have been using under their present contract and the other two are to be modern boats of a high class. These new boats are to be of British register one hundred 'A 1' Lloyds, of not less than 4,500 tons gross register and 5,000 tons dead weight capacity, with refrigerator chambers, electric light, and al! modern conveniences, capable of steaming twelve knots per hour, with passenger accommodation of fifty first-class, forty second-class, and a hundred steerage.

When will these new
boats be put on?

The contract starts the
1st of July.
They will be secondhand boats, they will be bought in the Old Country?
I am unable to say as to that. They may be chartered boats.
They cannot be new boats.

I quite understand that, but Mr. Black had in mind to discuss the matter with the Royal Mail and Elder-Dempster people. For the two new boats we are to pay $75,000 each per year. After considering the matter for a long time it seemed to me this was a reasonable temporary solution of a problem which presents a great many difficulties. As I view it, the heavier part of the cost is because we are trying to get a good passenger service. I believe that a freight service could be profitably run to the West Indies without very much subsidy, provided it was understood the Government would not subsidize some other line, but when we endeavour to get modern passenger boats to compete with the vessels running from New York and Boston, we find it costs so much to run these ships that the steamship .men ask very heavy subsidies. Under this plan we will be able to see whether these good passenger ships will get reasonable patronage from Halifax and St. John.
The subsidy you pay is $300,000 a year.

It comes to $200,000-
$150,000 per annum for the two better-class boats and $50,000, or one-half the present subsidy, which we give to the two other boats.
Mr. PERLEY
Is not the present subsidy more than $50,000?

The present subsidy is
$100,000 for four boats, and we are paying half of it for two of the present boats, and $150,000 for the two better boats.
To my mind this is a passenger problem. Can we by putting on first-class boats get enough passengers to make these boats pay, because we can get a good freight service for much less money-in fact, for a comparatively small sum, if we eliminate the question of passengers? By this method, the problem is settled for this year and we shall know a little better whether these boats will attract to themselves the passengers necessary to make them pay.
My hon. friend has referred to the reports about certain tenders that were put in. I will give a short resume of what happened when these tenders were asked for and of what offers we got. In the first place, the present contractors, Messrs. Pickford and Black, put in tenders for services of varying frequency and vessels of different speeds. One was for a twelve-knot service every twelve days for a subsidy of $315,000 per annum. None of these tenders provided for cold storage in the vessels, and the itinerary was to remain as it is at present; that is to say, a boat comes from the West Indies to St. John, discharges its cargo, takes on board cargo for the West Indies, then goes to Halifax and sails from there. We did not consider it wise to enter into a long contract on these terms. If my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) would arrange that either Halifax or St. John would give way to the other port, and have the ships sail from one port only-
That is impossible.

-it seem3 to me it would be a fairly easy task to arrange, but the present itinerary does not seem to be very satisfactory.
