The Royal Mail Steam Packet Company did not put in a regular tender; but they afterwards made proposals to provide next July a fortnightly service of eleven-knot steamers for two years for $300,000 per annum. with the condition that the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company would have the option of declaring at the expiration of one year whether they would continue the contract for a further period of ten years with steamers of an average speed of twelve knots at sea. The Government did not consider it advisable to enter into a two-year contract with any company on these terms. We offered to arrange with them for a two-year service on the understanding that we would get together afterwards and try to arrange for a ten-year service; but we did not consider it advisable to give them the option, and I [DOT]TO sure that the hon. mem-

bexs will feel that we were justified in our action.
Another tender came from the Canada-West Indies Syndicate for a fortnightly service to commence in eighteen months with vessels capable of steaming fifteen knots, for a subsidy of $300,000 per annum for fifteen years. This was coupled with a condition that they should receive a further sum of $150,000 per annum from the governments of the British West Indies and British Guiana. The Government did not consider it wise to accept their tender with a condition of that kind attached to it. My hon. friend has said some nice words about the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and I quite agree with him that anything that that company undertakes is well done. This tender, however, was not received from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company but from the Canada-West Indies Syndicate, composed of prominent gentlemen in Montreal some of them are affiliated with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; but that company would not have been responsible for this contract. The connection was that the Canada-West Indies Syndicate had a traffic arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
Is there any mention in that tender about a call at tbe port of Boston?

The original offer made
by the syndicate provided for a call at Boston; but the Government refused to entertain such a suggestion, and afterwards the syndicate withdrew that condition. The present contract into which we have entered with Messrs. Piekford and Black is improved, as I said, with regard to the class of vessels that are to be put on, and in one or two other ways. For instance, clause 5 of tbe contract says:
It is declared to be the intention of the contractors, and the contractors undertake to associate with themselves certain other responsible persons and with them to form a new steamship company for the purpose of carrying out this contract in a thoroughly satisfactory way and the minister agrees to consent to such assignment of this contract,1 provided it is shown to his satisfaction that such company is able to fulfil all the obligations of this agreement.
In order to help out the difficulty in St. John, I have inserted clause 7, which reads as follows:
It is further understood and agreed that the contractors shall at all times, when so required by consignors and at the expense of the contractors, pay the freight charges by rail from St. John to Halifax on all perishable goods intended for shipment by their steamers.
The same provision has been in tbe contracts for some years.

I have been told that it
has been done in certain cases, but it has never been in any of the contracts.
That does not help out the difficulty.
I quite understand that the matter is full of difficulty, but my hon. friend will agree with me that it will make some difference to the people of St. John.
What is the date of the agreement?
It is dated the 14th day of April, and is made between the present contractors, Messrs. Pickfo-rd and Black, Limited, and tire Government, for one year.

I desire to
say a few words on the third reading of this Bill, particularly in reference to the treaty as it may be affected by the steamship service carried on between Canada and the British West Indies. In some respects I agree with the observations made by my hon. friend from Carleton (Air. Carvell) in regard to the value of an efficient steamship service between Canada and the West Indies and its effect in developing trade. But I am not disposed to agree with him in hig views respecting the decree of efficiency in the past years nor with what I think are probably his views as to the kind of service we want between Canada and the West Indies. A feeling prevails that if we had a very high-class steamship service between Canada and the West Indies it would do a great deal for Canadian trade. To some extent that is true; but there is a point at which the increase of efficiency must cease, a time when contractors, to be practical and successful in their operations, must cease raising the standard of the service. I think there is altogether an absurd idea as to the character of the steamship service that we should have between Canada and the West Indies; and I do not think anybody has been more mistaken in this respect than the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster). I gather from the proceedings of the West Indian Conference and from returns I have perused that that hon. gentleman was under the impression that the main thing was to have a first-class steamship passenger service between the two countries. There is nothing whatever to warrant an expensive and high-class passenger service between Canada and the West Indies. If we are to develop and increase our trade there it must be by paying more attention to an efficient commercial service. For many years to come the number of passengers travelling between Canada and

the West Indies must necessarily be small. It is small to-day, between the United States and the West Indies, with the exception of a few months in the winter, and during that time the extra passenger ^service is carried on by special boats placed on the West Indian route. I assume that the greater portion of Canadians desiring to travel to the West Indies during the winter season will do so via American ports, largely the port of New York. If it is desirable to have a corresponding passenger service from a Canadian port it would be far sounder and more businesslike for Canada to pay a special subsidy for a special service for two or three months during the winter season. In the very nature of things there cannot be a great deal of passenger travel between Canada and the West Indies, or between the United States and the West Indies, on account of climatic conditions. One reason why the Pickford and Mack services operating from Halifax have not been able Ito meet the demands- of some of the travelling public is that for nine months in the year /practically nobody travels from Canada to the West Indies, nor do they desire to travel; and it would be a great burden upon any contractors-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that no Canadians go to the West Indies during nine months of the year ? Is it not a fact that a large number of Canadians go to the West Indies but that they go by American lines.

Not all the year round. They go only in the winter season. But during the summer season, of course, business men, and especially commercial agents, have occasion to go to the West Indies, and they might go there via American ports, but the number going to the West Indies during the summer season must be small, because nobody desires to go to the West Indies during the summer months unless it is absolutely necessary. Therefore, in considering what should be the character of the steamship service between Canada and the West^ Indies, too much stress should not be laid upon the consideration of providing a service that would equal, say, the boats sailing from the port of New York during the winter months-. It would be an unfair imposition upon the contractors and no good service would be performed for the country.
My hon. friend from Carleton, N.B., complains about the character of the service now being performed between Canada and the West Indies, and I have no doubt that in many respects his criticism is justified. The service, perhaps, was not what it should have been, but there are a good many reasons for that. I think that if my hon. friend from Carleton and my hon.
Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
friend from St. John would agree, I could suggest a very cheap and easy remedy for many of the defects in the steamship service now operating between the Maritime provinces and the West Indies. In the first place, this service, perhaps, has not been what it should be because the term of the contract between the Government and the company has not been sufficiently long. I regret that the agreement recently entered into between Pickford and Black and the Government is not for a longer period of time. It is hardly fair to the contractor, and hardly fair to the publio who are interested, to have a contract covering so short a time. One could hardly expect a contractor to make the investment necessary to put desirable steamships upon this route unless there is some certainty as to a long tenure of the contract. I submit to the Government that unless they very shortly enter into a contract covering a considerable number of years with some contractor, they will hardly get the service which we deserve. There is this further to be said in reference to the criticisms directed against the Pickford and Black service from Halifax, and that is that these steamers are obliged to call at two ports, St. John and Halifax. If that can possibly be avoided by the selection of one port, which, I would suggest, is the proper course, or by the establishment of two services, one from St. John and the other from Halifax, many of the objections to this service would be removed. >Some hon. members well know that the trade between the West Indies and the Maritime provinces ports a great deal of sugar cargo is carried. That is considered by ship-owners a very dirty cargo. It has a bad effect upon other cargo carried in the ship, and I have noticed myself that on these West Indian boats on arriving at Halifax with a cargo of sugar, considerable of the woodwork would be turned to a leaden colour owing to the escape of gas from the sugar. Then, owing to the fact that these steamers must go to St. John, and from St. John to Halifax, little time is left for cleaning the steamer between the trips. This lenders the ships less desirable for passenger and freight traffic; the contractors realize the force of the objection and its effect upon the ships and their business, but owing to the loss of time incurred in calling at the two ports, practically no time is left for the cleaning of the steamers. When I say it is in the interests of Canada generally that the ships of the West Indian steamship service should leave the port of Halifax, I know that I shall be charged with sectionalism and undue interest in the constituency which I represent. However, if the facts support the contention that there should be but one port of departure, namely Halifax; then, even were I anima-

ted by sectional motives, that would count for nothing in the end. I believe that a service amply sufficient and efficient for all Canadian trade interests can be obtained
by a service, sailing from Halifax to the West Indies throughout the whole year.
Would the hon. gentleman tell us what kind of boat would be the most useful in connection with this service?

I do not presume to
offer an opinion on the strength of the assumption that my knowledge of the matter is sufficiently great to ask hon. gentlemen to accept it, but I have frequently discussed this matter with importers and exporters at Halifax, and it is generally considered that a twelve-knot boat will meet the demands of the Canadian trade. It should be remembered that only steamers drawing a limited depth of water can enter some of the West Indian ports. For instance, at Bermuda, steamers drawing a certain depth of water only can enter the harbour there, and it would be useless to subsidize large and expensive steamship lines if the steamers could not enter the harbours of the respective ports.

They do not go to the
wharves, do they?

They do at Bermuda.
In the West Indian Islands it rarely happens outside of Bermuda, that steamers have access to wharves to load and unload; the loading and unloading is performed by lighterage. These islands are not very far apart, and the practice is to load and unload during the day and sail from port to port during the night, and therefore a twelve-knot service or even one in which the ships attain a lesser speed, will meet the demands of all these islands. As I have said, I have discussed this matter with a great number of exporters and importers in the city of Halifax who know this trade better than any other people in Canada; who have been connected with it for a great number of years and who are familiar with every detail of it. I think it could.be demonstrated that a twelve-knot service is amply sufficient for the needs of this country, and if a faster service is required for passenger trade, possibly some other plan can be worked out, particularly for the winter service. I believe that an efficient service can be operated between Halifax and the West Indies which for a great number of years will meet the demands of this country, and I believe that that service can be carried on just as well by the present contractors or by other Canadian companies as it can be done by the Canadian Pacific railway. I do not know of any reason why
the Canadian Pacific railway can perform that service better than any other people. The rail freight rate from all Canadian ports to Halifax and St. John is as good as it is to New York; it must of necessity be so, otherwise our exporters could not engage in, nor would Canadian steamships get any of that trade.
I have frequently heard the argument made by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) respecting the supposed differential rate in favour of New York as against Canadian ports. I have not carefully investigated the matter, but I did about a year ago, and the impression I then formed was that there was not such a differential rate as my hon. friend from Carleton stated.
I think that with a service operating between Halifax and the West Indies all the year round, the company would be very glad to absord the differential rate, if any, for the privilege of entering and departing from one Canadian port all the year round, just as they have agreed to absorb the differential railway freight rate between St. John and Halifax in order to catch the departing steamer from Halifax, having regard to perishable products, which I understood the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce to mention as being a part of the new contract.
It was rumoured a few months ago that one of the companies tendering for this West Indian service desired to call at the port of Boston. The minister assures that that proposal did not meet with favour on the part of the Government; I am glad to have that assurance, although I am inclined to believe that the Government was very much impressed with the proposal at that time. I am glad however, that they have abandoned that idea, and I trust that they will not again return to it.
Representations were also made, according to the press, by business interests in Montreal, urging the establishment of a service between that port and the West Indies. I do not know what grounds were urged by the Montreal business interests in favour of the establishment of such a service, but I would be very much surprised if they could make out half a case in favour of their contention. I would say that for a great number of years it would be impossible for a steamship service between Montreal and the West Indies to obtain sufficient cargoes to pay any r.ppreciable portion of the cost.
A very foolish opinion obtains to some extent in Canada as to the volume of trade between Canada and the West Indies and the possible extension of this trade. It is true that we have a gross volume of import and export trade with the West Indies amounting to probably twelve or thirteen millions of dollars, but our ex-

ports to the islands mentioned in the convention with the West Indies, amount to only $2,145,000, and this consists largely of the natural products of this country. The export of fish alone amounts to about $800,000 a year, and the item next to that in amount is flour. All the articles produced or manufactured in the western provinces of Canada, including Ontario and Quebec, can be forwarded as cheaply to the West Indian islands, via Halifax or St. John as they could be from Montreal if there were a steamship service from that port direct. I also think that some of our Canadian business men are in error when they assume there is an opportunity for a great development of trade in manufactured products with the West Indies. Under this treaty Great Britain obtains the same preference as Canada. Several splendid lines of steamships ply between Great Britain and the West Indies, and a very considerable trade is done between the two countries, the freight rates being extremely light. In manufactured articles I see no possibility of Canadian manufacturers successfully competing with British manufacturers, in many lines at all events. It is quite true that a considerable part of the trade done by the United States with the West Indies might be captured by Canada. For instance, whereas we export to the West Indies about $700,000 worth of flour, the United States exports about $2,000,000 worth. Our exports of meats again are rather a negligible quantity, whereas from the United States the export of meats, amounts to considerably over $1,000,000. Respecting the last item. I do not think there would by any possibility of Canada obtaining that trade. However, the point I wish to make is that with a Canadian-West Indies steamship service operating from one Canadian port, all Canadian exporters would obtain just as great advantages as they would if there were a steamship service operating from Montreal.
I made a suggestion a moment ago, and I wish to amplify it very briefly, in favour of the proposition that in this service there should be one Canadian port of departure and call, and I say that it should be Halifax.
I say so because you can obtain companies to perform that service for a lesser sum of money from the port of Halifax than from the port of St. John. On looking over a return tabled at my instance, and referring to the tenders asked for some months ago for the West Indies steamship service I find that when tenders were first solicited, nobody except Messrs. Pickford and Black, of Halifax, put in any tender. There was a tender,
I think from some company in St. John, who apparently were not steamship owners or who were not in the steamship business, and their tender was disregarded by the Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
department. I find that Messrs. Pickford and Black made four distinct offers, and I wish to give them to the House for the purpose of showing what in their judgment would be the difference if they were permitted to operate from the port of Halifax as against a two-port service, from Halifax and St. John. The first offer was a twelve day service by four steamers of ten knots, the price being $225,000 per annum. From Halifax the price was $195,000. The second offer was a twelve-day service by four ships of twelve knots the price being $315,000. From the port of Halifax alone the price was $285,000. The third offer was a ten day service by five ships of ten knots. The price mentioned was $360,000, but from Halifax it was $324,000.

I think my hon. friend
will find that there is just $1,000 a trip extra for calling at the second port.

At any rate it is quite apparent that if any steamship company were permitted by the Government to use but one port of departure and call, the services could be performed for a considerably less sum of money annually by way of subsidy, while the efficiency would be increased. I do not wish to labour this point too much. I could show that this West Indies steamship service was begun at the port of Halifax, and that it could scarcely have had a beginning if it had not been for the Nova Scotia trade.

When was that? My
impression is it was started at St. John.

The trade between the Maritime provinces and the West Indies was established many years ago. I find that by far the greater proportion, of trade carried between the West Indies and Canada to-day originates at the port of Halifax. The amount of local trade originating at St. John is considerably less than at Halifax. It cannot be said that any western interests w-ouild suffer by reason of the selection of one port, because I assume that arrangements could readily be made between the steamship company and the railway companies for a satisfactory export rate. If that were done, as I have already said, a more efficient service could be given to the public, and one which would meet the passenger traffic demands. However, I do not want to be accused of approaching this matter in a sectional way. It is quite true that in the event of the selection of Halifax as the one port, some disadvantage might accrue to the business interests of St. John, and rather than have the combined two-port service, as it now exists, I think it would be preferable to have two separate services. At any rate, I think it will always be found that froln either St. John or Halifax, or from the combined ports, a West Indies steamship service can

always be obtained to meet Canadian requirements, and that there never will be any necessity for the establishment of another service from the p-ort of Montreal which could have only one ending, a division of the traffic with great injury to both services, and a very considerable lessening of the efficiency of both. I am very glad to learn from the minister that he has entered into an arrangement for a continued service. I think it is extremely unfortunate that the agreement is for a period of one year. It is hardly fair to the public or the contractor, and I think the department might as well make up its mind to enter into a long term contract and thus insure a better service and one which will better meet the Canadian requirements, than will a contract for such a short term as one year.

Mr. Speaker, before the representative of the other rival port speaks, I would like to make a few observations on the treaty now before us. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster), continued negotiations where they had been left off by his predecessor with the result that an arrangement has been made which at the very best can represent but a petty cash business for Canada. A people are only able to buy and sell in proportion to their earnings. A year and a half ago we refused to trade with 90,000,000 people whose earnings are probably greater per capita than those of any other people on this continent and to-day we are trying to make ourselves believe that Canada has made a fair bargain because we have negotiated a treaty with about 1,250,000 people living in the West Indian islands, where the head of a family earns from sixpence to a shilling and sixpence per day, and is satisfied if he works four days in the week. The West Indies is a country so rich in vegetation and favoured in climate that the native lies down under a tree and, if hungry, opens his mouth and the fruit falls into it. These are the people with whom we have completed this trade arrangement.
It has already been pointed out that our two chief items of trade under this arrangement are flour and fish. I am sure that we all must admire the unanimity with which our friends from the Maritime provinces agree with the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Perley), that either Halifax or St. John must be the starting point of the steamship service. I hope the members of the House will keep in mind, in connection with the flour business that, whatever may be the profits from the fish business, flour is handled at an average profit of about ten cents a barrel and sometimes less. Under this trade arrangement, while we have a preference of twenty-five cents a barrel, let us not
forget that we are coming into competition with the southern and southwestern states which are tributary to the Gulf of Mexico and the south Atlantic ports where they have vessels going out every second day, and sometimes every day. Let us not forget that the people of the West Indies are not buyers of the same quality of flour as the people of Canada or of the United States. At the very best they take but a moderate quality of flour. In our country we handle flour in barrels and bags. Down in the West Indies, flour is sold on the market place by women in cup measures of about a pint. It is wholesaled largely by Chinamen. We are coming into competition with millers who are tributary to the large corn-growing states which grow a quality of wheat which is not suited for northern and United States markets. While we have an advantage of twenty-five cents a barrel we must take care that we are not going to lose that advantage by establishing a freight rate which will give our United States competitors an advantage over us. The minister, some moments ago, said that he had not been offered any evidence that Halifax and St. John were at a disadvantage as against New York in the matter of freight rates. I would like to point out to the minister that the freight rate from Fort William to New York, via Buffalo is twenty-one and a half cents per hundred, and from Fort William to St John twenty-five cents. To Halifax the rate is twenty-seven cents, or two cents over that of St, John. From New York to the West Indian ports the rate is twenty-two cents per hundred pounds. That is the competition that we are up against in so far as the northern states and Canada are concerned. But, when you go down into the southwestern states, which have their outlet by way of the ports of the Gtuif of Mexico, you find another condition of affairs. While the people of New Yorlr complain that we are taking away a part of their business, let me explain that the business may be handled through a New York commission house, but the flour goes out from New Orleans or Galveston at the rate of seventeen and a half cents per hundred from New Orleans and twenty-two cents from Galveston to West Indian ports. If we cripple the flour trade by compelling it to pay freight from Montreal to St. John or Halifax, we are either going to drive the Canadian business down to New York or we are going to allow the United States people, who have that business now, to keep it. I would point out that while St. John and Halifax are splendid shipping points for fish, as far as flour and cereals are concerned, there are no mills of any capacity east of Montreal and it will be much cheaper for the western Ontario and Manitoba miller to route his stuff via New

York than to route it by way of St. John of Halifax.
I do not think it is.

Well, I have the quotations here. I would also call the attention of the House to other rates. Take, for instance, the second and fourth-class rate, which includes dairy products, textiles, &c.; the car load rate on dairy products over Montreal to St. John is thirty-six cents per hundred and to Halifax thirty-eight cents;, while on textiles, it is fifty-one cents to St. John and fifty-three cents to Halifax. These are not local, but export rates. The first and third class rate, which includes boots and shoes, is forty-four cents per hundred for carload shipments to St. John and fifty-eight cents for less than carload. The carload rate to Halifax is forty-five cents and the less than carload rate iar sixty cents. The fifth-class carload rate is twenty-nine cents to St. John and thirty cents to Halifax. I want to point out to the minister that he is proposing to hand over all this ' business to the Maritime provinces. While I admire the hon. member for standing up for Halifax, I must say that the general complaint is that the contractors for the service in the past have had a general monopoly of the Canadian business with the West Indian islands, and that when shippers applied for freight rates they were generally met with the reply that the space was all taken. It is said that, this firm which had a subsidy from the Government were both merchants and shippers, and in that way controlled the Canadian business with the West Indies.
What is that statement?

I am told they had a merchant business in connection with their steamship business. I have no practical evidence of that; I am simply voicing the complaint I have heard. Another complaint is that when a ship is going out and a man gets an order to put goods on that ship he must see to it that the goods arrive in time for the sailing, and the difficulty about that is that when a carload of goods starts from Toronto or any point West it can be traced as far as Montreal, but as soon as it gets on to the Intercolonial, it is lost track of entirely. You can go to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's offices and ask where a car is that left Winnipeg on a certain day and they will tell you where it was the day before yesterday, but as soon as that ear gets on the Intercolonial it is sometimes put on a siding and is lost track of, and the shipper who is sending the goods to Mr. ROBB.
Halifax for export is at the disadvantage that he cannot trace it and have it forwarded in time for the West Indian boat.
The hon. member foT Carleton (Mr. Carvel!) found fault with the Government because they did not give greater concession to the West Indian islands under this treaty. I am quite in sympathy with that view, the more so that had the Government treated the West Indian people more generously they perhaps might have obtained more from the West Indies in return. The people of the West Indian islands on account of the climate, find cotton the most satisfactory fabric for clothing, and cf the total imports of the different islands, about one-third to one-fifth are imports of cotton. I have been wondering why the Government, in these negotiations, neglected the cotton industry of Canada. I notice they took care of the boot and shoe people and allowed them to deal with the people of the West Indies who go practically barefooted. But, these people do require to wear clothing, and I submit the Government has lost a splendid opportunity to provide larger and wider markets for the cotton people of Canada. It seems to me it is a very unfair return to the cotton industry of this country, that in the very first treaty which this Government negotiated they neglected the very people who stood loyally by them during their fifteen years in opposition and who made every effort to get them back to power. I hope that if negotiations are re-opened, the Government will make an attempt to let our cotton industries share in the business of the West Indian islands. I trust the rival interests of the ports of Halifax and St. John will not have such influence with the Government when they give a larger steamship subsidy for .a tehm of years, as to cripple the trade of Canada.
1 am in sympathy with the hon. .member for Halifax when he says that the passenger business is comparatively of very little importance so far as the West Indian tourist trade is concerned, and that the freight business is the real business that we should ic-ok to. I submit that the Government should take into consideration the ports of Montreal ami Quebec, which are open for seven months in the year and which are most central for the export of the general products of this country affected by the treaty.

I wish to ask the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce if it would not be possible for these boats in running to St. John to stop at the port of Yarmouth. On their way to St. John these steamers pass and repass Yarmouth, which is at the mouth of the Bay of Fundy, so close to the shore that they can be seen with the naked eye. The de-

lay caused by their coming in and going out of Yarmouth would be very short, and I think they would get sufficient freight there to pay them for the stop. Many years ago the trade between Yarmouth and the West Indies amounted to a considerable sum, and in fact it was the largest business of the port, being carried on by brigantines and schooners. That is out of date now and our West Indian trade to-day is very small. A large quantity of molasses is used in the western part of the province and Yarmouth is the natural distributing centre for that trade. Occasionally a cargo of molasses comes to Yarmouth by sailing vessel, but it mostly goes to St. John and Halifax and has to be reshipped, which adds to the cost. I respectfully suggest to the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce that in making this new contract he should consider the proposal to have these boats stop at Yarmouth. As to the existing service, I have no doubt that Messrs. Pickford & Black give as good a service as they are' paid for but there is no doubt that the service has not been up-to-date. I trust that under the new contract a better class of boats will be put on. Two years ago a friend of mine went to the West Indies from Halifax and this ear he wanted to return with his family; ut his previous experience deterred him from taking that route, which no doubt applies to a great many who travel between Nova Scotia and the West Indian islands. I might mention that a twelve-knot boat is not a fast boat for this age, not much faster than the usual tramp freight boat, but with the increased subsidy which the Government is paying, and to which I have no objection, trust the service will be improved. I repeat that the time occupied by the stop at Yarmouth would be very short and if provision was made for the steamers calling there, it would help to revive the old time trade between Yarmouth and the West Indies.

There is some explanation due to
the House as to why the goods which are to be admitted under this preference, small though it is, are so limited. Why, for instance, are cottons not admitted at a preferential rate? That is a very important-point raised by my hon. friend from Huntingdon (Mr. Robb). It seems to me that, if there is one class of goods which would naturally attract the attention of anyone seeking to develop trade with the West Indies, it would be cotton goods which we so largely manufacture in Canada and for which there is such a demand in the West Indies. Yet there is not one word in the agreement with reference to that. What is the reason? It seems to me that the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce ought to tell us why the Minister of Trade and Commerce in negotiating this agreement has so limited the scope of the trade development which he has sought to bring about. I only mention this as one instance.
The more you examine this much lauded agreement, the less you will think of it. It really gives to the West Indies nothing whatever, and to Canada very little. As far as the exports from Canada to the West Indies are concerned, it gives only the small preference of twenty per cent of the duty which is imposed against other countries. That is not large enough to turn trade from United States channels into Canadian channels. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce really had in mind the negotiating of a treaty which would be of benefit to Canada and to the West Indies, he would have adopted a much more liberal policy. What has he given to the West Indies? It is no wonder they do not give us much because he gives them so little. He does not give them anything but what they have to-day and what they have enjoyed for fifteen years, namely, the British preference of thirty-three and one-third per cent without giving anything in return. Under this agreement they get the British preference of thirty-three and one-third per cent as long as that preference continues. If for any reason it should be discontinued, the preference which they get is reduced from thirty-three and one-third to twenty per cent. There is absolutely no advantage given to the British West Indies in this agreement over what other British colonies, which are not parties to it, now enjoy. It is rather a travesty on the agreement that we should have found, only a short time after the House was called upon to consider this Bill, that an Order in Council was passed extending the British preference to many of the British possessions. This is the list of countries to which the Government has extended the British preference by an Order in Council which was passed only a few months ago:
Switzerland, Basutoland, Beehuanaland Protectorate, Northern Rhodesia, Navasaland Protectorate, Unganda Protectorate, East Africa Protectorate, Protectorate of Northern Nigeria, 'Colony and Protectorate of iSouthern Nigeria, Gold Coast, Sierra Leonne, Gambia, Somaliland Protectorate, Federated Malay States,

I can understand extending the British preference to the Malay states, because this Government is linking itself up with the Malay states in other particulars

-British North Borneo, Mauritius -and Dependencies thereof, Seyshelles, St. Helena, Ascension, Friendly or Tonga Islands, Fiji, Falkland Islands, British Honduras.
I do not know why the Government has done that, but it is giving to many comparatively unknown portions of the world identically the same benefits as are being extended to the West Indian colonies, under what some are pleased to call an agree-

merit conferring great benefits upon oui brethren there.
The list of articles which we can send to the West Indies under this twenty per cent preference is also exceedingly limited in its extent.
With regard to the steamship service, I would like to ask the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce whether the subsidy to the steamship lines is to be paid entirely by Canada, or whether any part if it is to be . paid by the British West Indies.
The entire subsidy is to be paid by Canada. There is a clause in the ontract which says that the contractors shall not receive any subsidy from the West Indies.

Has the arrangement,
which was approved by the commissioners, that there should be a service from Halifax all the year round and a service between Montreal and St. John and the West Indies, to which the British Government was to contribute, been abandoned?

The British Government have definitely decided, and have so communicated to this Government, that they will not consider paying any portion of a subsidy for a service between Canada and the West Indies. The British subsidy was discontinued about two years ago. We asked them if they would care to consider giving some help towards this service, and they replied that they did not see their way to do so.

So that it is a matter entirely for Canada to deal with, in so far as the steamship subsidy is concerned.
The acting minister, I presume with the view of showing that there was no necessity for the amendment moved by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), has made the statement that the Government had never thought of allowing subsidized steamers to go to Boston. It is within my own knowledge that not many months ago, the boards of trade of St. John and Halifax-St. John at all events, and I was informed that the same was true of Halifax-were requested to send delegates to Ottawa for a consultation in regard to the service. After they came here and had interviews with the Minister of Trade and Commerce and possibly with other members of the Government, they returned home and one of the most influential delegates from St. John gave an interview in the papers in which he made the positive announcement that the Government had decided to give the subsidy to a steamship line which intended to make Boston a port of call. That was announced publicly by this delegate and apparently with all the authority which would be attached to the position of a delegate who had come to Ottawa for the purpose of consulting the Government at its request.
Mr. PUGSLEY.
I am, however, very glad to have the positive assurance of the minister that the contract provides against these steamers calling at an American port. We fought out that question in St. John many years ago, and the principle was pretty well established that it was in the interest of Canada that no subsidized steamers should be allowed to call at ports in the United States. I am disappointed that the minister has not given us assurance that in the immediate future the provisions of the treaty under which the preference is to be allowed only upon goods coming direct from the West Indies to Canadian seaports may be brought into operation. That provision is to be brought into operation by Order in Council. Is it intended that the present arrangement shall go on indefinitely and that goods coming through the ports of Portland, Boston, and New York, to points in Ontario and Quebec and the other Provinces shall enjoy the same advantage as though coming direct through Canadian ports? Surely when we are taking this new departure, making arrangements with the West Indies-our West Indian brothers being satisfied that the preference shall be restricted to goods coming direct-this is the time when we should take a determined stand and make a patriotic effort to turn the trade into Canadian channels; this is the time to act vigorously; this is the time to make sacrifices by giving larger steamship subsidies if necessary to bring the goods to Canadian ports. But, instead of that, it is contemplated that the imports from the West Indies shall still be made through American ports and that no advantage shall be given on goods brought through Canadian ports. This is to go on indefinitely and Canada is not to get the benefit she might get if this preference were limited to goods coming through Canadian ports. I know that there are some importers in Ontario and the West who say that they ought to be allowed to get their goods through American ports if they wish to do so, and that no preference should be given to the Canadian ports. But I think that is not the view of the great majority of the people of Canada. In order to build up this country it is necessary, owing to the fact that these great ports of Boston and New York are nearer to Canadian commercial centres than are the ports of the St. Lawrence and the maritime provinces, that some sacrifices should be made to build up the trade through Canadian channels. Whenever the people of Canada have been appealed to, they have taken strong patriotic ground, and have been willing to make sacrifices in order to bring about such a result. If the Government had said at once to the stea.rn.ship owners and to the railways companies such as the

Grand Trunk railway and the Canadian Pacific railway who might be disposed to engage in the steamship business: 'Now, it is our intention to avail ourselves of the provisions contained in this agreement and to provide that the preference shall only be given to goods going direct from the West Indies through Canadian ports, and in order to obtain that object we are willing to give larger subsidies to the steamship line; 1 I believe that they would have been able to secure the establishment of such a line. Because we know that if, in addition to a first-class steamship service, there is a preference on goods, the effect must be to enlarge the irrofits through Canadian ports to which these steamships would come, and so in a few years, to make the steamship business more profitable than it can be so long as the bulk of our goods come from the West Indies into American ports. But, as I have said, we have no hope, so far as any statement of the Government is concerned, that in the near future this preference is to be limited to goods coming through Canadian ports. The view 1 have expressed now with regard to the West Indian agreement, I hold also with regard to the preference with Great Britain. I believe that the Government should take a firm stand and make the announcement that at a certain time in the near future, the British preference will be limited to goods brought direct through Canadian ports. We should take a firm, patriotic stand, and say we are determined, as far as it can be done by preferential tariffs or steamship subsidy, that the trade shall be brought to Canadian ports.
Now, a word with regard to a very interesting statement of my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) as to the advantages which would accrue from making Halifax the one port for import and export from and to the West Indies. I do not think my hon. friend has demonstrated very clearly that Halifax has any very great advantage over ports in New Brunswick in this particular. I could name two or three ports in New Brunswick which would have considerable advantage, in my judgment, over the port of Halifax, or at least would be at no disadvantage as compared with that port. There is the port of St. John, the port of L'Etang, and the poit of St. Andrews, all of which are very much nearer Canadian centers, so far as the railway haul is concerned, than the port of Halifax. And it must never be forgotten that, while it is of enormous advantage to have a natural harbour like the harbour of Halifax, we can always create a harbour if necessary. The ability of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works to utilize modern. engineering skill and appliances would give a harbour any depth of water
you like or any protection you like in places where, perhaps, there are not the natural advantages; but you can never annihilate distance. And so it will always be an advantage to a port that the rail haul is less than from some other port that may have other advantages. Therefore, the fact that St. John and other ports in New Brunswick are nearer the commercial centres than is Halifax will always be to a certain extent in favour of those ports. I do not wish to say a word against the port of Halifax, as a very considerable West Indian business can be done through that port. But what I do wish to contend against is the continuance of the policy of having steamers call at both ports. With the remarks my hon. friend made in that respect, I entirely agree. But the remedy is not to take out either St. John or Halifax. The remedy is to give an independent service to each port-one week or fortnight to Halifax and the next week or fortnight to St. John; but let each service be a direct and independent service. In that way, you would give far greater satisfaction and would be able to do a very much better business. It is the trip around the Nova Scotia coast from St. John to Halifax or Halifax to St. John that is the great handicap. The same is true of the Atlantic liners. If I had my way, I would divide the steamers into classes, let one class call at Halifax, direct call, and depart for Great Britain direct from Halifax, not making a call at the port of St. John. I would let the other class of steamers go direct to St. John and depart direct from St. John. There is no reason in the world why that should not be done, and in that way we would enable the people to develop a freight and passenger traffic through each of these ports.

Upon what principle
of freedom of trade does my hon. friend base his argument in favour of legislative interference?

I was not aware that
my hon. friend belonged to a party strongly in favour of freedom of trade. I do not sufficiently understand my hon. friend's question to reply with any advantage to him, but I do think it is the duty of public men in a country situated as Canada is to endeavour, by legislation and by subsidies, to turn Canadian trade into Canadian channels. At the time of Confederation, Portland, in the state of Maine, was the winter port of Canada. We had no railway connection between Montreal and St. John and Montreal and Halifax, and the Grand Trunk was extended to Portland with a view to giving to Canada a winter outlet. But the efforts of public men were turned in the direction of creating Canadian winter ports. This has cost a good

deal of money and has required a great deal of effort, but everyone will admit that the country has been fairly successful in that direction. I desire to move the following as am amendment or addition to that proposed by my hon. friend the hon. member for Canleton (Mr. Carveil).
And also to amend the same by inserting the following as sub-section 2 to section 3 thereof:
2. Provided that if and whenever, during the term of said agreement, the said colonies shall agree with the Government of Canada to admit into any of the said respective colonies the goods enumerated in schedule A to said agreement, being the produce or manufacture of Canada, at rates of customs duties not exceeding fifty per cent of the duties imposed in the colony on similar goods when imported from any foreign country, the goods enumerated in schedule B being the produce or manufacture of any of the colonies, parties thereto, when such goods are imported direct from any of the said colonies, shall, so long as said agreement as so midified remains in force, be admitted into Canada free of customs duties.
The effect of this sub-amendment would be to place upon the statute books a standing offer to these West Indian colonies that whenever they increase their preference to fifty per cent, all the goods enumerated in schedule B shall come into Canada free of duty. These goods are all enumerated in schedule B, and instead of some of them, as at present, coming in free, and being subject to duty, they would all come in free. I think that in considering this agreement we are apt to forget the interests of the consumer. We ask ourselves what the West Indies is giving to Canada and what Canada is giving to the West Indies, but we do not ask ourselves what benefit the consumer of Canada gets from this arrangement. I think it is just as important as the matter of finding a market for our manufacturers and our producers. Here was an opportunity for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to say to our friends of the. British West Indies: * Give us not a mere preference of twenty per cent, which will not have any material effect, but give us a substantial preference of fifty per cent, and we will allow the goods mentioned in this schedule to come into Canada free of duty.' Here was a splendid opportunity to confer a substantial benefit upon the West Indies and at the same time to confer a substantial benefit upon the consumers of Canada. Why should we not do that? Today we have such a revenue that we surely do not need to increase it. The hon. the Minister of Customs said yesterday that during the year ending March 31, last, the customs revenue alone amounted to $115,000,000. What does that mean? It means that the consumers-the workingmen of Canada, the farmers, the miners, the fishermen, the millions of hard-working people of
Mr. PUGSLEY
Canada-have been obliged to put their hands in their pockets and pay in taxes this enormous amount of money. Anyone who observed the satisfied air of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs when it was stated that this huge amount was collected in customs duties might have thought that by means of some magic wand they were bringing this great sum of money into the treasury, and that in some way they were entitled to credit for its receipt. But one must not forget that the people of Canada are paying this large amount of money; in customs revenue alone for every mail, woman and child in this country there was paid in taxes last year the sum of $14. And yet the Government neglected the opportunity of providing for the free admission of West Indian products into the country-products which do not compete or unduly compete with those of Canada-and for the sake of getting a mere pittance by reason of the trade of our people with the West Indies, they have made this arrangement whereby they give them in return nothing whatever beyond what they have enjoyed for ,Jhe past fifteen years. What are the products enumerated in schedule B? Let me enumerate them, and ask hon. gentlemen why they should not come in free; why that offer should not have been made to the West Indies. Listen to this list:
Sugar, molasses and syrups; shredded sugar eane; fresh fruits of all kinds; cocoanuts; asphalt and manjak; coffee; cotton, raw, cotton seed and cotton seed meal; cotton seed oil; rice, uncleaned, rice cleaned, and rice flour and rice meal, and rice bran; petroleum, crude; oils, coal and kerosene, distilled, purified, or refined petroleum; copra and eo-cocanut oil; rubber, raw and batata; bulbs; logwood and logwood extract; annatto; turtle shell, unmanufactured; ginger, nutmegs, and spices, unground; arrowroot; salt; sponges; vegetables, fresh, of all kinds; tapioca and cassava; tapioca and cassava flour; honey and beeswax; oils, essential, including bay oil and otto of limes; tamarinds, fresh or preserved; cattle food containing molasses; peanuts and kola nuts; diamonds, uncut; timber or lumber of wood not further manufactured than sawn or split; timber or lumber of wood, dressed; vanilla beans; bay leaves; papaine; lime juice, fruit syrups and fruit juices, non-alcoholic.
I am aware that, aside from this arrangement, some of these products come in free of duty. But, in consideration of getting a substantial preference in the markets of the West Indies, why should not the Government have agreed that all those articles should come into Canada free of duty, thus, as I have said, securing greater benefit in the West Indian markets, and at the same time lightening the burden of taxation on the consuming public of Canada. So far from looking towards the benefit of the consumer, the Government has actually raised the duty on one or two articles of

consumption, so far as other countries are concerned, and in that way they are giving a preference to the British West Indies. But it seems to me that that was a narrow position to take, and that the minister ought to have taken a broad view, and ought to have dealt in a broad and generous spirit with these West Indian colonies. The Government ought to have given them a substantial benefit by admitting their goods free of duty into Canada, and in that way induce the Islands to give to Canada a substantial benefit in the way of preference in their markets. We ought to have protected the interests of the consumer. We talk about our great and growing revenue as if that were something to be proud of. I saw it stated in the newspapers that the Minister of Finance will bring down his budget in a few days and will say that Canada is to-day enjoying the most prosperous year in her history. That is not true, Sir. It is true that the Government is wringing a greater amount of money from the pockets of the people of this country than any government ever did before, but the condition of affairs in Canada to-day is not one which ought to be satisfactory to the Government. The financial condition in Canada to-day is serious, but it is not different from what might be expected when the imports are so enormous compared with the exports. No country can continue to be prosperous so long as its imports are so vastly greater than its exports. Here was a small opportunity, not a, large one I admit, for the Government to deal with the question of the increase of our exports in a generous spirit, and at the same time to reduce the tariff on goods from the West Indies, thus lightening the taxation of our own people. Instead of doing that, all they seem to have had in view was to make a sort of picayune arrangement with our brethren in the West Indies which we could boast of, but which would confer no substantial benefit, either upon the people of Canada, or upon the people of the West Indies.

speechtext:
I do not rise so much
for the purpose of discussing the amendment to the amendment originally proposed by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) as for the purpose of saying a few words on the question which was presented to the House this afternoon in a very reasonable way by my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvel!), in the amendment which he proposed. My hon. friend from St. John has experienced a very sudden change of heart, even for him, when he comes to the conclusion that within the period which elapsed between the speech of my hon. friend from Carleton and his own remarks, the amendment which he had seconded ought itself to be amended. However, I am not disposed to dwell upon that, nor do I intend to touch very much on what my hon. friend from St. John said except in one or two respects.
My hon. friend has desired us to take a very firm and patriotic stand upon the preference to the British West Indies, and I gather from his remarks that the only firm and patriotic stand that can be taken, according to his conception, is to provide that the preference shall not have effect unless goods are shipped through Canadian ports. It seems to me remarkable that for fifteen years my hon. friend was never conscious that that, firm and patriotic stand was one which should have had the consideration of the late Government, for during the years from 1908 to 1911, it would have been perfectly possible for the Government, of which for many years he was a member, to have taken that particular stand, to the importance of which he seems to have suddenly awakened this afternoon. It would have been well for my hon. friend to have explained to the House why it was that the importance of such a course so suddently dawned upon him, and why, to a man of his remarkably acute mentality, such a plain conception as he regards it to-day, should never have presented itself before.
My hon. friend also deplored the existence of surpluses in this country. But I have seen him year after year vigorously applaud in this House when the predecessor of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance was announcing those very surpluses. _ No one was more active than my hon. friend in giving .his acquiescence to that condition of affairs in those days, although now he explains that such a condition outrages every fine feeling which he possesses. It occurs to me that during the period of fifteen years, to which I have alluded, and certainly in the ten years during which my hon. friend was a member of the late Government, it would have been perfectly proper JEor him to have urged upon the then Minister of Finance
I have a letter from an importer in St. John in which he states that the rate on scrap iron to St. John is nearly double what it is to New York.

As to the service furnished by Messrs. Pickford & Black, I agree entirely with what the bon. members for Halifax and Carleton have said. For the past six or eight years the contract with Messrs. I hope this service will give more satisfaction than it has in the past.
My hon. friend from Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) was rather despondent as _ to the possibility of developing trade with the British West Indies. I would point out to him, for example, that the export in cereals from Canada to the West Indies, has, developed very much of recent years. In 1908 Canada exported wheat flour to the British West Indies to the value of 8334,948, and in 1912 we exported $1,595,000 worth, or nearly 400 per cent more. I would not be at all so pessimistic as the hon. gentleman as to the possibilities of this trade; I think we may look forward to the trade of Canada with the West Indies developing not only in cereals but in fish and various articles of agricultural produce. Sir William Van Horne, who is thoroughly familiar with the conditions in the British West Indies and the other West Indian islands, is of the opinion that for agricultural produce which can be raised in abundance in the maritime provinces and other parts of Canada, there is a much better market in the West Indies than we have at present any idea of. I not only hope but believe that our trade with the West Indies will, in the near future, develop very greatly indeed; I trust the service which is now being provided, and even a better service in the
Mr. WHITE (Minister of Finance! [DOT] When I rose at six o'clock to speak on the third reading of the Bill vaadating the agreement between the Government and the West Indian colonies, I was under the impression that no other hon. gentleman opposite desired to speak. I was informed subsequently that my non. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and possibly some others desired to speak, so I am very glad to yield the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to support the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley). In doing so, I wish with all respect to refer to the criticism of tiie hon member and of _his amendment by the right hon. the Premier. If I remember correctly, that criticism was that the hon. member for St. John was not eligible to discuss the desirability of reducing the cost to the consumer and at the same time of reducing the burden of taxation on the citizen because, during the term of office of the Government of which he was a mem ter, means had not been taken such as he suggested should he taken on this occasion. This is a line of argument that my right hon. friend invariably uses. In my humble judgment, it is invariably futile and ineffective as argument. If our appreciation of our business is that we are' sent here to consider what the governments of years ago did, I do not think it is the appreciation of the people who sent us here. Our business here is to deal with questions, as they exist and as they have arisen, on their merits. The question of what somebody did on a presumably similar occasion at some past date is not really to the point.

My hon. friend perhaps
misunderstood me. I said that I was not going to deal with that phase of the hon. gentleman's speech; that it would be dealt with later on by the hon. Minister of Finance. I simply alluded to it in passing, saying that these ideas had not occurred to him in past years.

That is exactly what I am dealing with. If the right hon. the Premier meant his remarks as criticism, and I take
Mr. BORDEN.

it that is what he did mean, I am arguing that his contention was not well based.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I was merely calling attention to a phenomenon.

I am taking the liberty
of calling attention to the fact, which is known to hon. members, that the Premier and his colleagues, on every occasion when any question arises as to a matter of administration or policy on their part, answer that the Government of some previous day had taken similar or somewhat similar action. This is just as good an occasion as any for dealing with that particular line of argument. The statement that circumstances are similar to-day is no evidence whatever that they are similar. It is in the nature of things that conditions have changed as time has passed. Surely there is a vast difference between a condition that arises under the circumstances of a trade treaty being negotiated and circumstances that existed without any such consideration. When the Government of the day undertakes to negotiate a trade treaty and claims before the public great credit for doing so, then surely is the time for it to defend the merits of that agreement: and the question of previous conditions or previous actions by anybody else is no defence whatever. Am I going too far when I say that, when no defence is offered, when the only defence that is pretended is an attack upon previous actions, the logic of the case is that no defence is possible, and that as a matter of fact, when the treaty is criticised in the terms of the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. John, the Government has nothing whatever to say in defence of its treaty or of the position which it has taken?
Now, I have no immediate interest in this particular treaty; but as a member of this House I have a veTy deep interest in the principles which are involved in it; and it is to those principles that I wish to draw the attention of the House. This is called a reciprocity treaty, and it expresses, I have no doubt, the ideas of this Government in regard to reciprocity. If it can be taken as doing so, I want to express my dissatisfaction with the views of the Government in that regard. It will be remembered that the attempt to carry into effect the reciprocity arrangement between Canada and the United States met with very strong and successful criticisms at the hands of some of our friends on the other side who now occupy the treasury benches. That arrangement for reciprocity with the United States expressed Liberal principles with regard to reciprocity. The principles of Liberalism as manifested in the reciprocity arrangement with the United States involved a reduction in the cost to the consumer; that is to say, food
278J
products, speaking at large, were made free of duty on both sides of the line. By the application of that treaty the burden of taxation would have been correspondingly reduced. Therefore the principle of the treaty of reciprocity as embodied in the action of the Liberal Government meant reduced taxation and free trade in food, reducing at once the cost of living and the burden of taxation. I dwell on that point for a moment because my right hon. friend in his criticism of my hon. friend from St. John suggested that that hon. gentleman, or the Government of which he was a member, had done nothing to reduce the burden of taxation upon the people of Canada. The Government of which the hon. member for St. John was a member went out of power, let it be distinctly understood, on a question of the reduction of the taxation on the people of this country. They went out of power on the question of reducing the cost of living and the burden of taxation. It is because they embodied that principle in legislation and stood by that principle in this House and before the country that they are in opposition to-day; it is because of that that our friends opposite are in office to-day. And, speaking as one of that party which has upheld that principle, and which went out of office because of it, I want to say on my own behalf-and I believe I speak for my colleagues on this side of the House-we have absolutely nothing to regret in the advocacy of the principle that we stood for.
Now, what is the principle embodied in the treaty before the House? If I were to undertake to describe the merits of this treaty, and the principles involved as they appear to my mind, I am afraid I should be ruled out of order. But first of all we find this principle, that by schedule (c) of the agreement the cost of living to the Canadian consumer is specifically increased. It is true, the amount is not much, but the principle is there, and it is a leading feature of this trade arrangement. By schedule (a) the cost of living is not reduced to the Canadian consumer. I do not suppose that the people of Canada realize that to-day the Canadian consumer enjoys the benefit of a preference of thirty-three and one-third per cent, speaking generally, on goods imported into Canada from the West Indies. And this remarkable reciprocity treaty provides for a preference of twenty per cent-that is, this grave and- and I was going to say reverend, but I will not say that-this grave and supposedly earnest Parliament is ratifying to-day in the name of reciprocity of trade an arrangement which provides for less preference on goods coming from the West Indies than actually exists at the present time. I was sure, that you, Mr. Speaker, would rule me out of order if I expressed my opinion of such a position, but I will risk this so far

as to say that, to speak of this as a trade arrangement or as a reciprocity arrangement, having'in mind the idea of reducing the cost of living to the consumer, is simply humbugging the people, or an attempt to humbug the people; neither more nor less. If Canada is to increase the cost of living in order to get this treaty and does not in any case decrease the cost of living by these provisions, we must receive the benefit that we are going to receive from it through the expansion of trade we shall get under its terms. Our trade is to get a preference in the markets of the West Indies. So, if the consumers of Canada do not get anything by a reduction of the cost of living, the producers of Canada are expecting to gain something because of the preference we receive in the markets of the West Indies.
For what purpose are we negotiating this treaty unless it is to secure a market in the West Indies? I have already shown that it is of no benefit to the Canadian consumer; unless, therefore, it is a benefit to the Canadian producer it is of no benefit at all. Why do we want a trade treaty with the West Indies? Because their trade has already been captured by the United States. For one reason or another, whether it be greater proximity, better transportation, or greater enterprise, the trade of the West Indies desired by Canada is to-day held by the United States, and the whole purpose of this treaty, if it has any purpose, is to enable Canada to get that trade with the West Indies which to-day is being held and carried on by the United States. Are we going to get that trade by reason of a twenty per cent preference for our goods in the West Indian markets? We have found by experience that we have to give the West Indies a thirty-three and one-third per cent preference in our markets, or no good to them will result; yet we expect to get a benefit in their markets because of a twenty per cent preference, against the fact that this trade is all absolutely held by the commercial interests of the United States. It is absurd on the face of it. Unless we are to have a greater preference than twenty per cent we cannot expect to overcome the advantage that the dealers of the United States have to-day by reason of transportation facilities and proximity. If the islands of the West Indies had a high tariff, a reduction of twenty per cent might be of some value, but everybody knows that the West Indian islands have low tariffs, and the lower the tariff the smaller the value of a trifling reduction. Assuming that the duty on a barrel of flour is $1, a twenty per cent reduction would make the duty eighty cents; if the duty were $5, a reduction of twenty per cent would be an important one. The lower the duty the smaller the value of a preference, and of course the smaller the preference, the less the value. We are Mr. OLIVER.
entering into a treaty with the West Indies under which we give no benefit to our consumers, and by which we hope to benefit our producers by a reduction of twenty per cent on a tariff that is already very low, as against the competition of the people who at the present time control the market, and who have the facilities for controlling it in the future.
Under these circumstances, can any person who favours reduced cost of living and reduction of taxation do other than support the amendment of the hon. member for St. John, which declares that upon the West Indies giving us a fifty per cent reduction we will give them free entry into our markets for their products? Certainly by that means we would reduce the cost to our consumers, and we might reasonably expect to confer some benefit upon our producers in the increase of trade by the substantial cut of fifty per cent in the tariff of the West Indies. If we are not to confer any benefit upon either our consumers or our producers, why put ourselves before the world as negotiating a treaty which has no value?
Following upon this treaty is an arrangement whereby Canada is to provide better steamship accommodation between this country and the West Indies. It strikes me that the acquiring of a more efficient steamship accommodation, lower rates and better transportation, is the true method of securing trade as between Canada and the West Indies; but if we are to depend on improved steamship communication, why go through the farce of negotiating a treaty, professing to the people of Canada that a reciprocity agreement has been negotiated when, as a matter of fact, that treaty under no circumstances can benefit either the consumer or the producer of Canada? if that is merely an excuse for doubling the amount of the steamship subsidy without increasing the efficiency of the service, I must say that the whole transaction is one that does not appeal to me either as economic or advantageous; neither does it appear to be one that will tend to the progress or welfare of Canada or to the increase of trade between this country and the islands of the West Indies. It would have been better for the Government to have passed a pious resolution that there ought to be increased taade with the West Indies, and let the matter go at that. It would have cost less and would probably have been productive of as good results. I wish to support the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. John, the terms of which call for a substantial reduction in the cost of living to the consumer and hold out a reasonable prospect of increasing and widening the market to the Canadian producer.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have had a delightful little lecture from my hon. friend the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) as to the impropriety of the Prime Minister's references to the advocacy on the part of my hon. friend from St. John, when the previous Government was in power of different opinions from what he advocates here to-day. My hon. friend from Edmonton has stated that we should deal with questions as they are, and not with the policy that hon. gentlemen may have advocated some time ago. He says, using his own words, that what the previous Government did under circumstances said to be similar is not to the point, and he insists that all questions of this kind should be dealt with on their merits. I entirely agree with my hon. friend that they should be dealt with on their merits, and I can assure him that this particular amendment will be dealt with by myself, entirely, I hope, on its merits. But my hon. friend misses the view that some of us have on this side of the House, that when hon. gentlemen opposite oppose measures that we are introducing, it is a proper method of testing their consistency to call attention to the fact that they took a diametrically opposite view when they were in power, a comparatively short time ago. It is not that we decline to discuss these matters on their merits, but that we desire to point out the inconsistency of hon. gentlemen opposite in opposing them. That is the reason why my right hon. friend the Prime Minister referred to the position taken previously by tne hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) with regard to a matter which I shall mention a little later. My hon. friend from Edmonton has been inconsistent in many ways in his political career. I understand that a few years ago he was a free trader.
I have always been a protectionist.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He is a protectionist today and he belonged to a protectionist government.
I believe in protecting the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let us understand what
my hon. friend means, because I am advised ihat he was a free trader, and he was afterwards a member of a protectionist government. Is that correct, or not?
It is not correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no question that
the late Government was a protectionist government, is there?
I think there is very great question. My hon. friend will admit thai the late Government went out on a policy of ducing the tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let us see how far my
hon. friend is correct in that. He says it was not a protectionist government in any degree at all and that it went out on a free trade issue. Let me read a few remarks of my predecessor, the late Minister of Finance whom he followed, from his budget speech of 1909. I happen to have them here:
Those who refine sugar in all forms, the eastern refiners, and those on the Pacific coast, will import their raw sugar under the preferential tariff, paying only the preferential rates, and the duty on the British refined sugar is adjusted accordingly, so that our refiners may have what is deemed a moderate degree of protection.
So if my hon. friend did not know it, there is no doubt at all that the late Finance Minister believed in a moderate degree of protection. I do not suppose that anybody ever heard my hon. friend protest in this House against the views held by the late Minister of Finance with regard to tariff matters. So I say it is in order to test the consistency of hon. gentlemen opposite, when they rise in their places and oppose measures as my hon. friend does, that we recall what they did on other occasions when they happened to be^on this side of the House.
Then my hon. friend has also become an economist. He has suddenly become possessed of views of economy that he did not hold some years ago, and which the Government to which he belonged did not hold. I have heard a great deal of criticism of hon. gentlemen when they were in power, but I never heard that they were commended particularly for the economy which my hon. friend now puts forward as the most desirable thing imaginable in government policy. He will hardly say that they were economical in connection with the construction of the National Transcontinental railway from Winnipeg to Moncton, which cost about three times what it was originally estimated to cost. I am merely calling attention to this to test his consistency by referring to statements which he, or other hon. gentlemen opposite, made on previous occasions, and not with the view of avoiding discussion of these questions upon their merits. My hon. friend has referred to reciprocity. 1 have a sort of tacit agreement with my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) that we should not discuss the question of reciprocity any more than we are absolutely obliged to.

I have not
understood that agreement to exist, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I accept entirely what my hon. friend from Red Deer has said, from his standpoint, but at any rate I have an understanding on my part that I will not discuss it any more than is necessary.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Because, as I said before, it is a dead issue, and we do not like to say anything but what is good of the dead. My hon. friend from Edmonton has said that he has nothing to regret in his advocacy of reciprocity. He has said that so often that I think sometimes of Shake' speare's line, slightly changed: ' He doth protest too much.' I think perhaps he does sometimes regret his advocacy of it, unconsciously, because, of course, I do not believe he is making a mis-statement when he says that lie has not regretted it. My hon. friend has referred to the cost of living, and one of his strong points against this agreement is that he says we are increasing the cost of living. Look at schedule ' C ' he says, you are increasing the cost of living to the people of Canada. One of the principal items in schedule ' C ' is fresh limes. We are giving to the West Indies a preference of not less than 10 per cent ad valorem on limes.
