I do not know how the cost of living is going to be increased under that item, unless in connection with gin rickeys. It seems that limes are used-in the concoction of what we call gin rickeys, but I do not think my hon. friend from Edmonton is specially interested in fancy drinks, and therefore I do not believe that the cost of living is going to be increased to him by reason of that item.
So much for my hon. friend from Edmonton, and now I come to the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). I shall say nothing on the amendment of my hon. friend from Carle-ton (Mr. Carvell) except that we are entirely in accord that it is extremely desirable that the best steamship facilities possible should be provided in connection with the trade between Canada and the West Indies, and especially in view of the completion of the agreement which we have now under consideration. The matter has been very fully discussed this afternoon, aind I do not think I can add anything to the arguments which have been advanced by my hon. friend the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Perley) and my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. With regard to the amendment of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), it is a very curious thing that hon. gentlemen opposite should take such diverse views as to the character and nature of this agreement. My hon. friend from Carleton, New Brunswick, said that it was a niggardly agreement, that we do not give enough to the West Indian colonies. On the other hand my hon. friend from St. John complains that we do not secure the admission under preferential rates of more articles to the West Indian colonies. In other words my hon.
Mr. WHITE (Leeds*
friend from St. John takes the view that we do not get enough, and my hon. friend from Carleton, New Brunswick, takes the view that we do not give enough. It is fairly difficult to please all our hon. friends opposite in the views that they take in regard to this matter. The hon. member for St. John is disposed to regard this agreement from a very hard, commercial standpoint. There was a very great deal of goodwill in connection with the negotiation of this agreement on both sides, and let me commend to my hon. friend the example of my predecessor, the Hon. Mr. Fielding, in dealing with this question of the British preference and its extension to the British West Indies. Mr. Fielding, and the Government of which he was a member, extended the benefits of the British preference to the British West Indies without getting anything whatsoever in return and it was properly counted to them for righteousness in the Empire.

That was reducing the
tariff, was it not ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was reducing the tariff, but my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has not followed my argument. This afternoon the agreement has been subjected to criticism because, on the one hand, Canada did not obtain a preference on certain articles not included in schedule 'A' in the West Indian market, and I am pointing out that for many years the late Government, of which both my hon. friends were distinguished members, extended the British preference to the West-Indies without getting any consideration at all, and that act was imputed to them for righteousness. In that they showed that they were not disposed to look at this matter in the hard, commercial way that the hon. member for St. John was looking at it this afternoon. They said they would like to assist the British West Indies and they felt a sense of obligation towards them having regard to the languishing condition of the trade in the colonies ten or twelve years ago-I think in 1898 and 1899. The result which followed was an increased demand in the markets of Canada for products of the West Indies, and particularly sugar. This matter had never been approached by the two parties, the Canadian Government and the West Indian colonies, in any hard, commercial way. We sat down together at the convention in Ottawa in April last in no huckstering spirit, but in a very friendly fashion, all as members of the same great family, with the view of -reaching an agreement which would be beneficial from the standpoint of mutual trade in both countries and also from the standpoint of Imperial unity and solidarity. I cheerfully testify that I never met a more genial and agreeable lot of men in my life than the

representatives of the West Indian colonies. I cannot imagine anything more pleasant and agreeable than our convention, and both the representatives of Canada and the British West Indies were entirely satisfied at its conclusion.
The only regret I have heard expressed, the only criticism that I have heard made of this agreement, has been from a few hon. gentlemen opposite this afternoon and previously in connection with the discussion of this Bill in the House. My hon. friend from St. John said: What did we give to the British West Indies more than they had before ? He said that they had the benefit of the British preference. With all due respect and with a great regard for the industry of my hon. friend from St. John, I do not believe that he has gone into this question as thoroughly as he should have. I do not blame him very much because, to have gone into it, he should have read over all the proceedings of the Imperial Commission and the proceedings of the convention here, and he should have posted himself with regard to the sugar tariff of Canada. That he has not done, as I propose to show very conclusively before I conclude. If he had consulted with the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) he would have been in a better position to deal with this question in connection with the amendment which he has proposed; in fact, I think that, if he had consulted with the hon. junior member for Halifax, in all probability he would not have moved the amendment at all. Let me say to the hon. member for St. John that my predecessor, Mr. Fielding, under circumstances which I shall detail at length a little later on in the course of my remarks, gave to the sugar refineries of Canada a twenty per cent preferential rate upon foreign grown raw sugar. The hon. gentleman will observe by the agreement that the privilege has been terminated; in other words, that the British West Indies obtain an exclusive preferential market in Canada for their raw sugar and sugar is the commodity in which they are principally interested. Nine-tenths of the imports into Canada from the British West Indies are composed of sugar and the principal advantage which the West Indies were desirous of obtaining was the advantage of an exclusive market in Canada at a preferential rate as against all non-British raw sugar.
Does that mean that in addition to the items included in schedule 'C' we are to have an increase in the cost of sugar as the result of this treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would be a very long discussion at the present stage which would be necessary to make my hon.
friend acquainted with the intricacies of the sugar tariff and with all due respect I do not propose to discuss that question tonight. If my hon. friend will look at the provisions of the Bill-I think it is section 3-he will see what is there provided and I shall deal with it a little later on. I shall try not to overlook the point. As I have pointed out to my hon. friend from St. John, the object of the British West Indian colonies was to obtain a preference in the growing market of Canada for their raw sugar as opposed to non-British or foreign raw sugar and as a result of that it is provided that the so-called twenty per cent privilege of the refiners of Canada shall be taken away by tariff change. In addition to that my hon. friend knows that there was a certain privilege which comes to an end at the end of next year to the beet sugar refiners of Canada. That privilege we have agreed not to renew by the express terms of the trade agreement so that there is a very decided advantage to the British West Indian colonies in that agreement as it now stands over and above the position they enjoyed before the agreement was negotiated. The hon. members for St. John and Edmonton have both referred to the twenty per cent preference, but I would call attention

Before the minister departs from this, would he tell me whether or not he would consider it desirable to make sugar free and whether or not there is any difficulty about it for the reason that he has mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Before I conclude I will
show my hon. friend that his amendment precludes the possibility of making sugar free.

I would be very glad
if my hon. friend would show that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall not overlook it. I intend to take the matter up fully, I have it in my notes and I will show that it ofiers an insuperable objection to the amendment of my hon. friend. But, let me call the attention of niy hon. friends from Edmonton and St. John to section 3 of the Bill, which says that:
There shall be levied, collected and paid, after the said agreement is in accordance with its terms brought into operation, and so long as it remains in force, on all goods enumerated in schedule f B J to the said agreement being the produce or manufacture of any of the colonies parties thereto, when such goods are imported direct from, any British country into Canada or taken out of warehouse for consumption therein if imported as aforesaid, duties of customs-
(a)	at the rate of four-fifths of the several rates of duties, if any, imposed on similar goods when imported from any foreign country ; or
(b)	at the several rates of duty, if any, set opposite to each tariff item respectively in

the column ' British Preferential Tariff ' in schedule A of the Customs Tariff, 1907, and in any amendment thereof, whichever shall be the lower rate.
We are not taking away from the British West Indies the benefits of the British preferential tariff if it happens to be the lower rate as it would be on substantially all the articles that are not on the free list. That being so we come to this advantage to the British West Indies-in the first place this provision as to giving them an exclusive market, with the preference as against any foreign-grown raw sugar, involves the abolition of the twenty per cent, clause in favour of the refiners. Then under schedule ' C,' in order to meet the case of the important colony of Trinidad chiefly, we have provided that 'cocoa beans, not roasted, crushed or ground,' which are now on the free list, shall continue to come in free from the British West Indies, but that iso far as foreign countries are concerned there shall be a duty of not less than seventy-five cents per hundred pounds.
Do they make gin rickeys out of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I understand it, they
do not make gin rickeys out of cccoa. My hon. friend may have drinks of that kind in his private recipe-book, but I never heard of them.

The reason I asked my hon. friend was that, in referring to the remarks of the hon. member from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), lie said the only articles as to which there was an increase in the cost of living was that out of which gin rickeys were made, but now there is an increase on cocoa beans.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend was guilty of a wilful mis-hearing.
In that I want to support the hon. member for St. John; I understood it exactly as he did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I never knew my hon.
friend to fail to support anything that came from his side of the House. I mentioned that there were three items, one of which was limes, and another of which was ' cocoa beans, not roasted, crushed or ground,' and these are on the free list and will continue to be there so far as the British West Indies are concerned. The British West Indies claim they can produce all the cocoa beans Canada can consume, but it would not be fair to leave it at that because our manufacturers who use the raw cocoa beans require different blends, and the cocoa bean of the West Indies being of a dark colour our cocoa manufacturers will require blends to make their jiroduct of lighter colour, and on foreign-grown cocoa beans there will be a duty imposed of not less than seventy-five Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
cents per hundred pounds. Trinidad would not come into the agreement if that concession had not been made, these being the instructions to its representative, and Trinidad is one of the most important colonies in the West Indies. Then, we have ' lime juice, raw and concentrated, not refined,' which comes chiefly from Montserrat, and there is to be a duty on foreign ' lime juice, raw and concentrated, not refined,' of not less than five cents per gallon.
What do hon. gentlemen now think of the contention that by this inoffensive little schedule ' C ' to which so much reference has been made by hon. gentlemen opposite, we have increased the cost of living to the people of Canada? My hon. friend in his amendment admits that it is not of course in any way necessary to validate this agreement. The Bill before the House is for the purpose of giving effect to the agreement which was entered into by the Convention of April, 1912. My hon. friend said this afternoon that his desire is simply to insert in the Bill what would be a standing offer to the British West India colonies so that when they gave us a fifty per cent, preference upon the articles in schedule ' A '-which are the articles on which Canada enjoyed a twenty per cent preference in the British West India colonies-then the articles mentioned in schedule ' B ' shall come into Canada free. I have no doubt my hon. friend thought he was doing a most commendable thing in that; he did it in his offhand jovian way, and he said: Oh, let them give us fifty per cent preference and we will admit all these articles free. That sounds very well; the only difficulty about it is that it is absolutely not feasible. In the first place, if there is anything abundantly made clear by the evidence taken by the Imperial Commission and by their findings, and the evidence of the representatives of the West Indies at the convention in Ottawa, it is that the people of the West Indies cannot stand more than the twenty per cent preferential rate already provided for in this agreement. So that when my hon. friend says: wait till they give us fifty per cent before the articles are to come in here free, he would know had he read all the proceedings, that would mean never, because they would never be in a position to give us a fifty per cent preference. I should like to read from part VII. of the report of the Royal Commission on the trade relations between Canada and the West Indies. My hon. friend from Edmonton apparently does not know that his Government was a party to the report of the Imperial Commission upon which this agreement is founded, and, that (except that we have added articles to schedules ' A ' and ' B ' and inserted schedule ' C ') this identical agreement was recommended by

the Imperial Commission, the report of which is signed, among others, by his colleagues in the late Government, the Hon. W. S. Fielding and the Hon. William Paterson. My hon. friend should know, if he does not, that the commission prosecuted extensive inquiries in Canada and in the British West Indies in order to make themselves acquainted with the situation.
Does the recommendation made by Messrs. Fielding and Paterson include this preference with regard to sugar?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the point exactly. My hon. friend lias not read the sugar tariff; it is the most intricate part of the tariff and I do not blame him for not having read it; but had he read it and the report of the Imperial conference he would have realized that the sugar question is the question in connection with this agreement. The Imperial Commission had in its membership the Hon. Mr. Fielding and the Hon. Mr. Paterson, and this agreement now before the House-extended as to the articles in schedule ' A ' and ' B '-was recommended in the report of the Imperial Commission.
Did the recommendations of Messrs. Fielding and Paterson include those readjustments of the Canadian tariff in regard to sugar?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They recommended the fifteen cents preference on sugar and for the reason which I shall give later.
The minister is wrong there; they did not recommend fifteen -cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend from Halifax knows that a combine was alleged among these planters, the contention put forward being that they took the whole or the greater part of the preference of thirty-one cents existing between the British preferential rate and the foreign rate on raw sugar, and if my hon. friend will read over the proceedings of the commission, he will find that they concluded that they would not be in a position to take that advantage, which would be serious so far as the refiners in Canada are concerned, if instead of that thirty-one cents a preference of fifteen cents were granted.
The difference is trivial; I thought it was stated in the draft to be twenty cents per hundred pounds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was about half of the thirty-one cents, as my hon. friend knows, although perhaps other hon. gentlemen opposite do not know it.
Let us deal with the question raised by my hon. friend from St. John, of giving
the West Indies a fifty per cent preference. The people of the West Indies are poor. They will have to impose additional taxation upon foodstuffs in order to make up the loss of revenue by reason of this twenty per cent preference which they are giving us. Yet my hon. friend from St. John, deploring the poverty of these people and saying that we have been unfair in making such a bargain with them-my hon. friend from Carleton calls it a niggardly bargain-says:	Let us give them
fifty per cent. They might say:	Thank
you for nothing; we are absolutely unable to do it. I propose to read part VII of the report of the Roval Commission, section 109.
Is it because these people are poor that they are not able to reduce the taxes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have answered my hon. friend a number of times. With all due respect to him, I propose to make my speech in my own way. (Reading):
The preference, as stated elsewhere, might be established either by reduction of duties on imports from Canada and the United Kingdom, or by adopting the existing rates on such products and higher rates on similar articles of foreign origin, or by a combination of these measures. A proposal for reducing the existing duties by 10 per cent in favour of Canada and the United Kingdom, and increasing them against foreign countries by an equal amount was put before us. We thought it well worth careful consideration, where the finances do not permit of an immediate reduction of the full 20 per cent on Canadian and British goods. We suggested it to a considerable number of representative witnesses, and we found it received with a large amount of favour. If it were understood that a preference would in all cases have to be created by an increase of existing duties there would undoubtedly be strong op-osition to the movement. It must be remem-ered that the mass of the people inhabiting the West Indian colonies are poor and therefore unable to bear any considerable burden of taxation. Their sources of public income being limited, a considerable portion of the revenue has to be raised by taxation on imported food. An increase of the duties on such articles would naturally meet with much objection.
Not only does this note run through all the proceedings of the Royal Commission and the evidence taken by it, but it is the note running through the proceedings of the convention held here. It was repeatedly brought to our attention that the people of the West Indies could not give more than the preferential rate of twenty per cent to Canada. If my hon. friend from St. John had read the evidence taken by the commission and had carefully considered the proceedings of the convention, he would have realized that it is useless to talk of the British West Indian colonies giving us a preference of fifty per cent.

Was any offer made to
the British West Indian colonies to admit the articles in schedule B into Canada free of duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No such offer was made
to them because we were rational men, acquainted with the evidence taken before the Imperial Commission. Does my hon. friend mean in return for fifty per cent preference?
Was any offer suggested to the delegates that they should proceed to negotiate upon the basis of free entry into Canada of the products of the West Indies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Most certainly not, as I
shall show my hon. friend in a moment. In the convention, Mr. Chandler, repeatedly pointed out that a very large proportion of the revenue of the West Indian colonies was derived from the duties on fish, lumber, soap, boots and shoes. It was also pointed out to' what an extent the twenty per cent preference would embarrass their revenues. I think it may be taken as conclusive that there would be no chance whatever of inducing the British West Indian colonies to give a fifty per cent preference or indeed any greater preference than the twenty per cent which had been found by the Imperial Commission, which was appointed for the very purpose of investigating it, as a reasonable preference for the British West Indian colonies to give.
As I have pointed out, sugar from the British West Indies is 9/10 of the value of their importations into Canada. The British West Indian colonies are not concerned about free raw sugar as far as Canada is concerned. What the British West Indian colonies are concerned about is preferential raw sugar. In other words, it makes no difference to them whether their raw sugar comes in here free or subject to a duty, as long as they enjoy the preference. That is a point which was entirely overlooked by my hon. friend from St. John, As long as Canada takes their sugar and gives them a preference, they are mot concerned whether the duty against them is high or low. A preference is what they want and that is what they have obtained by this agreement. My hon. friend asked me some time ago if this necessarily meant dearer sugar. It does not. We have the adjustment of our tariff in our own hands, only we must give them this minimum preference of twenty per cent. Let us take it from the standpoint of Canada. In order to deal with the objection to this .amendment which makes it wholly impossible of acceptance by this House, I desire to call attention to what transpired in connection with the British preference upon raw sugar. In his budget Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
speech of 1909, my predecessor the Hon. Mr. Fielding, called attention to the fact that the preference of thirty-one cents upon raw sugar was being largely taken by a combination of planters in the_West Indies. Consequently, instead of being of advantage to our refineries, it was a disadvantage, because the duty on refined sugar was fixed having regard to the amount of the preference upon raw sugar. Therefore in his budget speech of that year, he provided that the sugar refiners of Canada should be entitled to import foreign-grown raw sugar at British preferential rates in order to meet a situation created by the combination of the planters. The Imperial Commission, of which I have spoken and of which the Hon. Mr. Fielding and the Hon. Mr. Paterson were members, investigated that question thoroughly and their report shows without question that that combination existed among the planters and that they took in some causes the whole and in most oases a substantial part of the preference. In the report they recommended practically a cutting down of the preference upon raw sugar from the West Indies in order that such a combination might not be as effectual as it had been in the past to the detriment of our sugar refiners. If any hon. gentleman desires to take up this question, he will find by the most incontrovertible evidence taken before the Imperial Commission, and in their findings, that such a combination existed. Mr. Parker admitted that he thought it was quite proper to take the preference; that the preference was for the West Indian planter and not to mure to the benefit of the Canadian refiner or the Canadian public. What was the result of that ? Here is the point to which I want my hon. friend from 8t. John to have regard in connection with his amendment. The ex-Minister of Finance, Mr. Fielding, pointed out that the duty upon refined sugar in this country was fixed having regard to the preference upon raw sugar used by the refiners at Halifax and Montreal. My hon. friend, I believe, expects a sugar refinery to be established at St. John; and I want to show him how seriously his amendment would affect that sugar refinery-in fact, prevent its establishment. Now, bear this in mind, this is an agreement to afford the British West Indies a preference on raw sugar in the markets of this country. That is to say, there must be a duty in accordance with the terms of this agreement upon all foreign-grown raw sugar imported into Canada. That is to say, when sugar refiners, during the period of this agreement buy raw sugar, they must buy it, so far as the amount they take from any other producers is concerned.

Not twenty
per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, twenty per cent
preference.
Fifteen cents per hundred pounds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the twenty per cent I am using.

I do not understand
that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will
find that it is twenty per cent, and not less than fifteen cents.
I have not read it that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is the trouble. The
hon. gentleman has not read the agreement. The hon. gentleman is better informed than the others, but apparently he has not read it. This is a technical question. In the future the Canadian sugar refiner must buy his raw sugar under a preferential rate. It has been shown conclusively that the planter in the West Indies will take a certain considerable proportion, if not all that preference, at certain seasons. Our Canadian sugar refiners are in competition with the Greenock sugar refiners, who are subject to no preferential rate. Now, in drafting his amendment, the hon. member for St. John has overlooked the fact that sugar includes raw as well as refined sugar. He proposes that sugar admitted from the British West Indian islands should be free. He knows that whatever concessions are given to the West Indies aTe given to the United Kingdom. That is an unbroken usage which I think he would not controvert. Therefore we must give the same advantage to the United Kingdom which we give to the British West Indies.
I do not see that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman
say that we are not to give to the United Kingdom preference equal to that which we are to give to any other country or colony? Can he find a precedent for such a view?

I say it is quite open
to the Canadian Parliament, if they think it desirable, to make a preferential arrangement with sister colonies by which we give a preference on raw sugar. There is no raw sugar imported from Great Britain. It would be quite open to us to make an arrangement, so far as that is concerned, that would not apply to Great Britain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does he know of any precedent for that?
I know of no objection to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the report of the Imperial Commission are these words:
It is, of course, a cardinal point in the policy of Your Majesty's Government that any concession which is made to imports from the Dominion would also he extended to like products of the United Kingdom. We were glad to find that this principle obtained practically universal recognition in the West Indies, and we need hardly add that it has never been disputed in the Dominion.
If the hon. gentleman is desirous to be critical from a legal standpoint, I take up the Bill-and his amendment relates to the Bill-and I find that it provides:
The advantages or concession granted by this Act to the colonies parties to the said agreement shall extend to the United Kingdom and such of the other British colonies and possessions as may be admitted thereto by proclamation published in the Canada Gazette so long as the colonies parties to the agreement continue to be entitled to such advantages or concessions.
I do not know of any case in the history of this country in which this Parliament has given a concession to any other country or coloiw which has not been extended to the Unified Kingdom.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask another question? He says that the term 1 sugar ' includes the refined sugar. Grant that that is correct, it would be easy for my hon. friend to make a change. Suppose it were limited to raw sugar, and that applied to the United Kingdom, it would have no effect, because they do not produce raw sugar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is rather a late repentance after all this discussion. Perhaps the hon. gentleman now begins to see my point that his amendment would put the sugar refiner in Canada in this position, that he would have to pay higher than the market price at which the British refiner can buy raw sugar in the world's markets, because no combination of West India planters could affect him. The Greenock refiner would not be subject to the combination which would raise the price to the refiner in Canada, and yet his refined sugar would come in free. So, the hon. gentleman has moved an amendment which would prevent the establishment of a refinery in St. John and would close up our sugar refineries generally.
It would give the people cheaper sugar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman means well, but I fear he has not looked into this tariff question.
We want cheaper sugar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He wants cheaper sugar. It- is impossible to please the hon. gentleman. He was finding fault with me because I am going to be able to show in my annual statement an abounding revenue.

But he would be the first to raise his voice to high heaven if we had a deficit. Good management of the country's affairs on this side of the House has-

You are not going to
make a budget speech now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can always rely on the
good sense of the hon. member for South Renfrew. But the management of the country's affairs ably, economically, prudently-these are the stock terms-has had its effect. I see no reason why we should not have every advantage we may fairly claim from the fact that we have an abounding revenue and a large surplus. My hon. friend from Carleton, New Bruns-wisk, has moved an amendment, but in view of the statement made by the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, supplemented by the right hon. Prime Minister, it would seem to me inexpedient and unnecessary to add the amendment that he proposes. For, after all, this Bill is simply to confirm and bring into effect an agreement. Why should it be thought advisable to commit ourselves in any way as to the future? It is open to us to do any of these things at any time. These proposals that have been made have not been considered by the other parties to the agreement, they have not been before them and have not been agreed to by them; in other words, they are entirely ex parte. What is proposed here is proposed to be added in the Parliament of Canada. I submit that it is inexpedient to add to the provisions of this validating Bill an offer, whiclr as I have shown in the case of the amendment of the hon. member for St. John would not be acceptable to the people of the British West Indies. All this afternoon we have been discussing matters of inexpediency. I would not say that we have wasted the time of the House, because I suppose that any discussion of this kind is enlightening, but, as was pointed out by the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce and the right hon. Prime Minister, there is no intention in connection with the steamship service of doing what my hon. friend desires to avoid. The amendment of the hon. member for St. John, while specious on the face of it, and seeming to have connected with it some probability of its acceptance, is in reality a provision that could never be accepted by the British West Indian colonies, even if we were disposed to accept it ourselves. It seems, therefore, that it is useless to cumber the legislation that is necessacrv to validate this simple trade agreement with provisions or with offers which probably would not be accepted by the other parties to the agreement. I submit also, quite apart from that, that it is inexpedient to fetter ourselves in anv way Mr. WHITE (Leeds)
in advance. My hon. friend from St. John has referred to the high cost of living. We all know that the cost of living has been very high, but it has not materially increased within the last year or so and I am inclined to think that conditions are better than they were twelve or thirteen months ago. The hon. member for Edmonton referred to what was done when his party was in power. I would remind the hon. gentleman that it is not so very long ago-only eighteen months-since his party was in power. My right hon. friend referred to the zeal of the hon. member for St. John this afternoon in his apparent desire to extend the British preference only to such goods as might be brought without transhipment to Canadian sea or river ports. As pointed out by my right hon. friend, the hon. member for St. John was a member of the Government for many years, and in the customs' tariff of 1907, I find this:
Section 5. On and after a date to be named by the Governor in Council
That was before I came into the Government.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But it continued in force during the time my hon. friend was in the Government, and I never heard of my hon. friend rising in his place and criticising the Government for not bringing this provision into effect. Let me read it to my hon. friend:
On and after a date to be named by the Governor in Council in a proclamation published in the Canada Gazette, the British
referential tariff shall apply only to goods
rought into Canada by ship direct to a Canadian seaport.
That is the customs tariff of 1907, and it has been there ever since, so that the late Government, by proclamation could have confined the benefits of the British preferential tariff to goods brought into Canada by ship direct to a Canadian sea or river port. But my hon. friend sat still during all that time. Does he mean to say he did not know that was in the customs tariff? I hesitate to call the attention or my hon. friend to the celebrated tale of Rip Van Winkle, who was asleep for so many years that when he woke up he found things very much changed. My hon. friend was slumbering during all the time he was a member of the late Government, at least in connection with section 5 of the customs tariff of 1907, and when he wakes up he chides this Government for not immediately bringing into force that provision. Why did my hon. friend sit still during all those years and not proclaim in the Canada Gazette, as required by this section, that the British preferential tariff was to apply only to goods brought into Canada by ship direct to Canadian seaports? I would call

his attention to some of the debates that took place in this House a few years ago; I think my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition took the view that it was inexpedient to_ carry this provision into effect. He said that the Grand Trunk Pacific was not completed; that the country wanted to get the benefit of the completion of that through route, and my right hon. friend objected at that time to bringing that clause into operation by making the proclamation to which I have referred. The hon. member for St. John cannot deny that. The Grand Trunk Pacific is not yet completed, and if my right hon. friend were sitting on this side of the House I have no doubt he would oppose my hon. friend's suggestion. I would suggest when my hon. friend visits his condemnation upon this Government, that he call to mind the position taken by hon. gentlemen, including himself, when they occupied this side of the House, and that he read the arguments then advanced for and against this proposal of his.

I do not object to my
hon. friend's referring to my position on the matter of the preference being allowed only to goods coming direct to a Canadian port. As my hon. friend knows, upon matters that may not be regarded as essential members of the Government may entertain different views. Many years ago a resolution was passed, unanimously, I think, in favour of the limitation of British preference to goods coming through a Canadian port. I have taken that ground on the public platform, and on proper occasions I have urged it from time to time upon the favourable consideration of my colleagues I was pleased when the then Prime Minister made the announcement in Parliament that the Governor in Council, at a date which would synchronize with the completion of the Grand Trunk Pacific, would limit the British preference to goods coming direct to Canadian ports. My views to-day are exactly what they were as publicly expressed some fifteen years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White), has labored for over an hour to prove to his this House that it would be impossible to accept the proposed amendment of my hon. friend the member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley). I am in the class of the Opposition opposed to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), and I must say that to me the Minister of Finance has made the matter about as clear as mud Possibly to a man'of the intellectual ability and knowledge of the West Indian trade possessed by my hon. friend from Halifax, it may be a little clearer than that, but I know I am voicing the sentiment of every other hon gentlemen on this side of the House. I will not follow my hon. friend in his remarks relating to the transportation problem, because I have already discussed that, and I understand I would be out of order if I did so again. If I followed my hon. friend at all, I understood him to say that he could not adopt this amendment because, if he did so, the whole treaty would fall to the ground, or could not be put through. If he is going to prevent this Parliament and

the people of Canada from changing their tariff so that it will decrease the cost of living, the sooner we know it the better. For all the advantages we are going to get from this one-horse agreement the thing is hardly worth discussing. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has laboured for a year and has brought forth a mouse.^ He wants reciprocal trade with the British West Indies whose total trade, including imports and exports, amounts to something like $13,000,000 while our trade with the rest of the world amounts to a billion dollars. He says we must put our.selves_ in a position where we cannot do anything to reduce the cost of living. Why Sir, I do not think there is anybody in Canada who would lose much sleep, or even a penny to give away to a passing beggar, if this thing did not go through. It is such an infinitesimal thing compared with the trade which Canada does with the rest of the world. It is not worth the time we have taken to discuss it in this House, but as my hon. friends brought it down as the great achievement of their 18 months rule, it was worth the while of the Opposition to discuss it to some little extent. My hon, friend could not resist the temptation to have another fling at what he calls the corpse of reciprocity, to which he refers every time he gets on his feet. He had something to say about reciprocity in the earty part of this session when I took the liberty of giving him some of my views, and I think I convinced a good many people, and raised some suspicion in the mind of my hon. friend himself, that reciprocity is not as dead as he thinks. I want to tell him tonight that it is not half as dead as the naval bill, and I hope that he will have an opportunity of finding that out within the next three or four months. He will find that the naval emergency was buried six months ago, if the people of Canada have a chance of expressing their views, and I hope they will have that opportunity in next few months. However, I am not going to discuss reciprocity now, I shall probably have another opportunity of doing so before the close of the session. I simply wish to tell my hon. friend that where I come from it is a much more active issue than ever it was before, and that it is becoming more active every day, and I think that what is true of my own portion of Canada is true of other portions.
I want to come back to the task oi making it clear that sugar could be admitted from the West Indies free. My hon. friend says that the British West Indies are not concerned about whether the duty on sugar coming into Canada is high or low, but that what they are concerned about Mr. CARVELL.
is that they must have a preference. I think that is exactly what he said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it is substantially
correct. It is the preference they want.

All right. As I understand it, the duty on raw sugar under the seventy-five standard, amounts to about fifty-two cents on the 100 pounds, or practically one half cent a pound, and under this agreement the British West Indian islands must have a preference of twenty per cent. In no case must it be less than fifteen cents per 100 pounds. All my hon. friend has got to do is to reduce the general duty on sugar coming from the rest of the world, so that there will be fifteen cents per 100 pounds left, and then he can make sugar free from the West Indies to Canada. Is there any objection to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Even if that weTe doneand I do not say it would be advisable to do so- -the point I am making is that the fifteen cent preference would still be taken by the planters.

That is a point which my hon. friend did not make before. He read extracts from something which Mr. Fielding said three cr four years ago, which may have convinced him, hut which, I am satisfied, did not convince anybody else in this House. When he attempts to tell this House that we cannot make sugar free from the West Indies because of this agreement when he could do so, so long as he left 15 cents per 100 pounds as against the rest of the world, I must say I cannot follow his logic. Under this agreement he could make sugar free so long as he left a duty of fifteen cents per 100 pounds as against the rest of the world. The West Indies would still get a preference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is misrepresenting entirely what I said. I was dealing with refined sugar which would be included in the sugar in schedule B. The point I was making was that if the refined sugar were admitted free, as it would be under the amendment of the hon. member for St. John, it would have to be admitted free from the United Kingdom, and the sugar refiner in the United Kingdom, having the advantage over the sugar refiner here, would be in a position to cause the latter to give up business. There is no doubt about it.
That is the first time I have heard refined sugar mentioned in this debate. I never suggested for a moment that we were dealing with refined sugar. It is raw sugar we are talking about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What does it say in
schedule B ?

No refined sugar comes from the British West Indies. My hon. friend is quibbling. I do not wish to use harsh language, but there is no other word in my vocabulary which defines his attitude better. We are talking about raw sugar, and my hon. friend knows it. He knows that the duty c.n refined sugar is about one and one quarter cents per pound, and he knows that we are talking about raw sugar, the duty on which is about one-half cent per pound. I could not understand what he meant by saving that if sugar were admitted free into'Canada, the refiner in Canada would be driven out of business. As I have already said, he knows that he could admit raw sugar free from the British West Indies, so long as he left fifteen cents per 100 pounds on the sugar coming from the rest of the world and by doing so he would not affect any sugar refinery in Canada. But if he went so far, he would have to go further for the benefit of the consumer.
Do they produce refined sugar in the British West Indies ?
How would that affect the beet sugar industry in Ontario ?

If there were any industry to affect, possibly that question would be worth answering, but the industry is so infinitesimal, when you consider the great sugar consuming people of Canada, that it is scarcely worth while discussing at all. If there is such a thing as protection run mad, it is the protection of a few people who raise beets in the province of Ontario, while the people who use the sugar have to pay a big price for it. That may be according to the logic of a high protectionist such as my hon. friend, but it does not appeal to the ordinary business sense of the sugar consumer in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will my hon. friend look at the first item of schedule ' B '-molasses and sugar ? Does my hon. friend mean to say that the word ' sugar ' would include refined as well as raw sugar and that if the benefits of that schedule were extended to the United Kingdom it would not apply to refined sugar ?	.

I am not going to
quibble about it at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a matter of interpretation.

Well, it may be a matter of interpretation, but if the amendment is not just right there is no trouble about amending it. The hon. gentleman is trying to get out of a hole by quibbling and nothing else. If the term he refers to in schedule ' B ' means refined sugar all that my hon. friend (Mr. Emmerson) has to do is to change his amendment so as to say raw sugar, because that is all the amendment is intended to include.

I do not believe that
there has ever been one hundred pounds of refined sugar produced in the British West Indies. Even if the interpretation did include refined sugar it would not affect the sugar industry in Canada in the least. I submit that this amendment should be adopted, and if it is adopted then let them go a little further and reduce the duty on refined sugar just to the same extent, or a little more possibly, than the duty is reduced on raw sugar because, if you do not reduce the duty on refined sugar the people of Canada will not get any benefit and you will simply be making a present to that extent to the refiners. They will get their raw sugar cheaper but they will charge the same price to the consumer. I hope the hon. Minister of Finance will follow this up by reducing the duty on refined sugar to the same extent. The result will be that the people of Canada will be relieved of nearlv $2,000,000 annually which they are now paying upon molasses and sugar. If you leave a reasonable protection on the refined article-and I am not asking that it shou.d be made free-you protect the Canadian manufacturer against the competition of Greenock and everybody else in the world; we would still have the sugar industry in Canada and the people would their sugar cheaper to the extent of $-,000,000 You may say that that is not. much, but $2,000,000 is quite an item to the consumers. It is not the rich man alone who is a consumer of sugar. The poor consume sugar in greater proportion than do the rich. Therefore, it is quite an item. It is also quite an item from mv hon. friends surplus. My hon. friend from Edmonton referred to the fact that every time an argument on a matter of policy is raised on this side hon. gentlemen opposite always fling back-you did it when you were in power. I would really like to see some important matter of policy brought up in this House when hon members opposite would not fling back to us the answer, 'You did it.' Surely hon gentlemen opposite ought to have sufficient ingenuity to originate some. legislation which could depend upon its merits and not say, if it is bad, ' You did it,' and if it is good, You did it.' I would like to hear some hon. gentleman opposite try to justify the retention of the duty on refined sugar coming into Canada. The Minister of Finance has absolutely failed to justify it. Probably he is in the same class as my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean); they may understand what they are talking about, but if so they are the only two members of the House who do. I would like somebody who does not understand if so

well to explain it in ordinary language so that we could all understand it. _ The Minister of Finance has discussed it along a line that is not intelligible to the rest of us any way. My hon. friend attempted to show that we could not reduce the duty because we would have to give the same preference to the rest of the United Kingdom which we gave to the British West Indies. I presume now that he made use of that argument in reference to the refined article. Of course, if he did, it would not be necessary to make the comments that I intended to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is in this Bill.

I know it is in this Bill. We are not through with this Bill yet. There are lots of opportunities of amendin'* this Bill in order to make it meet the requirements of the people of Canada This is not a matter of the laws of the Medes and Persians which cannot be amended and I hope that my hon. friend will be convinced that it ought to be amended. At any rate, we will do our duty m pointing out desirable amendments and possibly we may succeed in convincing him. We ought *to " be open to conviction when a reasonable line of policy is placed before us but when you mention the word 'reciprocity' to the hon. Minister ot finance it rather gets into his blood and affects his thinking powers. It may he that he is confusing reciprocity with the United States with reciprocity with the West Indies and that may possibly be! the reason for his not being able to think along proper lines as lie does on oidinary occasions. I think that he has got this microbe in his blood, but the people ot Canada, when they get the opportunity, will take it out of his blood or they will put him m a position Where it will not make any difference whether it is there or not. He cannot give us a chance to perform that operation upon his anatomy too soon. _ To show my hon. friend how little tins living of a preference to the rest of the British Empire amounts to, I would quote to the House something from the trade returns. I have not those for the present fiscal year and therefore I am compelled to use those of the former one, but I presume that the proportions would be about the same in the two years. The total amount of raw sugar imported into Canada in 1912, was $13,300,000, on which a duty of $3,000,000 was paid. Of the importation about $9,500,000 came from British Guiana and the British West Indies, or those countries included in this agree-memt. I assume that the words British West Indies ' mean all the British West Indies. Some of these are not parties to this agreement, but they are parties to it Mr. CARVELL.
for the first three years _ and therefore In the compilation I am taking them as being in the agreement. In other words, out of. $13,300,000 worth, $9,500,000 came from countries included in this agreement which leaves only $3,000,000 or $4,000,000 to come from the rest of the world. Of that amount, from British East Africa there came only $240,000 and from British Oceania $192,000. All the rest came from foreign nations. Practically the only raw sugar which we get from abroad comes from the British West Indies and British Guiana, or countries included in this trade agreement. Therefore, the argument that my hon. friend wished to make that we would have to extend this free sugar to the rest of the Empire means nothing at all because, if you give free sugar to the West Indies, you give "it to the whole of the British Empire as far as Canada is concerned. Of course,
I am not applying that to the refined article.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the point.

Then, my hon. friend
says this agreement does not increase the cost of living to the people of Canada, m contradiction of the statement made by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). I cannot read the trade figures without coming to the conclusion that the Minister of Finance has not been paying attention to the facts. Cocoa beans have been free for a great many years past, and if this agreement goes through they will be dutiable from every other country except the British West Indies. Last year we imported from the whole world $691,000 worth of cocoa beans, and of that the magnificent amount of $85,000 came from the British West Indies, from the United Kingdom $79,000, or from the British Empire all told there came $164,000 worth compared with half a million dollars worth from the rest of the world. In order to allow $160,000 worth of cocoa beans to come from the British Empire free, we are imposing a duty of seventy-five cents per hundred pounds, or three-quarters of a cent per pound on the half million dollars' worth that we get elsewhere. And yet the Minister of Finance says this is not increasing the cost of living.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How much?
Three-quarters of a cent per pound on half a million dollars worth. The same thing applies to limes. Limes and lemons are included together in the trade returns, and therefore I cannot separate them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Keep away from the
lemons.

The people of Canada
are getting the biggest lemon to-night they

have ever got since I have been in Parliament. The Minister of Finance has become such an ardent protectionist that everything that increases the duty appeals to his imagination, and it will no doubt be pleasant for him to hear that last year from the United Kingdom we imported, of limes and lemons, $14,981 worth, from Australia and Tasmania $97 worth, from the British West Indies $1,051, from British Oceania $10 worth, or about $16,000 worth in all from the British Empire, whereas from the rest of the world we imported about $730,000 worth
How much from Italy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Of limes and lemons
together.

I have already stated that the figures for limes and lemons are not given separately, but under this agreement we will still be able to bring in $16,000 free from the British Empire, and we will have to pay a duty on limes and lemons from the rest of the world. To carry out this little one-horse trade agreement, you are taking limes ofi the free list and putting them on the dutiable list, and increasing the cost of living.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If it has any effect at all, it will be to advance slightly the cost of gin rickeys?

The Minister of Finance has spent a year over this and I do not wonder that he is proud of his child, but I say it is a lemon which he is handing out to the people of this country. We are making a trade agreement with a country which only takes $3,000,000 worth of goods from us in the whole year, and from whom we import $9,000,000 worth at an average of thirty-three and one-third per cent British preference against the rest of the world. Of course they say the British preference shall govern instead of the twenty per cent which they stipulate as an alternative, but what guarantee have we that the British preference will remain if the Conservatives stay in power for a year or two longer? I would not be surprised to see the whole British preference wiped out, if we can believe the statements of their prominent politicians and newspapers. If the Minister of Finance is satisfied with an agreement like that, well and good, but I do not believe the people of Canada will be satisfied with it. The only thing in its favour is that the whole business is so small that the newspapexs will not discuss it, the politicans will not notice it, and I presume if the Bill goes through this Parliament you will never hear of it again. It amounts to nothing to the people of
Canada, and it amounts to very little to the people of the West Indies. If the Minister of Finance accepts the resolution of the hon. member for St. John, and changes it if necessary in order to make it explicit, he will be doing something for the people of Canada. From the trade returns of 1912 I find that we imported the year previously of syrups and molasses, sugar above No. 16 Dutch standard, including all refined sugars of whatever kinds, grades or standards, $814,000 worth, and of that amount we imported from the British West Indies only $2,534 worth. From the United Kingdom we imported $657,000 worth. If if were made free, we would save in duty about $200,000 because practically all our sugar, molasses, and goods of that character come either from the British West Indies or from other parts of the British Empire. Let us take the raw sugar, that is sugar not above the sixteen Dutch standard, which I think means raw sugar; we imported $13,300,000 worth. From British Guiana and the British West Indies alone we imported $9,500,000 worth. From the British Empire we imported somewhere over ten million dollars worth. Therefore practically three-quarters of all the raw sugar which we imported from the whole world came from the British Empire. On that we paid duty of about $2,500,000. If this amendment were adopted, we would save that duty, which would be of some value to the consumers of tnis country. Hon. gentlemen opposite say:	You did not do
it_ when you were in power; when Messrs. Fielding and Paterson were on a commission representing Canada, you did not make any proposition like this. Things are very different to-day in Canada from what they were three years ago. To-day the revenue from customs and excise is about $50,000,000 more than it was in 1910. In other words, this Government has to-day over $50,000,000 more actual hard cash with which to carry on the business of the country than the Minister of Finance had in 1910. A remission of $2,500,000 of duty in 1910 might have been a fairly serious matter from the standpoint of the Minister of Finance; but, with such an enormous revenue as we have to-day, it is a mere bagatelle. I do not think that it is necessary to bleed the people of this country white in order to have a big surplus. I assume that the duty of the Minister of Finance is to raise sufficient revenue to carry on the business of the country. It seems to me to be good politics to give the surplus to the people or to remove from the people any burden of taxation which is not necessary. If there was a case in which the Government would be justified in doing so, it would be in the case of raw material. There is no article which enters

so much into the ordinary life of the poor people. We have only to look to our friends to the south of us to see what they are doing. Hon. gentlemen opposite want no truck or trade with the United States. You may say: Well, they are a sugar producing country. That is true, but they do not produce more than one-third of what they consume; yet they are making sugar free. They are grading it; they are cutting it down a little now, and they will have it free in three years. My hon. friends opposite might well take a leaf out of their book and attempt to make sugar free in Canada and relieve the people of a certain amount of the burden of life. Tire cost of living has reached a state in Canada when it becomes a menace to the ordinary labouring man and people of small means. There is nothing on which you can reduce the cost of living more easily than on sugar, and I do not know of any better opportunity to do it than by adopting the amendment proposed by the hon. member for St.	John. The more	you	lookinto	this	matter, the	plainer it
becomes the duty of the Government, if they want to carry out their pledges and to do something for the common people, to accept this amendment and in some way to relieve the burden imposed on the people at the present time.
I hope my hon. friends opposite will accept the amendment which I proposed at the beginning of the debate this afternoon, and will agree that the amendments shall become a part of the statute. It is all very well for my friends opposite to say:	We
are going to do it anyway; there is no difference of opinion between us and therefore you should take our word for it and not insist on having it put in the form of a statute. That reminds me of an argument which they used in regaTd to another measure before the House. They did not want us to bind them down by a statute. On this side of the House we prefer to have these gentlemen on record in the form of a statute. We have had so many promises of no value at all, promises made only to be broken, that we have become a little suspicious when these gentlemen come offering us gifts. We would like to have these amendments crystallized in the form of a statute. Then we would know that hon. gentlemen opposite are sincere. I know from the serious look of my friend the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, that he is sincere. Therefore I see no reason why he should not be willing to incorporate these amendments in the statutes. If the rumours in the papers are correct that there is going to be a change in the Government, a new set of men will come in who will not be bound by what the present Government say is their intention. We do not know what might happen in Mr. CARVELL.
that ease. As long as my hon. friend the Minister of Railways is in the Government, I know he will stand by his promises, but he may not be here another ye?.r. When the Government come to renew this agreement with another company a year from now, they will say: It is true the promises were made but we were not bound by them. I hope my friends will let my amendment go through without division, and for once we shall be in accord and shall have something which I submit will be of lasting importance to the people of Canada as a whole. We can make this little treaty of any value only by going at it in a wholehearted manner. If we have to force trade through channels which may be a little unnatural, if we cannot trade in natural channels, if we cannot trade with the hundred million people who want to trade with us, let us do it in such a way that the people of Canada will get the benefit of it.
