Hon. FRANK COCHRANE moved the third reading of Bill No. 32, to encourage and assist the Improvement of Highways.

I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Pardee:
That the said Bill be not now read a third time, but that it be recommitted to the Committee of the Whole House with instructions that they have power to amend it in the manner following: (a) by inserting the foU lowing words as sub-section 2 of section 3: The sums of money voted in any year to be expended under this Act shall be apportioned among the different provinces of the Dominion according to the population of the said provinces as established by the last census for the time being.
(b) By striking out clause 6.
I have made the amendment in a form which includes all I have to say and places it before the House in a manner in which I can discuss it with expedition and the House can deal with it conveniently. There are really two points involved in the Bill, and only two points, which seem to divide the parties. So far as the principle of the Bill is concerned, there seems to be no division in the House. We all agree that out of the abundant revenues of the country we can afford to pay to the various provinces of Canada a substantial amount annually to be expended in the work of constructing roads and bridges. We differ, however, as to the application of that expenditure. We do not agree with the Government in its proposal that the money shall he spent as laid out in the sections of the Bill as it came from the committee. I would just like to emphasize the only points of disagreement so far as I understand it.	.
Mr. BUREAF.

In the first place, the Bill provides for an annual appropriation, but it does not provide that the appropriation shall be expended between the various provinces according to population. I think I have heard the Minister of Railways state in the House that it is the intention of the Government that this money shall be expended as subsidy to the various provinces, having regard to the population of the provinces according to the last census. That would be satisfactory if it were so expressed in the Bill, but it is not so expressed in the Bill, and the object of the first sub-section of my amendment is merely to make it plain that the money shall be expended among the provinces of Canada according as they are entitled to receive it proportionately under the last decennial census. I think my hon. friend the Minister of Railways might accept that amendment. The Bill as drawn states that this payment is a subsidy, but the word * subsidy ' does not mean a proportionate payment, and under the Bill as drawn, there is nothing to compel the minister or the Government to make a proportionate distribution as between the provinces of Canada. We disagree upon that point, and a very slight amendment, such as I have proposed, will cure the defect and allow us to agree upon it.
The next proposal in my amendment is to strike out clause 6 in the Bill altogether. The objection to clause 6, in my judgment, is that it gives to the minister and to the Government unlimited, unnecessary and improper power in regard to the expenditure of this money. Those who sit to your left, Mr. Speaker, believe that this money could best be spent and should be spent by the provincial authorities. Under clause 6 of the Bill, which I now propose to have stricken out by my amendment, the minister has exceedingly large powers, so large that I think he could of his own motion, at all events with the consent of the Government of which he is a member, spend the whole amount, which one province or all the provinces are entitled to receive in any given year on a single work as he might determine, or, if he saw fit, he might refuse altogether to expend it. The clause reads as follows:
The minister, with the approval of the Governor in Council and upon such terms'and conditions as are prescribed by Order in Council, may undertake the construction of any new highway or the improvement of any existing highway in any province, and may expend in such improvement or construction the whole or any part of the sums voted by Parliament for such subsidy to that province: Provided, however, that the minister shall first obtain the necessary authority from the legislature of such province and the consent of the Lieutenant Governor in Council.
We on this side of the House believe that this money may best be expended
by the various provinces. I do not see why the Minister of Railways or the Government should insist upon controlling the expenditure of this money which is to be given to the provinces by way of a subsidy special ear-marked for expenditure on roads. The other subsidy which we annually grant to the provinces goes to them with full liberty to expend it as they see fit. Why should this additional subsidy not go to them on the same principle? Why should the Minister of Railways and the Government, engaged in the various works which occupy their attention throughout the Dominion of Canada, charge themselves with the comparatively small matter of expending road money in the various provinces of the Dominion ? Does it not seem reasonable and proper that this money should be granted to the local administrations which, under the British North America Act, are charged with the maintenance and construction and care of roads and bridges, for the purpose of expending it. I do not go so far as to say that the Government should give up all control. The Bill gives the Government or their inspectors the right to inspect and pass upon the work before the money is expended, or even to pass upon it before the work is undertaken at all. Surely that is enough, so far as this Government is concerned. Why not trust the provinces themselves with the actual work; with the laying out of the actual work ? I do not know what knowledge my hon. friend the Minister of Railways has with regard to road work. I fancy he has some knowledge of it in regard to the province of Ontario, but this applies to all the provinces of Canada, east and west. We, on this side of the House, are quite prepared to entrust Ontario's share of this money to the Conservative Government of that province. We believe that proper expenditure in the interest of the province would follow. We are just as prepared to trust the Liberal Administration of Quebec to-day with the expenditure of that money, or the various other provincial governments throughout the Dominion. We believe they are the proper bodies to expend it, and that the Minister of Railways and the Government are not.
When the late Government voted money for the improvement of Ottawa, why did they not hand it over to the city of Ottawa rather than to a commission ?

I do not know that the oases are quite parallel. I think the idea of the expenditure in the city of Ottawa largely came from the policy which the United States adopted in the city of Washington. I believe that that was rather an exceptional case. But the frapiers of Confederation had no doubt in their minds as

to what was the proper legislative body to take charge of roads and bridges in this country. They did not hesitate about the matter; they placed the roads and bridges under the provincial Parliaments, and there they have remained with very few slight exceptions ever since. The Minister of Railways pointed out that there have been some exceptions, but they are slight exceptions. Here we are laying down a policy which is to be followed as a settled policy for a number of years. Let us see that we proceed upon proper lines. The provisions of this Bill, and particularly of section 6, would enable an evil-minded minister or an evil-minded government to use the powers given to them as a huge electioneering machine in any province in the Dominion.

It has been used to
the limit already.

I do not say that the
present minister would so use it, but the Bill puts it in the power of the minister or the Government to do so. Why not remove this Government from temptation altogether and place the money in the hands of the proper authorities and not make another exception under the British North America Act as I maintain you are doing?
There is just one other phase of the question thait I would like to mention and I do so because on a former occasion in this House I mentioned something in connection with trunk lines. On two or three occasions since then hon. members have asked me whether I was not joking on the subject. I certainly was not joking. But when I came to look up the pages of ' Hansard ' I found that the Minister of Railways and Canals had expressed a very strong opinion in this House that it would be a ' grand thing ' to establish trunk line roads. He said that there was a great demand for the establishment of such roads and he suggested one might be constructed between Windsor and the city of Quebec. Immediately the thought crossed my mind that the only useful purpose that such a trunk road would serve in this country would be to accommodate the automobile traffic in the summer months and that it would be most largely used by the joy riders of Chicago and Detroit on their way down to the lower provinces. I do not believe that at this period in our history we are called upon to expend this country's money on trunk roads through the older portions of the older provinces of the Dominion of Canada when we have so much to do in the newer and unsettled portions of Canada in giving the settlers ordinary accommodation to get to their markets. I would rather, for that reason, have this money left in the hands of the provincial Mr. GUTHRIE.
legislatures 'to expend than have it placed in the hands of the Minister of Railways who thinks that a trunk road from Windsor to Quebec-as reported in ' Hansard ' at page 8805-will be such a ' grand thing.' That is a matter in the future and in the far, far distant future too.
This money, if it is going to be used to the advantage of Canada at the present day, has to be used largely for agricultural purposes, for the purpose of enabling the agriculturist in the remoter sections of the country to travel to and from his nearest market and in this way help to bring about the settlement and development of Canada. If you allow these provinces to expend the money it is in that manner that they will expend it, but I am afraid, from the language of the minister himself, that it will run rather in another channel and that what appeals to him is the accommodation of the richer portion of the population in the older settled portions of the Dominion-good roads for automobiles! That policy does not commend itself to me and I do not desire to give the minister the power, whoh this section will give him, to expend all the money in any province on a single work, or a particular line of work, as he may see fit. My hon. friend may say that under section 6 he has to get the consent of the Lieutenant Governor of the province before he can make the expenditure. But if he goes to the Government of tlie province of Ontario and says: I propose to expend this money on a trunk line from Windsor to Quebec, and 1 want to get the consent of the Lieutenant Governor in Council to that, they may say: No, we will not consent to that, we want this money spent in New Ontario and in the badly served portions of old Ontario.

Is my hon. friend
aware that the former Government assumed and took over a considerable portion of the very road to which he is referring?
Yes, I am well aware of that but the fact of their having done so does not answer my argument.
And that they did not even ask the consent of the province?

There was a reason for that. The road that my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) refers to is the old Toronto and Kingston military road, built by the old province of Canada, always looked on as a government or military road and built for that purpose, and if the Dominion Government did assume control, or partial control over that road, it surely does not give us the ground work to defend this policy and the method by which this expenditure will be made. Under this section the minister has it in his power to say to the province

of Ontario: If you do not consent to the work I propose, you will get no money at all. Accept the amendment that I offer and the minister cannot say that. Then each province will have the right to receive annually its proportionate share according to the last census. If you strike out section 6 tach province will have the right to expend that money as it sees fit and the Dominion Government will have the right te put on its engineers and inspectors, prescribe proper conditions and see that the money is not improperly expended. That will give the power to the province and it will relieve the minister and the Government here of a great deal of anxiety and unnecessary work and trouble.
I suppose that the principle that is going to be urged against my proposal is that, as the Dominion Government owns the money, it must keep control of its expenditure. I submit that such an argument has no force. If you read section 3 you will see that this money is called 'subsidy.' You give subsidy for what purpose at present?-to assist the provinces? Yes, and you allow them to expend that money as they think proper. Therefore, if the argument that this House must keep control of the money it votes has any force, you should keep control of the subsidies that you vote to the different provinces.
Will the hon. gentleman say that in voting a railway subsidy we should give the control of it to the province in which the railway is located?
No, I do not put a railway and a highway on the same basis.
What is the distinction in principle? If we vote railway subsidy, why should we not say to the province: You spend this money because you can spend it better than we can?
The two are quite distinct. We of right are in control of the railway systems but we are not in control of the highways and bridges in the provinces.
' We ought to be in control of our own money, no matter what it is for.

Well, I have made that distinction and if it does not appeal to my hon. friend I cannot do anything more. Nothing could be better settled by the framers of Confederation, and nothing was settled better by the Confederation Act itself, than that roads and bridges belong to the provinces.
We do not take away from that in any sense of the word.
You are going pretty deeply into the business of making, maintaining, repairing and constructing roads in the provinces when you ask them to consent-
By their consent.

And if they do not consent to the minister's proposal he can say to them: Very well, I will not give you anything. He is really placing himself in absolute control of the highways and bridges in the different provinces if the Bill goes through in it3 present form. 1 doubt if it is good policy for my hon. friend to adopt such a course. What advantage will the public get out of it?
They will get good roads.

Does not my hon.
friend think that Sir James Whitney will spend the money properly?
I think that if it is our money we should have control of it.

Then my argument in regard to the subsidy must hold good. We grant a large amount to the provinces each year and although it is our money we still give it to the provinces. If it is our money, and if my hon. friend's argument is a good one, we should keep control of it and spend it. This is the old principle of centralization, while the principle that has been adopted in this House more and more as the years have gone by is one of decentralization. Likewise it is an expenditure to meet the local demand. I know that the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) would trust the Whitney Government absolutely with the expenditure of this money and would consider that it would spend it for the benefit of the province and the advantage of the people. I am also willing to trust them. The British North America Act, our constitution, says that they are the people who should control the highways.
The province does not take hold of the county roads although it supplies the money to be expended upon them.

That strengthens my argument. The Province of Ontario had adopted the principle in its legislation that the counties and the townships can best say what their local needs are, and instead of assuming control at Toronto of the roads in the County of Carleton for example, they say to the authorities of that county: there is your money; spend it where it is most needed.
Not at all.
They do in my county.
They do not in your county.

If it is a provincial road they send an inspector, and I do not know if we have built any of those provincial roads in our county; but the Municipal Act of Ontario gives absolute control of the county roads to the county, the township roads to the township, and the urban roads to the urban municipalities. The title of the land is in the Crown but the sole control, management, and liability for repairs of the road is in the municipality and not in the Province of Ontario.

In the county of
Wellington do you not get one-third from the Ontario Government under certain restrictions as to supervision and expenditure?
We get the road grant and it has to be expended according to certain prescribed standards which the Ontario Government has set out.
And under the supervision of a Provincial Government appointee.

And nobody would object to such a provision in this Bill. I have said time and again that the minister should have the right to put his engineers on to inspect the road, but he goes further because he controls the expenditure and he can say to a province: you do this or you will get nothing.

And so says the
Province of Ontario in regard to the roads in the County of Wellington.
Indeed it does not.

Yes it does. In nineteen
counties in the province of Ontario that have come under "the good roads system

My hon. friend (Mr. Edwards), had better let me go on without interruption. The Province of Ontario pursues what I maintain is the proper system and the system that should be pursued by the Minister of Railways in this case. The Provincial Government has this to say in its favor, that it is the body specially created by the British North America Act to attend to roads, and the Federal Government is not in any way charged with that duty.

Is it not a fact that
when a county in Ofitario wishes to share in the Ontario grant for good road purposes it lays out a county road system and that system must be submitted to the Ontario Government for its approval and sanction?

I should think that is
so, and the provincial government is the Mr. COCHRANE.
proper authority to look after roads and the Dominion Government is not. The first difference between us is that we say the provinces should be treated equally and that each province should receive its money annually on the basis of population. .That is what the minister says he intends to do but it is not in the Bill.
No he does not.

I do not think you
have any right to make that statement.

The Bill is so framed
that he need not do it unless he wants to.
No.
The minister said in the House that his intention was to treat the provinces according to their population at the last census.

And the money was
so voted last session.
If that were in the Bill it would do away with my first objection.
But it is not in the Bill.

Will the minister put
it in the Bill?
No.
Then that is the difference between us.

The vote of money
has to be brought before the House every year.

Yes but that leaves to the minister power to strike out one province this year and another province next year, and it enables him to refuse to consider the basis of population in the various provinces.
Is the hon. gentleman (Mr. Guthrie) unwilling to accept the word of the Minister of Railways and the word of the Prime Minister also?

Just on that point; if
the word of the Prime Minister and of the minister were binding in the interpretation of a statute I would accept it without the slightest hesitation, but my fear is that we may not have the Prime Minister next year, and it is rumoured we are going to lose the Minister of Railways in the near future and we cannot tell who his successor may be. If the Prime Minister were sincere, and I assume he was; if the Minister of Railways were sincere; and I assume he was, when they stated their intention was that each province should be treated on an equal basis according to the population at the last census, why do they object to crystallizing that statement in the legislation? It is much better to have it in

the statute than to depend on the memory of man for it, or on the debates of ' Hansard ' which are not binding. We do not object to your expenditure; we approve of it, and I wish to emphasize that fact in view of the statements that appear day after day in the Conservative newspapers. The Toronto Mail stated recently that the Liberal party was opposing and obstructing this Highways Bill.

The Senate did it last
year surely.

The Conservative press of the country and Conservative speakers have been most unfair to the Senate in that regard. The Senate made seven proposals by way of amendment and the minister has accepted five of them this year.
I did last year.
It should be recognized that five of the amendments having been accepted by the minister the Senate did a good work.

Why did they not
quit at that?

If the Senate last year took the view that this money should be expended by the provinces the Senate was right, and if the Senate takes the same view this year it would still be right. We want the people of Canada to know that the Opposition in this House does not oppose this money grant, but that we insist that the provinces shall have the control of the expenditure and that they shall have the money distributed to them on the basis of population.
The farmers who are paying the taxes will know all right what they are doing.

We want the farmers to know that the misrepresentation that has been indulged in during the last twelve months is a slander against the Liberal party because the word has been passed- to the reptile press as the Minister of Public Works would say-to state that the Liberal party opposed the passage of the Highways Bill.
They killed it last session.
It was the Government that killed it.

And if we can kill this proposal as it is in the Bill at present we will kill it, and if we can amend it we will amend it and bring it into conformity, not only with common sense, but with the provisions of the British North America Act, leaving the provinces to expend their own money on the roads as they see fit. I fear that the minister does not feel disposed to accept our amendment.
I do not think he will.

He should consider that matter very carefully because I believe I am making a reasonable request. All I isk is that he put his own promise in this legislation and then my first objection will have disappeared. The second would stand because that is the question as to whether [DOT] he will spend the money or whether the provinces will do so.

By the majority of the inhabitants of rural Canada this Bill to encourage and assist the improvement of highways is, I believe, regarded as the most important measure in the Government's legislative programme, the Naval Bill not excepted. This Bill has been pretty generally discussed during the three several occasions when it has previously been before the House this session. Hon. gentlemen opposite have taken the very extraordinary ground that, while they admit that the highways are in need of improvement, they oppose this means by which they might be improved.
The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) in moving his amendment has made two principal points. He says that this money should be apportioned to the various provinces, according to population as disclosed by the last census. It will be remembered that legislation of this character was before the House last session, and in order to provide for the expenditure of the money which was to be appropriated under that legislation, the Government included in the supplementary estimates the necessary sum of money apportioned to the various provinces according to population. Making a total of a million dollars. That was based upon the population of Canada as disclosed at the last census. The purpose was to meet the very object in connection with which the hon. gentleman has moved this amendment.
Why not put it in the Bill?

Parliament should have the voting of this money. If at some future time it might in the wisdom of Parliament be desirable to depart from that principle

of distribution, there is no reason why that attitude should not be open to Parliament without amending the legislation.
My horn, friend asks that clause 6 of this Bill should be struck out. Clause 6 says:
The minister, with the approval of the Governor in Council and upon such terms and conditions as are prescribed by an Order in Council, may undertake the construction of any new highway or bridge, or the improvement of any existing highway in any province, and may expend in such improvement or construction the whole or any part of the sums voted by Parliament for such subsidy to that province:	Provided however
that the minister shall first obtain the necessary authority from the legislature of such provinces and the consent of the Lieutenant Governor in Council.
It is to be observed that in every case where the expenditure is made under the direction of the minister, it shall be done by and with the consent of the legislature of such province and the consent of the Lieutenant Governor in Council of such province.
My hon. friend, in asking that this clause be struck out, makes this point. He says: This is in the nature of a subsidy; why not treat it as all other subsidies are treated when payable to the provinces and place it absolutely under the control of the provinces. There is this distinction, that the general subsidies which are payable annually to the provinces are fixed under the terms of the British North America Act. This is a special and additional subsidy, voted by this Parliament for a special purpose, and it seems to me that it is only right and proper that the Parliament which votes the money should retain some control over it.
When the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) spoke on this measure a few days ago, he gave what appeared to me to be a most novel reason for not supporting it. He said that it would be a most unpopular thing for any provincial Government to refuse to accept any money from the federal Government for such an excellent purpose as the improvement of highways. I think the hon. gentleman was right. I think hon. gentlemen oppositj have discovered, since legislation of a similar character introduced by this Government last year was defeated, that it was a most popular measure and that its defeat, as a result of amendments in the Senate, was most unpopular.
The hon. member for Humboldt presented to this House a resolution from the legislature of Saskatchewan, the effect of which, if it were adopted by this Government, would be to postpone indefinitely any legislation or any grant along these lines. He thought that this Government should consent to that proposition, which would defeat the very purpose which they Mr. JAMESON.
have in view. It seems to me that that would be obviously a most unreasonable proposition and contrary to every rule of reason and every principle of common sense. I .have always understood that every legislative body should proceed upon its own authority and that it should be responsible for its own acts. I do not think that the legislature of any province, not excepting the legislature of the province of Saskatchewan, has the right to dictate to this Parliament, or to the Government of Canada, how they shall exercise their functions, or what their legislative programme shall be.
This Government will pass this Bill in aid of the highways. It will appropriate one million dollars fox highways, and if the Government of any of the provinces of Canada refuses to enter into an agreement with the minister, for the acceptance and expenditure of that province's share of any sum appropriated under this Act, I believe that the people of that province will deal with such a Government at the earliest opportunity.
My hon. friend the member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney), propounded a most unusual doctrine. He said that if this money were coming from outside of Canada he would approve of the expenditure, but inasmuch as it was coming from the pockets of the people of this country, he did not feel that he could support it. He thought it should rather be applied in the reduction of the cost of living. I do not know how my hon. friend is going to find a better means of decreasing the cost of living than by improving the means of. communication between the producer and the consumer.
I do not know whether my hon. friend really considered where his line of reasoning was going to lead him when he advanced that doctrine. The city of Saskatoon at this time is asking for a very considerable grant for the construction of a public building in that city to meet the requirements of a growing community. But if the doctrine which the hon. gentlemen propounds were carried out, there would be no expenditure of public money for the construction of that building; there would be no publics works; there would, indeed, be no highways. I do not think my hon. friend could have been serious when he put forward that proposition.
The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) spoke on this Bill a few days ago and he opposed it because of its form. He said the	Bill should
be made satisfactory to hon. gentlemen opposite. I think he has set a pretty difficult proposition to this Government, to satisfy hon. gentlemen opposite. If any member of the Government were to seriously contemplate attempting to satisfy hon. gentlemen opposite-and I have

sometimes thought that occasionally they make an honest effort to _ do so, more particularly in the case of my hon. friend from Pictou, but with rather indifferent success-I would advise that member of the Government to first sit down, square the circle, and work out the problem of perpetual motion, and after he has disposed of these comparatively easy exercises, he might attempt the more difficult one of satisfying hon. gentlemen opposite.
Hon. gentlemen opposite are not here to be satisfied, they are here to be dissatisfied; the moment they are satisfied their functions as an opposition cease.
My hon. friend from Pictou might have had legislation of a form to satisfy him had he and his party desired it. For sixteen years hon. gentlemen opposite were in nower, and during a part of that time the hon. member for Pictou sat as a supporter of that Government in this House.
To what extent did they increase the provincial subsidies in that time? [DOT]

Let him tell. During all that time did they bring down any legislation in respect to the highways? No; but now that this Government has brought down this legislation, hon. gentlemen opposite see that they missed . a grand opportunity _of meeting the needs and requirements of the people of this country, and I have no doubt they feel somewhat sore in consequence.
The objections of hon. gentlemen opposite when weighed and sifted), come down to three:	First, partyism, which
prompts them, not unnaturally, perhaps, to oppose everything that this Government proposes; second, remorse, because they did not, when in office, bring down legislation of this character and for this purpose; third, jealousy, because this Government will obtain the credit for this legislation which is, I am sure, meeting the approval of the people of this country.
At the last session of Parliament, hon. gentlemen opposite opposed a Bill along the same lines as this. They moved certain amendments in this Chamber, which amendments were voted down. Having done that they had discharged their duty to the country, as they saw it. The Biil went to the Senate; their political influence followed it, and it was amended, and amended in such a manner that this Government would not accept the amendments and take the responsibility for those amendments.
My hon. friend from South Renfrew referred to what he was pleased to term the ' obstinacy ' of this Government in not accepting the Senate amendment. Sir, I say that while nominally the amendment which was objected to by this Government was a
Senate amendment, in reality it was an amendment of the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, and it was an amendment by which he was trying to frame legislation which he could have framed to suit himself at any time prior to the 21st of September of 1911, had he had any desire to do so. But if it were not, Sir, I say the people of this country will not stand to have the action of this, the popular chamber, the chamber elected by and responsible to the people, defeated, hindered, and delayed by the action of a chamber which is not responsible to the people of Canada, but which is responsible to the grim reaper and to the grim reaper alone.
When, some years ago, the proposition to create the Commonwealth of Australia was before the people of the island continent, a cartoon appeared in one of the Sydney papers which illustrated the stand of the anti-federal party. There was a picture of a boy standing on a railway track regardless of a fast approaching express train. Another picture alongside showed the train at a standstill and the engineer down examining the driving wheels; and underneath were these words:
The boy stood on the railway track He heard the whistle squeal-
The engineer got slowly down,
And scraped him off the wheel.
The anti-federal party in Australia was steam-rollered by the people when they went to the polls, and I firmly believe that the political party which opposes this legislation will receive similar treatment from the people of Canada when they go to the polls, and when the real test as to the popularity of this legislation is had.

I am sure the House has listened with interest to the versatile address of the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) who addresses the House all too seldom, and who, when he does claim attention brings to the debate a spice of interest and a touch of humour which is too often lacking in speeches in this House. The hon. gentleman seems oppressed with some feeling of sympathy for hon. gentlemen on tjjis side. I assure him that hon. gentlemen on this side are all very well and very good-humoured, and not worrying about any of these sad policies which in his imagination he attributes to us. The only people who are worrying about whether this legislation will pass or not, are some whom we might call the heelers of the Conservative party who anxiously await the division of the spoils and the use of this million dollars which would be such splendid election material in the hands of these workers for the Conservative party. These are the gentlemen who are worry-

ing about this measure; these are the gentlemen who were disappointed last year when this measure was not passed in the form in which hon. gentlemen supported it, and these are the gentlemen who will be disappointed this year if it fails to pass in the form in which it is now proposed. The House is in a peculiar position in respect of this matter. Hon. gentlemen on the other side say: 'We have here a wonderful Bill; nobody ever thought of it before. We charge hon. gentlemen on the left of the Speaker that although they were in power fifteen years, such a brilliant idea never came into their minds as the one which now possesses us. When you analyze the matter, the whole of this wonderful policy consists in the fact that, according to the preamble of the measure, hon. gentlemen propose to take a million dollars out of the treasury and give it to the provinces. There is nothing very mysterious or wonderful about that. The subsidies for the different provinces have been increased at different times, after conferences with the provinces, and the increased amounts which Parliament voted from time to time were for the betterment of the roads of the different provinces of the country and for the betterment of all the institutions which are committed to their care. By this measure hon. gentlemen are taking a million dollars, and, without any regard to subsidies paid in the past, they say they propose to give this sum of money to the provinces for the purpose of having the roads improved. When it is desired to ascertain the alleged intention of hon. gentlemen in proposing a Bill, it is rarely necessary to go to the preamble. They say that the highways of Canada are an important part of the facilities of transportation; everybody agrees with that. Then they say:
And whereas, with the increasing progress and development of the country it is desirable and expedient to improve and extend the existing highway facilities, and for that purpose to give assistance to the various provinces of Canada.
That is the preamble of this Bill, and they go on to provide for the voting of money to ^ive assistance to the various provinces of Canada. Hon. gentlemen
state that as the preamble of their Bill, but they come down with a measure which docs not provide what their preamble states they intend to provide for. My hon. friend the Prime Minister and the hon. Minister of Railways supplement the preamble of this Bill by saying: 'We intend to give this money to the provinces, we have no intention of doing anything else. Look, for instance, at the verification of our professions in that regard. Last year when we brought down the supplementary estimates, in furtherance of this Bill, w« Mr. MACDONALD
placed in them an amount to be given_ to the provinces, and we divided it according to the basis upon which the subsidies were voted; therefore hon. gentlemen on the other side have no right to question the procedure in the matter at all.' We all know the old saying that the road to Hades is paved with good intentions. Hon. gentlemen appear to be full of good intentions, but when it comes to putting down their real intentions in black and white, certainly they fall short of the ideal. If the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) had any right to believe that in the Bill now before the House there was a crystallization of the professions of the gentlemen whom he follows, there would be no division upon this matter. What a peculiar situation is presented to the House. It is that under this Government we must take the statements of the ministers as to the quality and effect of intended legislation, and then, when we come to look at the document which is to be placed on the statute-book, it does not matter if we find that differs entirely from their statements. When questions are raised as to whether or not the words of the measure which is to be the statute and the law of the country are to be interpreted as indicating the true objects and intentions of the Bill, hon. gentlemen say: ' It is not what you put on the statute-book under this Government that is to be the foundation upon which judges are to base their conception of the law; it is what the hon. the Minister of Railways and the Prime Minister choose to say, even if what they say is diametrically opposed to the words of the Bill. If the hon. the Minister of Railways had put in the Bill what he claims to be his intentions in the matter, then the hon. member for South Wellington would have had no need to present his amendment. Why should the Minister of Railways not put his intentions in the Bill? The hon. minister admits in the preamble of the Bill the purpose of this wonderful measure-this project of statesmanship the like of which has never been seen in this country; the concentration of everything that is wonderful and mysterious, but which, translated into plain English, means nothing more nor less than a proposition to take so much money out of the Dominion treasury and give it to the provinces. We are told that no one should question the qualities of this wonderful Bill, and that anyone who does will get into trouble. With any hon. gentleman who thinks that any hon. members on this side of the House are worrying about their opinion to this measure, I take issue fairly and squarely, and I am prepared to go into my constituency or any other constituency and ask the people of this country whether they believe what hon. gentlemen say or whether

they would rather look to what they do. Actions speak louder than words. Professions are not worth much when you come to deal with legislation; the question is what did you put in the document that is to control the expenditure of the money? Professedly this money is to be given to the provinces; actually hon. gentlemen want to keep it under their own control. They know that the right to deal with roads rests exclusively in each of the provinces, and in section 6 of this Bill they recognize the fact that the provinces own the rights of way of these roads and that no federal parliament or any other authority in the British Empire can interfere with the right of the provinces to deal with them. They admit all that, and yet they say: 'We want to put in this Bill something to give us the right to deal with the money. The issue as between the parties is well defined. The hon. member for Digby need not attempt by any method such as he has suggested so very adroitly to draw the attention of the House, or indeed of the country, from this measure. I may tell my hon. friend that there only as many people, outside of the political partisans who want to control the expenditure of this money, who will be offended by the nonpassage of this Bill, as the hon. gentleman can mislead by the statement that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House are opposed to federal assistance to roads, and by the concealment of the fact that we on this side of the House asked the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to put in this document the crystallization of the language which he used in this House as to what his intention is in Tegard to this measure. The statement that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House are opposing federal assistance to roads is untrue, and the hon. gentleman who makes it, and who lias heard this discussion, must hereafter know that it is untrue. I venture to say that at no time in the history of this Parliament has a Government ever come before this House and presented a measure under such conditions as those that exist in the present instance, whereby hon. gentlemen declare their avowed purpose and object to be one thing, and admit that the language of the Bill is not in the terms of their intentions, yet decline to put in the document a statement of the views which they allege to be their true convictions. That is the position here. We cannot tell what hon. gentlemen in the other legislative branch of Parliament may do in regard to this question. We know the view they took last year. We know that they recognized the constitutional right of the provinces of this Dominion. It is stated categorically in the preamble of this measure. They I
recognized their constitutional right to deal with the question of the rights of the provinces, and hon. gentlemen on the other side know that they were right in doing so.
No.

Perhaps my hon.
friend will tell me where they were wrong?

Where were they
right?
They were right because my hon. friends opposite put it in the preamble of the Bill but did not put it in the enacting clauses.
An excellent reason.

I aim surprised that my hon. friend from Toronto, whose partisanship sometimes runs away with his legal judgment, should think that he can put something in the enacting clauses of a Bill which is entirely contrary to what is contained in the preamble. My hon. friend who has had a good deal to do with private Bills, knows that he would not venture to put something in the enacting clauses of a Bill which was contrary to the preamble. That is what this measure does, and it is because of tho absolute anomaly in the drafting of the measure and because of the results that might follow, that those of us on this side of the House have no hesitation in stating that when a government comes before Parliament with a proposition they ought to put in the statute what they mean, and not leave it to the House, or to anyone else, to infer what they mean.

In view of the fact that many newspapers supporting the Government in my province, and indeed in all the provinces, are grossly misrepresenting the attitude cf the Opposition in regard to this measure, I deem it my duty to say a few words before the Bill is finally disposed of. The idea that seems to run through some of the articles that I have read, and which apparently runs through the minds of the men whe write them, is that the money proposed to be expended under this Bill, is a gift from the Government of this country, from the twelve or fourteen gentlemen who compose the Government, to the provinces, or to the 'people of the country. They do not seem to realize that all the money that is obtained by this Government, or by any government, is first obtained from the people by taxes, and the money that will go to the provinces is first taken from the provinces. It is simply a distribution. It is just as well to be plain and not mince matters in regard ta this measure. The Opposition are really under the impression

that the object of this Bill is to make a pawn for political purposes. That is one of the chief objects of the Bill.
Oh, oh.
There is no use in mincing matters.
That is a farfetched idea.

The Government say that the intention is to expend the money in the provinces according to population, and to expend the portion allowed to each province each year. But they refuse to put that provision in the Bill and they give no reason why they refuse. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) put a straight question to the right hon. the leader of the Government when he asked him in what way the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition would prevent the Government from carrying out what they allege they intend to carry out under this Bill. The Prime Minister did not answer him. Apparently he could not answer him. The only answer he gave was that the amendment was not necessary. There seems to be some reason why the Government refuse to accept any amendment to this Bill with the object of assisting them in carrying out the views which they say they intend to carry out Is the Opposition unreasonable in taking the view that there is a sinister object?

They are in wrong, that
is all.

This Bill had not been
brought down to Parliament last year, it had only been mentioned, when the election in South Renfrew took place and two ministers of the Crown went into that constituency-
Five.

The hon. member for
that riding says that five ministers went into his constituency and tried to influence the electors by telling them of the enormous sums of money that would be spent in that county under this proposal if they voted right. It was only this afternoon that I heard the Minister of Finance inform the hon. member for Halifax that the supplementary estimates were not yet completed, that they were still under consideration; and yet these supplementary estimates were published three months ago in the county of Antigonish to influence a by-eleotion. Is it unreasonable to suppose that a Government which acted in that way in these two instances would not make use of the money voted in this Bill for the purpose of influencing elections ? I do not think that anybody will say that the Opposition are not amply Mr HUGHES (Kings, P.E.I.)
justified in taking that view of the matter, having regard to all the circumstances.
Further than that, the tendency of legislation by this Government appears to be to encroach as much as possible upon the rights and privileges of the provinces, and to pass over to the Imperial Parliament, or to some Imperial body, the rights and privileges of this Parliament. The tendency of such legislation is dangerous. Further, the present Government in their legislation appear t-o wish to take away all the power they can from Parliament, to get Parliament to vote large sums of money without particularizing how it is to be expended. The tendency of such legislation is dangerous. For these reasons the Opposition are amply justified in opposing this Bill. We fear the uses that will be made of the money. Why, it was only a few moments ago that the hen. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) said that if the government of any province refused to accept the money under the conditions which this Government would impose, he presumed that the people of that province would take care of that government. Is it not a fair inference to draw from that statement that the conditions that this Government would impose, upon a provincial government in political sympathy with them, would be easily arranged?
Is that what the late Government did ?

But it might be very
hard and very difficult for a provincial government not in political sympathy with this Government to accept the conditions offered, and the object would be to make that government unpopular with the people of that province. That is what the hon. member for Digby intimated a few moments ago. Look at the measure in what way you will; there must certainly be something behind it when the Government absolutely refuse to accept any amendment whatever, the object of the amendment being to carry out the provision which the Government say they wish to carry out in connection with the Bill. They will retain the power in their own hands to make whatever changes they wish afterwards. We are justified in opposing it in every way we can. It may be worked as the most iniquitous measure that ever passed the Parliament of Canada and we have no assurance that it will not be so worked. Therefore, I repeat, we are justified in opposing it, I intend to record my vote against it, and these are some of the reasons I give for so doing to the people who sent me here.

Mr. Speaker, I just rise to give an instance of what my hon. friend from Kings, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes), has said, I went down to

my riding at the week end, and I was mot much surprised when I saw a man there, a Conservative and a friend of this Ministry, getting a petition signed by farmers in my riding. He was asking the farmers to sign the petition and for what reason? He would say to a farmer: You need not bother yourself about borrowing money under the law of the province of Quebec because you will have to pay interest on it. We have a Bill now before Parliament and, if it is not killed by the Senate, you will have all the money you want to improve your own roads and highways and it will cost you nothing. That shows you the spirit in which this Bill is regarded in some quarters. I rose only to give the House an instance of what my hon. friend from Kina's has stated. This Bill is nothing but a football to be played with when elections come on.

absolutely the amendment proposed by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). I am surprised at the minister refusing to accept the amendment to clause 3. He stated both last year and this that it was his intention to grant aid in the form of a subsidy according to population. Why he refuses to include that in the Bill is something I cannot comprehend. Some of our hon. friends are worrying because the Senate threw this Bill out last year, but I would just like to say that I endorse the Senate's action.
I am quite prepared to discuss it anywhere in the country and I have no apology to make. I think the Senate was absolutely right in trying to force the minister to put into the Bill the protestations he has made in this House as to what he intends to do. My hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson) said the subsidies were fixed by the British North America Act, and I will not answer that further than to say there have been a great many subsidies granted by the Dominion to the provinces since the enactment of the British North America Act. This subsidy should be given exactly in the same way as the other - subsidies. I pointed out in committee that clause 6 in my judgment was absolutely unnecessary because clauses 4 and 5 covered the question. I have no objection at all to the granting of subsidies in aid of good roads but I would have objection to the granting of subsidies towards the building of a trunk line at the present time. The probabilities are that if the money is left with the province the province will know how to expend it, and it will be expended on roads that are leading directly to the farmers' market. I repeat that I thoroughly and absolutely endorse all that has been said by the member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) and said much better than I can say it.

Is the hon. member (Mr. Nesbitt) perfectly satisfied, if the provincial government should get this grant, that it should expend it in the northern parts of Ontario and not in the older parts of the province.

I would be perfectly satisfied to abide by the decision of the Ontario Government as to where they thought it wise to expend that money. I would be very pleased to see them expend some of it in my county but I would not object if they would not.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite towards this Bill seems to have varied very much since it came up for second reading. At that time the right hon. leader of the Opposition used this language:
Let me assure my hon. friend that ve do not approach this measure in any factious
Mr. NESBITT.
spirit; we are willing to give the measure our support.
And then he went on to move an amendment which embodied a certain principle that he thought ought to be applied to the Bill. We now learn from several hon. gentlemen opposite that they are absolutely opposed to the Bill and that they intend to vote against it, and we are perfectly willing that they should do so if they desire. A great many bugbears have been conjured up with regard to this measure. It is said the money is to be utilized for some improper purpose; that these roads are local works within the meaning of the British North America Act, and that the Federal Government should have nothing directly to do with them at all. As a matter of fact highways in the province are not more local works than a great many subjects for which Parliament votes estimates every session. There is just as good warrant for the construction of a road by the Federal Government as there is for the construction of certain docks and roads approaching docks, and for the construction of cer-, tain bridges for which money has been voted over and over again by this Parliament. In the early history of Confederation works of that kind were not undertaken to any great extent by the Federal Government, but the practice began to creep in ten ..r fifteen years after Confederation, and since then it has grown until the present Federal Government are constructing a great many works that perhaps might be more particularly classified among the local works mentioned in section ninety-two of the British North America Act.
My hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), was very much disturbed about a road from Quebec to Windsor, and he imagined the Government were introducing this Bill for the purpose of constructing such a road. According to my conception of the British North America Act it would not be necessary at all for the Government of Canada to hand over money to the governments of the provinces for the purpose of constructing a road of that character.

Not that kind of a
road; that would be an interprovincial road.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend cannot
be serious in his suggestion that the object of a Bill which proposes to hand money over to the provinces is to 'carry out the construction of such a road.
It does not propose to hand the money over to the provinces; that is my objection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend has not
properly comprehended the Bill. The object is to hand the money over to the pro-

vinces for a particular purpose and to see that that purpose is carried out. The provision of a sum of money under these conditions is absolutely different-one would think any hon. gentleman would understand it without the necessity of such an explanation-is absolutely different from a permanent subsidy which is granted to the provinces with full right to appropriate that subsidy for any purpose whatever. Such general subsidies were granted in the first place by the British North America Act and afterwards by various arrangements which have ensued since Confederation, and they are of an entirely different character from this, because in every instance, so far as I can remember at the moment, such subsidies were moneys handed over to the provinces for their absolute disposition. This is not a subsidy of that kind; this is a subsidy handed over to the province, for the purpose of constructing works which, so far as most of these enterprises are concerned, are works of a local and private nature, and the object is that this subsidy shall be devoted to that particular purpose and no other. That being the object and purpose of the Bill it is manifestly desirable, and further than that it is manifestly necessary that there should be some safeguards in this statute, so that the Government of Canada, responsible to this Parliament, shall see to it that that money is devoted to that particular purpose and to no other. Further than that, it is the duty of this Parliament to see that this money shall be devoted to highways of such a character that they will be of permanent advantage to the people in every province. It is in connection with such a proposal, that all this discussion-a great part of which seems to me to be of rather a trivial character-has been expended on this Bill both last session and this. If the Government had any such idea as seems to be in the minds of hon. gentlemen on the other side, some sinister purpose in connection with this Bill, they would not have gone about it in this way. Hon. gentlemen opposite dwell too much on their own record when they make suggestions of that kind. The object of this Bill is simply to enable the various provinces of Canada to have placed at their disposal for a certain definite and particular purpose, namely, the improvement of the highways of this country, certain sums of money which will be allocated to them in accordance with their respective populations, and it is not only the right but it is the absolute duty of the Government of Canada who are responsible to this Parliament, to bring down that measure with necessary safeguards to ensure that that money shall be applied to that particular purpose and no other, and that it shall be expended in such 2804
a way as to result in permanent benefit and advantage. And, these hon. gentlemen opposite are spending hours and days in opposing that. I venture to think, notwithstanding what has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite, that they are reckoning without their host when they set up opposition, as they did last session and as they have done this session, to a proposal for the permanent improvement of the highways of Canada, They have mistaken the attitude and the feeling of Canada in that regard when they suggest to us that some of the provinces are opposed to this measure. I am quite conscious of the fact that the province of Saskatchewan some time ago and latterly the province of Nova Scotia have made a certain suggestion for a delay which would prevent this money from being voted at this session, and from being utilized by the various provinces of Canada during the present fiscal year. I do not think that even the people of these two provinces would support the governments of these provinces in their proposals. It was suggested by one. of these provinces that the governments of two other provinces were of the same opinion. I made an inquiry at once by telegraph and found that that statement was absolutely unfounded.
So far as the autonomy of the provinces is concerned, so far as their rights are concerned, the most absolute safeguards are provided by this Bill. Even in respect of section 6, how can any reasonable or sane man in this House say that the autonomy of any province is trenched upon in the slightest degree when it is absolutely impossible for this IGovernment or the Minister of Railways and Canals to lift one finger under that section without the authority	of the provincial	legislature
and without the consent of the provincial government? It is absolutely useless for any hon. member to make the pretense that there is any violation of provincial rights or powers with that absolute and distinct safeguard staring him in the face in the words of section 6 of the Bill. As hon. gentlemen have seen fit to take the attitude that they have taken with regard to this Bill, to obstruct it from the very first day on which it was presented to this House for second reading, all I have to say is that we are perfectly willing to accept their challenge, to place our attitude with regard to this measure in contrast with theirs before the people of this country and to left the people judge the policies and attitudes of the two parties with regard to this Bill when the propeT time shall come.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (South Renfrew) ; Mr. Speaker, if my right hon. friend would put the meaning of his words in the Bill, there would not be much objection.

The trouble -all through this session is that in half the measures "which the Government has proposed, they insist on saying one thing themselves and having their Bills say something else. That is what we object to. If the Minister of Railways would put his attitude so far as his words are concerned, into this statute, he would wipe away one objection of the hon. member for South Wellington. He absolutely refuses to do that.
I refuse to allow even the Prime Minister to tell the people of Canada that, because I, being a victim of corrupt practices on account of this Bill made a few remarks on it, I was obstructing this measure. I want to make myself clear on that point. This Bill had scarcely been presented to Parliament last year When men went from the city of Ottawa to the riding of South Renfrew and scattered over that riding promising men $100 to $500 under the measure before Parliament if they would turn out and attempt to defeat me in that riding.

Where is the proof
of that ?

I have met the men
who have been promised it. I do not need to give their names. It only shows what ministers of the Crown did in promising grants to that riding. _ Hon. gentlemen opposite, of course, did not succeed, but they made the attempt just the same. So far as I am concerned, I have the personal experience of knowing that under the terms of this Bill corrupt promises were, made to the electors of the constituency in South Renfrew in a futile effort to defeat me.
The Prime Minister should _ not make any charge of obstruction. This Bill has not been obstructed. Every time we have moved an amendment in this House during this session, we are charged with obstruction, or with doing something wrong. The Government has gone so far as to move a resolution to prevent even the leader of the Opposition from moving an amendment. That spirit runs all through their legislation. If the Prime Minister had been the attempted victim of corrupt promises in the same way as I was, I am sure he would not have sat silent without attempting to dehorn this Bill in such a manner that it could not be used in that way again. I decline to be told even by the Prime Minister that I am opposed to a grant of money for the building of good roads in the provinces. I am in favour of such a grant. Years before I was in this House I made such a proposal to the Government then in power. Although I was not a member of this House, I was a member of the Ontario legislature. I admit that it did not meet with favour, as they took the ground that the work belonged to the provinces.
Mr GRAHAM.
Let me call attention to what happened here the other day. A deputation waited on the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers). Their object was to get bridges constructed to connect the Island of Montreal with the mainland. They reported that they had been cordially received. They were told that if they could get the Senate to let the Highways Bill go through, without amendment, they would, have no difficulty in getting their money out of this appropriation.
I was present at the deputation. The bridge in question was an interprovincial bridge across the Ottawa river between the two provinces.

I know where the bridges are wanted. I travel over the territory as	many	times	in a	month	asmy hon.	friend	does	in a	year.	Anattempt is being made to have the island of Montreal connected with the mainland on the river road. At the present time automobiles or carriages cannot drive from the city of Montreal west; they have to cross by a rather old-fashioned ferry. I want to point out to	the Minister	ofRailways that if this Bill went through, he would not say that out of the grant given to Quebec according to population it	could	allow	these	bridges	to
be built. The grant would have to be enormous in proportion to the grants given to the other provinces. I am in favour of tnis Government giving a grant to assist in the construction of bridges at these two points, because they are badly needed, but they should not interfere with the Highways Bill, as they are very large works and would not properly come under this Bill.

speechtext: What are the two points?

The two branches of the Ottawa river at Vaudreuii and St. Annes. They connect the island of Montreal with the mainland. A promise w.as held out in order to get this Bill through. I submit to the Minister of Railways that the Minister of Public Works has no right to enter his preserves and to distribute the money of his department.

I will take care of
that.
I do not doubt that, but I want to point out some of the uses to which this Bill is being put already.

What election was
that for ?

You cannot tell; it is
meant for general results; it is a shot from a scattering musket with the hope that it will hit somewhere. What I object to principally in this Bill is section 6. I am going to point out to my hon. friend one

of the objections I have to it. The others have been pointed' out already. Under this section my hon. friend could select six counties in which he would spend say $20,000 each. If the governments of the provinces did not consent to that, my hon. friend could say: We will give you none at all of that $120,000. Now, that is hardly the intention of Parliament, or even of hon. gentlemen behind the minister, in passing this legislation.
Another point is this: This is along the line of one or two other measures in which the Government propose under certain conditions to take into their hands the expenditure of money without giving this House one iota of information as to how they are going to spend it.
That is what you advocated in Ontario.

The hon. gentleman is
harking back to something of years ago, and that is the answer of this Government in everything. Now, I want to make it clear that the case is as I stated. This is taking away the rights of the members of this Parliament to express their opinions on the Supply Bill. Suppose that $100,000 is voted for Ontario-it would be more than that, of course-and the province did not expend the money, or left a portion unspent, the minister and the province of Ontario might come to an agreement as to the expenditure of, say, $50,000, and the Minister of Railways could spend it wherever he likes in Ontario and this Parliament would not have a word to say about it and would not know where it was going to be spent. I submit to the Prime Minister that that is hardly fair to-[DOT]
They would not know if the province spent it.
But the provincial government would be responsible to the people of the province.

We are responsible
here.
But before the provincial government spent the money they would submit their estimates and explanations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I desire to follow the argument of my hon. friend* and would like to ask him a question. Suppose this money were handed over without restriction to the province, could not the provincial government do exactly the same thing as he complains of?
I should look to the legislature to look after that.
Why not look to this Parliament?

M>
right hon. friend goes further than I do. I do not blame the Government in appropriating this money, ear-marking it to be spent for roads, those roads to be built to a certain standard; I think the Government ought to keep control to that extent. But I take the other ease where the minister himself, under this Act, could spend up to $100,000 under arrangement with any legislature, and the members of this House would not have a word to say about where the money should be expended.

But under your plan
if Ontario spent $1,000,000 this House would not know where it was spent.
But the provincial minister pays out $1,000,000 for certain expenditure under certain conditions as provided in a statute which governs the expenditure of the money.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Does the provincial
statute define the locality in which the money is to be spent?

The provincial statute defines it in this way-they apply it under a statute fixing certain conditions under which the .money shall be given to the locality, just as the school grant is given to the locality according to the attendance of pupils and the qualifications of the teacher. I believe it would be better for the minister himself, and I know it would be better for this House, if in any work he is undertaking under the conditions of this clause he would agree that before work was undertaken it should be submitted to members of this House and let them pass upon it.
